articles.title: Pilandok won’t directly affect PH but habagat to prevail
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Depression Pilandok will not directly affect the country, while the southwest monsoon, or habagat, will continue to prevail over Luzon and the western part of Visayas…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Depression Pilandok will not directly affect the country, while the southwest monsoon, or habagat, will continue to prevail over Luzon and the western part of Visayas on Tuesday, according to the state weather bureau.

In the 5 a.m. weather forecast of the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration, weather specialist Veronica Torres said that Pilandok was last estimated 1,050 kilometers east of Extreme Northern Luzon. It maintained its strength as it was carrying a maximum wind speed of 55 kilometers per hour (kph) and gustiness of 70 kph.
“Walang direktang epekto sa ating bansa at napakababa naman ng tyansang maglandfall sa anumang parte ng bansa,” Torres said.
(This does not have a direct effect over the country and it has a low chance of making landfall in any part of the country.)

Torres also said that Pilandok will move east-northeastward and then northeastward in the next 24 hours. It may also traverse northwestward and exit the Philippine area of responsibility by Wednesday evening or Thursday morning.
It is forecast to intensify into a tropical storm in the next 12 hours.

Meanwhile, Torres noted that the habagat will bring heavy rains in the western portion of Luzon. She added that Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Batanes, Abra, Benguet, Zambales, and Bataan will experience 50 to 100 millimeters of rainfall on Tuesday due to habagat.
Weather disturbances outside the country
Torres also shared that there are currently three weather disturbances being monitored outside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR.

Tropical Storm Saudel, formerly locally named Obet, was last located 965 kilometers west of Extreme Northern Luzon as of 3 a.m. Torres said that because of its east-southeast movement, its chance of re-entering the PAR is not ruled out.
A tropical depression seen 645 kilometers west-northwest of Itbayat, Batanes is not forecast to enter the PAR.

Lastly, a low pressure area 3,000 kilometers east of Southern Luzon has a medium chance of developing into a tropical depression in the next 24 hours. Its possibility of entering the PAR is not ruled out. /jpv

articles.title: Colonel Raymund Lachica: The ‘missing link,’ and the trial’s wildcard
articles.summary: Can the prosecution navigate the unpredictability of Lachica's testimony? Will the defense risk giving the opposing camp a chance to cross-examine him?

items: Colonel Raymund Lachica, a key figure in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, is accused of mismanaging confidential funds, but his potential testimony remains uncertain as neither the prosecution nor defense has requested his appearance.
Lachica's background includes a long military career and direct involvement with the funds in question, raising concerns about the implications of his testimony for both sides in the trial.

The prosecution is hesitant to call Lachica as a witness due to the unpredictability of his testimony, while the defense is also weighing the risks of bringing him forward, leaving the court's potential involvement as a possibility.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Among the most frequently mentioned names in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte is the military man who has yet to take the witness stand — and it is up in the air whether he will actually have his day in this televised court proceeding.

Colonel Raymund Lachica, former security officer of the Vice President, is accused of unlawfully disbursing the confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President. The prosecution’s previous hostile witnesses — former OVP special disbursing officer (SDO) Gina Acosta and assistant chief of staff Lemuel Ortonio — confirmed that the secret funds worth half a billion pesos across four quarters in 2022 and 2023 were handed over to Lachica.

Senator-judges have expressed interest in hearing Lachica’s side of the story, with Senator Erwin Tulfo describing Lachica as the “missing link” in the story of Duterte’s alleged misuse of public funds.
Neither the prosecution nor the defense, however, has committed to making a request for the issuance of a court subpoena against him.
Calling him to testify carries great risks for the opposing counsels, despite the potential of his testimony bolstering their cases before the court.

blocks.caption: Sara Duterte trial: Will Raymund Lachica ever take the witness stand?

blocks.text: The 55-year-old Lachica hails from La Union, graduated from the Philippine Military Academy as part of the “Maalab” Class of 1993, and has built a decades-long career with the Philippine Army, holding various posts.

Despite his roots in the north, he’s been familiar with southern Philippines. His LinkedIn profile says he had been “company commander from 1996 to 1999 and also a field station commander of an intelligence unit operating in the provinces of Davao del Norte, Compostela Valley, and Davao Oriental in Mindanao.” He was also chief of operations for the Western and Eastern Mindanao Commands, the latter covering the Davao region, the bailiwick of the Dutertes. His family currently resides in Tagum City.

He became the commander of the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSPG) in July 2022, and held the post until October 2025, when the Armed Forces of the Philippines reassigned Lachica back to the Army after he was linked to the confidential fund scandal. While the AFP said it later subjected him to an investigation, it ended the probe and passed the responsibility to the Ombudsman.

Lachica’s role in the fiasco is crucial because he is alleged to have directly handled the funds turned over to him by Acosta, and exclusively liaised with supposed informants who were paid in cold cash on the ground.
Lachica provided acknowledgment receipts that became the basis of the OVP’s submissions to the Commission on Audit (COA), which later slapped notices of disallowance against the agency.

Even though Acosta was the SDO and Ortonio oversaw the financial services of the OVP, Lachica did not report to them about the confidential activities of the agency, which implies that the only other person who knew how the money was spent was Duterte herself.

blocks.caption: Colonel Raymund Lachica: The ‘missing link,’ and the trial’s wildcard

blocks.text: Lachica’s testimony could offer a fresh perspective on the longstanding allegations of confidential fund misuse by the Vice President. Such accusations have been hurled against her as early as 2023, but despite piling evidence, she remains the most trusted official in government.
But the prosecution team appears to stick to a talking point: downplay the importance of Lachica in building its case against the Vice President.

“I am more inclined not to present Lachica and (Colonel Dennis) Nolasco,” lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro said. “But this is just my personal position. As a matter of practice, we always decide as a team.”
Here’s the problem for the prosecution: Lachica is a wildcard whose unpredictable testimony could be a make-or-break move for Luistro’s team.

Unlike Acosta and Ortonio who already faced the House good government inquiry in 2024 and made on-record statements about the scandal, Lachica has not. Should the prosecution present Lachica as a hostile witness, it cannot know in advance what he will say before the court.
He could simply not tell the truth, and should he do that, there will be no prior testimony that the prosecution can compare to.

“He’s a military man, and these are wily characters. They are used to lying when necessary…. I think this kind of character can lie by concealment more efficiently and competently than anyone else. If I were in the prosecution, I will not call him to the witness stand,” constitutional lawyer Lulu Reyes told Rappler.

blocks.caption: Colonel Raymund Lachica: The ‘missing link,’ and the trial’s wildcard

blocks.text: He could also say the truth, but the prosecution has to be prepared to counter whatever damaging information that Lachica would provide outside the scope of its questions.

The prosecution asserts that the evidence it has presented so far is sufficient to establish that Duterte abused her powers and defied the joint circular that governs confidential spending when she allowed the handover of the important secret funds to a person other than her SDO.
Worse, Lachica is not covered by a fidelity bond, and is not even from the OVP, but from the AFP.

“I think they’re building a case on misuse and abuse of funds. So far, they have been succeeding in building that case, that story. I think they are building a case towards making it unavoidable for the defense to be the one to call Lachica. They want the defense to call Lachica,” constitutional lawyer John Molo told Rappler.
So if the prosecution won’t call him, maybe the defense will?
Duterte’s legal counsel Michael Poa said it’s not yet in their plans, as they will have to evaluate whether Lachica will be integral to the Vice President’s defense.

By letting the defense take the lead in calling Lachica to the witness stand, the prosecution gets to avoid the tradeoffs that come with examining a hostile witness, such as giving the defense a free preview of its theory, and a chance to rehabilitate the witness through its own follow-up questions.

“(The prosecution can be like) ‘Ask the defense, because our job is to prove the misuse of funds. Once that is established, the burden of evidence shifts. The senators will be asking, maybe Lachica should be called to testify,” Molo said.

blocks.caption: Colonel Raymund Lachica: The ‘missing link,’ and the trial’s wildcard

blocks.text: Lachica was listed as a potential witness by the prosecution in its pre-trial brief, while the defense didn’t. But should the defense team change its mind, there’s nothing stopping them from requesting the court for a subpoena against Lachica.
If that happens, the move comes with the risk of giving the prosecution a chance to pounce on the credibility of Lachica’s claims.

“If the defense calls him to the witness stand, that will subject him to cross-examination by the prosecution. If by that time, the prosecution has additional information regarding the actual usage of the P500 million, he will not be able to deny or refute anymore,” Reyes said.

Lachica has expressed willingness to take part in the trial and set the record straight. If neither the prosecution nor defense avails of the opportunity, the court has the residual power to call him only after both camps have presented their respective evidence. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Q&A: Canadian man held in ICE detention centres for 9 months shares challenges while detained
articles.summary: An Edmonton-born man who spent months in ICE detention is back in Canada, where he is now sharing his story about the conditions and hurdles he faced while detained. Curtis Wright, 40, who spent most…

image.caption: Curtis Wright, centre, his fiancée Kayla Thomsen and their daughter are pictured in this undated handout photo. Wright was recently returned back to Canada from the U.S. on a removal order after being detained by ICE for the past nine months. (Kayla Thomsen/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: An Edmonton-born man who spent months in ICE detention is back in Canada, where he is now sharing his story about the conditions and hurdles he faced while detained.

Curtis Wright, 40, who spent most of his life living in the United States, was held by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas for nine months after returning from a business trip to Mexico in November.
Wright said the reason he was detained stems from a misdemeanor drug possession charge from when he was 17 years old.
Wright said he was motivated to fight to remain in the U.S to try to be with his two young sons from a previous marriage, aged 8 and 11, who are in Texas.
Wright said he was returned to Canada in mid-August, and is temporarily staying at his parents’ house in Kelowna, B.C., with his fiancée, Kayla Thomsen, and their two-year-old daughter.
In an interview with Edmonton AM on Monday, Wright detailed the challenges he faced while struggling to remain south of the border.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
LISTEN | Curtis Wright ends up back in Canada after months in ICE detention:
Edmonton AM10:57Edmonton born Curtis Wright is back in Canada after nine months in ICE detention centres in the U.S.
What happened when you returned to Texas after a work trip to Mexico?
When I was going through Immigration and Customs, they asked me to go into secondary screening, which isn't uncommon. I've been through that before, but this began pretty differently.
He right away asked me, “Were you charged with misdemeanor possession back in 2004?”
I said “Yes, I was.”
He said, “OK, make a text to one of your family members. Let them know that this is going to be a while because we're going to have to investigate this further.”
Once I did that, they brought me into a back interview room where I was interrogated almost as if I were on trial, like I had done something wrong at that moment.

Then once the interview was over, he said, “As of this moment, you're now being detained. You'll be taken to a federal facility, and you won't have a court date until Dec. 3rd.” And this was on Nov. 6.

From that point, they moved me to a separate room and then from there they shackled me, put the waist chains around me, handcuffed me to my waist, put on ankle shackles, as if I was some kind of murder convict, and had me wait in a cell then took me to the facility.

items: 12 international students at Calgary protest referred to CBSA office after status check
On America's northern border, the threats are not unidirectional

blocks.text: Has anything like this ever happened to you previous to this encounter?

Never. I've gone in and out of the U.S. probably over 100 times since this has happened. I came to Kelowna to visit my parents at their home just this last summer just a few months before this detainment.
I was under the impression that they were focusing on the worst of the worst, like gang members, and people of that nature. I didn't realize that they were going to be detaining me.

items: Canadian man stuck in ICE detention centre for 4 months, awaiting deportation hearing

blocks.text: What options did they give you about what could happen next?
Really nothing. The guy informed me that because I was being federally detained there's no bond available to me because they marked me as a visiting alien reentering the country.
I was told later that if ICE had grabbed me in the country, I would have been able to get a bond potentially so I could fight my case outside.
But they purposely marked me as a visiting alien so that I couldn't get a bond. And then he said, “You're just going to have to go through the court case.” So that's essentially what I did.
Then that took this whole nine-month process to go through that court case?
They keep pushing your court case back because the whole idea behind it is they want you to give up. They don't want you to fight your case.

They put you in these horrible facilities and treat you very, very poorly, and they continue to push your court cases back. So you think you're going to court and then they say, “No, actually it's going to be in another three weeks. Oh wait, no, it's going to be in another two weeks.” Because they want you to give up and just go home.

items: Canadian who was held in ICE facility for months back in detention despite judge's ruling rights were violated

blocks.text: How many times did that happen to you where they pushed it?
For my first court date, it happened four times. I was originally scheduled to have it on Dec. 3 but didn't end up having it until Jan. 16.
After about five months, I finally went through the court case process and lost.

You’re supposed to get three dates and your third date is your trial date where a judge renders a decision. But I didn’t even get the opportunity to fight my case. On my second court date, they just said “Order of removal.”

Then I appealed after that and we tried to get a federal release through a writ of habeas corpus. The whole idea behind that was to get out so I could fight outside, and then we'd continue to do continuances and continuances and continuances waiting for the next political regime or hopefully winning my appeal. But I was never given the opportunity to do that.

items: How the U.S. secures its northern border
Canada's immigration 180: Part 1

blocks.text: You were fighting to be released back into Texas. That's where you called home. I understand that's where some of your family is as well?
The main reason that I was fighting to stay in Texas is because I have two sons with a previous wife.
I knew if I went to Canada they wouldn't be able to come with me. At the time I had 50/50 possession, so I got them half the year.
I fought because I wanted to stay in my children's lives as much as I possibly could, so that's why I stayed for nine months until we exhausted every option.

We had Republican senators write in asking for my release. We had Democrat senators write in asking for my release. We had Texas state representatives, even one individual who was on the board of commissions for Texas State prisons and detention centres, he wrote to ICE, the federal courts, the immigration courts. They all did.

Then I fought my case and we tried federal release. We went to the media. I exhausted every option because, to me, it was important to leave with no regrets, knowing that I did everything I could to stay with my boys. And that one day when I have to tell them why Dad had to leave, I can tell them with honesty that, “Your father did everything he possibly could.” But it just didn't work out.

items: How Trump’s mass deportation plan became big business

blocks.text: Can you tell us about what you experienced over those nine months in those centres?

It's the hygiene side of it. There's dirt, mould and grime everywhere. Everything's run down. I mean, you're sharing a small bathroom and showers with 100 men. There are a hundred men in the dorms. The food is just abysmal.

But more than that, it’s the officers that are there in place to be security for you. They yell at you. They curse at you. They threaten you. Solitary confinement is always one of their biggest threats, or moving you to different dorms or taking away privileges.

The lights are on 24 hours a day. You're sleeping in a steel bunk bed with no pillow. You're asked to be counted in your bed five times a day, and it's almost like a psychological and emotional beatdown.

Because, as I mentioned before, they want to make things as uncomfortable as they possibly can for you because they want you to give up and just go back to your home country. You feel like you're less than human.

items: How ICE detention is forcing immigrants out of the U.S.

blocks.text: When did you finally decide to be deported to Canada?
I finally made that decision about eight months in, and then it took about another month to get out.

Because my lawyer had informed me that in the federal courts there's an ongoing case right now pertaining to permanent residence and due process, and that the judge that had my habeas corpus for a federal release was waiting on the ruling of that case, and it had already been ongoing for several months.

The lawyer said the case “could go on for two more weeks or it could go on for two more years. So, you could wait another year, year and a half, let’s say, and then the ruling goes against permanent residents. And then you can’t get release on that anyways.”

items: Canada's immigration 180: Part 2

blocks.text: At that point, I realized it was just the best thing for my family because even though I'm the one locked up in there, my whole family's going through it. I feel like we were all stuck in this terrible, terrible nightmare.
I thought it was important for the whole family that we just kind of move on and find a way to just move forward with our lives the best way we can and accept what is, and so that's what we're doing.
But again, I love Canada and there was no concern about coming back here. It was simply trying to stay there for my sons.
What are your next steps from here?

My career has been in oil and gas and so, being from Edmonton, it's kind of a perfect spot to pick that right back up. Thankfully, my company that I was working for before in Houston, is going to be opening up a Canadian division just for me to run and try to grow here in Canada.

I've had a lot of wonderful people in my corner, including my employer, and they're going to continue to stick by me and most of my family is in Edmonton — all my aunts, uncles, cousins, my brother and his wife and children are there.

articles.title: Hiker, 91, becomes oldest person to complete grueling Appalachian Trail
articles.summary:
Dale Sanders said he fell 71 times on the trail, but completed the journey as ‘people are motivated … by my efforts’

A 91-year-old hiker has reclaimed his record as the oldest person to…

blocks.text: A 91-year-old hiker has reclaimed his record as the oldest person to complete the more than 2,000-mile Appalachian Trail.

By his count, Dale Sanders, of Tennessee, fell 71 times during the feat, six of which he said were hard falls and one which required a brief hospitalization and another just 200 yards from the end. The 2,193-mile trail runs between Springer Mountain in Georgia and Mount Katahdin in Maine.

The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines a thru-hike as completing all of the trail’s sections in any order within a year, allowing for pauses. Sanders began his hike on 6 September 2025 in West Virginia and, allowing for some brief breaks, he completed his journey on Monday atop Maine’s highest peak, where he paused to pray at the sign marking the summit.
“I had to thank God, and I had to thank my support team and everybody that got me here,” Sanders, whose trail name is Grey Beard, told the Associated Press.

blocks.caption: Dale Sanders celebrates after completing a difficult section of Mt Katahdin in Baxter state park in Piscataquis county, Maine.  Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/AP

blocks.text: Sanders first set the Appalachian Trail record in 2017 when he was 82, only to be overtaken four years later by his 83-year-old friend MJ Eberhart, whose trail name is Nimblewill Nomad.

Within months, Sanders announced his comeback plan. But despite six months of training, he told the AP, he still was not in the best condition. “And even today, I feel that I should probably be in better shape than I am,” he said last month. “But I just have to always go back and say: ‘But I am 91, so I’m blazing new ground hiking long distances like this.’”

In June, Sanders was descending Killington Mountain in central Vermont when he fell forward in a boulder field, scraping his legs, arms and hands. “Thank God nothing got broken, but I was banged up,” he said. “I didn’t rub the blood off, I just kept hiking.”

Weeks later, his left arm went numb and he ended up at a hospital in Maine with what turned out to be a pinched nerve. But although he was soon cleared to resume hiking, he at that point considered giving up.
When he returned home to Tennessee in early August to be with his wife, whose mother had just died, she convinced him to press on with his mission.

Some of Sanders’ best days were in Pennsylvania, where he said he enjoyed well-maintained trails and treats delivered by “trail angels”. “When people are taking care of you and bringing you caramel frappes on the trail, the rocks don’t matter,” he said.

Also pushing him to keep going were his thousands of followers on social media. “I wanna get [my record] back, but right now, that’s secondary,” he told the AP. “Right now, what’s the most important thing – and it’s one of the things that surprised me – is that people are motivated and given encouragement by my efforts.”

blocks.caption: Sanders takes a brief power nap near Monson, Maine, on 28 July 2026. Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/AP

blocks.text: Sanders was born in Kentucky in 1935, two years before the Appalachian Trail was completed. Bullied as a child for his small size, he gained confidence in solo sports such as acrobatics and swimming. He later served in the navy and retired in 2002 after a long career in parks and recreation.
He holds numerous other age-related records, including becoming the oldest person to paddle the entire length of the Mississippi River in 2022, an 87-day trip he started on his 87th birthday.
Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: US supreme court allows Trump to keep building $400m White House ballroom
articles.summary:
Justices’ 5-4 ruling permits Trump administration appeal to block lower court order halting above-ground work

A divided US…

blocks.text: A divided US supreme court has permitted Donald Trump to continue building his controversial $400m White House ballroom despite legal challenges, raising the likelihood it will be completed.

In a 5-4 ruling, the justices permitted the Trump administration’s request to ⁠block a lower court order which had halted above-ground construction of the project while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeks to block it.
The US president, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people.
Monday’s decision from the supreme court comes after the court’s conservative chief justice, John Roberts, issued a temporary order that had enabled work to continue.
However, Roberts joined the court’s three liberal justices in dissenting from the majority’s decision and wrote that the construction was “likely unlawful”.

The court’s decision may allow Trump to bring to fruition a project that is at the center of his ambition to remake the US capital in his image. Since taking office, he hass ordered the National Mall’s reflecting pool covered in blue liner, proposed a $250m renovation to the Kennedy Center performing arts center that would see his name emblazoned on its side, and is pursuing plans to renovate a golf course and build a massive arch.

While some projects have hit legal roadblocks, such as when a judge ordered Trump’s name removed from the Kennedy Center, or descended into farce, like when the reflecting pool line began falling off, the supreme court’s decision today is a victory for the president.

Trump celebrated Monday’s ruling in a post on Truth Social, boasting that the White House complex would be “one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington DC”, with construction to be completed by the summer of 2028.

In an unsigned opinion, the five conservative justices said the National Trust for Historic Preservation in the United States lacked standing to bring a lawsuit against the project. The trust had centered its argument on the declaration of a board member, the architectural historian Alison Hoagland, who said the ballroom was an “aesthetic, cultural and historical” affront because of its design, and that she would suffer “injuries” when viewing it in Washington DC.
“The government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks standing to challenge the East Wing project,” the majority opinion read.

“This court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury.”

The justices also agreed that the government would suffer “irreparable harm” if construction is stopped, or only allowed to continue on a military installation set to be built underneath the ballroom while the above-ground portion remains unfinished.
The majority ultimately side stepped the question of whether the president’s decision to tear down a chunk of a building that rotates between presidential officeholders was actually legal.
“Today, we do not pass upon the legality of the government’s East Wing project,” they wrote.

The dissenting justices – Roberts, together with Democratic-appointed justices Elena Kagan, Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson – argued that the project is unlawful because Congress has not approved it.

In his opinion, Roberts wrote that the construction is a “likely infringement of the legislature’s power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue,” and says the majority’s ruling “is no victory for the separation of powers”.

“The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds – President’s Park – in the District of Columbia. Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the executive’s construction of it,” the chief writes.

He also disagreed that the potential injuries to Hoagland are insufficient for the historic trust to sue, saying she was “deeply committed to the preservation of such historic American buildings” through her work with the association.

“Hoagland’s injury suffices for standing,” Roberts wrote, likening the impact of the White House’s transformation on her to how “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys”.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 20: What to expect
articles.summary: The prosecution will call to the witness stand retired Colonel Manaros Boransing II to testify on Article I of the impeachment case, which accuses Vice President Sara Duterte of committing…

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 6:09am

A new witness is set to be presented by the House prosecution panel on Tuesday, September 1, in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, this time coming from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP).

The prosecution will call to the witness stand retired Colonel Manaros Boransing II to testify on Article I of the impeachment case, which accuses Duterte of committing impeachable offenses due to systematic misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds.

To recall, in October 2024, lawyer Michael Poa told the House good government and public accountability panel that he asked then-Department of Education (DepEd) undersecretary and retired Major General Nolasco Mempin to request certifications from military units to back up the department's spending of the P15 million in confidential funds for informants in 2023.
The Senate impeachment court has also issued a revised subpoena for Colonel Magtangol Panopio. His testimony will come after Boransing.

Boransing and Panopio were among the military officials who previously said that they issued military certifications, but maintained they were not aware that these were used to liquidate the DepEd's confidential funds.

On Friday, House prosecution panel adviser and former Surigao del Norte Representative Ace Barbers and House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V of La Union said that the military certifications issued by Boransing and Panopio to justify DepEd's confidential fund spending carry great weight because, aside from these being public funds, it is not the job of the military to liquidate these confidential fund disbursements of DepEd.

The prosecution team also said that Poa, then-undersecretary and spokesperson of the DepEd, has a lot to explain before the Senate impeachment court on how the P112.5 million in confidential funds of the DepEd was used during the tenure of Duterte as Education chief. —LDF/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo
articles.summary: Wildfires in Indonesia have destroyed part of the natural habitat of hundreds of orangutans, risking the survival of the species.

blocks.text: A weak orangutan was found laying on the ground in Ketapang, West Kalimantan on Borneo island.
Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze from wildfires across six provinces in Borneo and Sumatra islands.
The wildfires have destroyed part of the habitat of hundreds of orangutans and risking the survival of the species.
"The situation is quite critical", said Karmele Llano Sanchez, CEO of the wildlife foundation Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI).
Sanchez said the fires are "leaving [the orangutans] without any food or water".
The orangutan found will be moved to a rehabilitation centre to get more treatment and will be released back into the wild after recovery, according to YIARI.

articles.title: How intense rains in the Grand Canyon turned into a deadly disaster
articles.summary: Flash flooding in Arizona tourist destination was likely triggered by compounding climate factors, such as drought and warming in Pacific Ocean

blocks.text: A deadly flash flood in the Grand Canyon over the weekend was likely driven by a confluence of climate factors, including drought, wildfire scarring and warming temperatures in the Pacific Ocean that can supercharge storms.

At least two people have died and 15 remain missing or unaccounted for after a surge of water and debris swept through the immensely popular tourist destination on Saturday, fueled by torrents of rain that hit the national park’s Bright Angel Creek area.

Flash floods are not uncommon in the region, especially during the monsoon season from June to September, when strong rains pummel the arid landscapes and can quickly fill narrow rock formations. Visiting the Grand Canyon – a crown jewel of the US national park system – can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding, when clear days can give way quickly to thunderstorms and downpours.
The steep, rocky nature of the canyon itself funnels water rapidly, transforming downpours into a charging wall of water.

blocks.caption: This handout image released by the National Park Service shows a storm system moving across the North Rim of Grand Canyon national park on 29 August. Photograph: J Baird/National Park Service/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: But Saturday’s strong storm also hit part of the burn scar of the Dragon Bravo wildfire, a destructive and fast-moving blaze that swept across nearly 150,000 acres (60,700 hectares) and consumed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge in July 2025.
Runoff tends to flow more quickly in the aftermath of a fire, especially in hotter burns where slopes are left barren of vegetation.

While it’s still unclear how directly long-term damage to the landscape from that fire played a role in last weekend’s disaster, federal models indicated a rise in the risks of debris flows in Bright Angel Creek.

blocks.caption: Floods sweeping through Grand Canyon national park

blocks.text: Teams with the Department of Interior charged to assess post-fire threats to “life, property, and critical natural and cultural resources”, found runoff risks would be between two and eight times greater upstream of Phantom Creek. “Hikers on the trails within or downslope from the burned area will experience frequent stabilization issues, especially hazardous rockfall for at least the first year,” the team wrote in a report on conditions.

Park officials were reportedly concerned at the start of this summer that stronger storms could create dangerous conditions near the burned areas. Hikers that had to be evacuated by helicopter after the rushing waters swallowed bridges and other infrastructure told the Arizona Republic that the creek turned black as it filled with runoff.

blocks.caption: This handout image released by the Grand Canyon National Park Service shows remnants of stone bridge pylons along Bright Angel Creek following a flash flood. Photograph: J Thompson, handout/National Park Service/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Scientists have long warned that the climate crisis will create stronger extremes and destructive shifts between wet and dry conditions. As temperatures continue to climb, extreme events will not just increase – they are more likely to overlap, causing more calamity and testing the limits of the nation’s resilience and recovery.
So-called “compound extremes”, where a combination of contributing factors come together, are on the rise, according to researchers.

blocks.caption: The sudden, heavy rainstorm that fueled this catastrophic flood may have been been supercharged by the historic El Niño. Photograph: J Thompson, handout/National Park Service/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Along with the potential impact from a previous fire, a severe drought that continues to affect the Grand Canyon region – and the Colorado River basin that runs through it – could have contributed to the disaster. The deluge unleashed torrents of rain on hardened and sparsely vegetated steep terrain that is less able to absorb and contain abrupt increases in moisture.
The sudden and strong rainstorm that fueled this catastrophic flood may have been been supercharged by the historic El Niño that has sharply increased sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean.

blocks.caption: The Grand Canyon national park in northern Arizona on Sunday, a day after it was hit by heavy flooding. Photograph: Craig Sanderson via AP

blocks.text: The climate phenomenon has the ability to affect weather systems around the world. But in the south-west, the higher amount of water vapor in the atmosphere due to El Niño is wrung out in the form of rainfall, Park Williams, a hydroclimatologist at the University of California, Los Angeles, told the Associated Press.

El Niño is part of a natural cycle, but models show there is a strong likelihood this will become one of the strongest on record. It layers on top of spikes in temperature fueled by the climate crisis. Together, the possibility of severe and extreme weather is expected to dramatically increase.

blocks.caption: Bright Angel Canyon, the scene of flash floods, runs into the Colorado River in the Grand Canyon on Monday. Photograph: John Locher/AP

blocks.text: The link to human-caused climate change and the heavy Arizona rain is moderately strong, said Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the California Institute for Water Resources.

Swain and colleagues recently published a study in the journal Weather and Climate Extremes finding that during the summer, short-term intense downpours in the US west – akin to the one that hit the Grand Canyon – have become 10% stronger since 2000.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Poa faces questions on P112.5-M DepEd secret funds
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson could emerge as a pivotal witness when the Senate impeachment trial enters its ninth week on Tuesday, as prosecutors turn to the paper…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson could emerge as a pivotal witness when the Senate impeachment trial enters its ninth week on Tuesday, as prosecutors turn to the paper trail behind the alleged misuse of P112.5 million in confidential funds at the Department of Education (DepEd).

Michael Poa, now also one of Duterte’s defense lawyers, is expected to face questions about military certifications he helped obtain for DepEd, where Duterte served as secretary for two years until June 2024.

Poa will be called to the witness stand after retired Col. Manaros Boransing II and Col. Magtangol Panopio, who are expected to shed light on certifications cited by DepEd in responding to Commission on Audit (COA) findings.
House prosecution adviser Robert Ace Barbers said prosecutors would examine certifications used to justify fund releases, including those tied to youth summits organized by DepEd.
Why Poa matters
The House prosecution team views Poa, who also served as an undersecretary and chief of staff at DepEd, as crucial because he figured in the agency’s response to the audit findings.
During a 2024 House inquiry, DepEd Undersecretary Nolasco Mempin testified that Poa requested military certifications for the agency’s response to a COA audit observation memorandum.
Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V described Poa as a “central figure” in the impeachment case, saying the Senate proceedings could clarify his earlier statements.

“His statements to the good government [committee] when he was a resource person are still incomplete … Now we are in the impeachment court and I believe this is the proper forum to clarify the questions,” Ortega said in Filipino.
Poa said last week he was ready to testify and did not intend to invoke attorney-client privilege unless necessary. Ortega said prosecutors were prepared for whatever Poa might say or invoke.

“He is the mouth of the Vice President and you cannot speak, you cannot defend, you cannot honor your words if you don’t know … all the details and you don’t know the whole process. That’s how important he is to the trial,” Ortega said.
Poa’s testimony could help establish who sought the military certifications, why they were obtained and how they were used to support the release and liquidation of confidential funds.
Fajarda sidelined
The prosecution’s original witness for the DepEd transactions, special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda, will not testify Tuesday after suffering a stroke. His appearance has been reset to Sept. 7.
Fajarda was supposed to testify on his role in disbursing and liquidating P112.5 million in confidential funds from the first to third quarters of 2023. /cb

articles.title: Lacson: P3.7B ‘wasted’ in Taguig reclamation
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — At least P3.713 billion in public funds may have been wasted on flood control and multipurpose projects in reclamation areas of Laguna Lake in Taguig City, according to Sen.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — At least P3.713 billion in public funds may have been wasted on flood control and multipurpose projects in reclamation areas of Laguna Lake in Taguig City, according to Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson.

Also on Monday, Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano welcomed the scrutiny of land titles in his bailiwick, noting that his wife, Taguig Mayor Lani Cayetano, had long wanted these properties examined.

The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has ordered a halt to reclamation projects in Taguig, saying it would soon “determine a way forward” on this matter after consulting with “different stakeholders.”

Posting on X on Monday, Lacson said: “WASTED PUBLIC FUNDS DUE TO MISUSE: Based on official records and our investigation, the total cost of Identified completed, ongoing (and suspended) DPWH Flood Control and Multi-Purpose Projects along the ‘illegal’ Laguna Lakeshore Reclamation Areas in Taguig City has so far reached P3.713 billion.”

“These do not include other anomalous Slope Protection and Flood Mitigation projects along Taguig River involving double appropriations and ‘ghost’ projects using recycled photographs in different ‘completed’ projects, for billing purposes,” he added.

Lacson’s latest disclosure came following Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon’s announcement of cease-and-desist orders issued on the said projects, in line with a directive from the Office of the President through the Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA).
Lacson said earlier that an investigation by his team has found reclamation activities on Taguig City’s side of Laguna Lake covering at least 85 hectares of land.
He said their latest findings would be among the evidence to be sent to the Office of the Ombudsman’s fact-finding team “for proper disposition.”
Contractors
In his post on X, Lacson also cited official records as well as his office’s investigation identifying the top five contractors involved in projects covering P2.372 billion:
1) Dahl Construction: P858.22 million covering five solo projects worth P571.5 million and four joint ventures totaling P286.7 million;
2) JC Uyecio: P483.1 million covering four joint ventures;
3) ToughBuilt: P434.2 million covering three solo projects;
4) Topnotch: P329.9 million covering two joint ventures with Core Check and one with Beam Team; and
5) GR Fervidal: P266.6 million covering five solo multipurpose building projects
Lacson said all of the multipurpose building projects of GR Fervidal were suspended due to a “revision of plans” involving soil reinvestigation.
He said the DPWH issued the cease-and-desist orders “to prevent further waste of government funds on contractors carrying out unauthorized or illegal activities.”

Lacson also said earlier he was told by PRA officials that all unpermitted reclaimed areas in Taguig City, whether belonging to the local government or to private individuals, are subject to forfeiture in favor of the national government.

On Saturday, he disclosed that at least four parcels of illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City had been initially identified as covered by “fraudulently” issued land titles, while at least four other parcels have no plotted title lots in the digital file of the Land Registration Authority (LRA).
‘Digging further’
In a statement on Monday, Cayetano said the government stands to gain if allegations of illegally titled properties along Laguna Lake in Taguig are proven true.

“Yesterday, there was something in the newspaper saying that there is a 181,000-square-meter, or 18-hectare, property that was supposedly ‘illegally titled.’ On one hand, we are also hoping that’s true. Why? Because if it is indeed illegal, it would go to the government. Then we would have 18 hectares now for the government,” said Cayetano, referring to one of the parcels identified by Lacson.
In another post on X, Lacson reacted to that statement by Cayetano.

“Maybe so, except that those titles (38.83 hectares total, so far) are registered to private individuals. We have their names as well as the OCT (original certificate of title) and TCT (transfer certificate of title) numbers. We are digging further deep into it,” said Lacson.
“What if it wasn’t exposed?” he added. /cb

articles.title: 2027 budget vulnerable to politicking, watchdog warns
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The proposed P7.2-trillion national government budget for 2027 is vulnerable to political manipulation ahead of the 2028 elections, with budget watchdogs warning that billions…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The proposed P7.2-trillion national government budget for 2027 is vulnerable to political manipulation ahead of the 2028 elections, with budget watchdogs warning that billions of pesos in discretionary and localized projects could be used for patronage despite shrinking fiscal space.
Kenneth Abante, coconvener of the People’s Budget Coalition, said the national expenditure program was not “people-centered,” as the Marcos administration claims, but “more centered on politicians.”
“We are worried that the 2027 budget will be politicized for the coming elections,” Abante told the Inquirer in a text message.
He said about P735 billion in discretionary funds could be exposed to “waste, fraud, abuse and patronage.”

Among the programs flagged as susceptible to political meddling are the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s cash assistance, the Department of Labor and Employment’s program for displaced workers, and the Department of Health’s medical aid for indigent patients.

Also at risk are infrastructure programs such as farm-to-market roads, health facility improvements and flood control projects.“It is striking that hyper-local, patronage-driven projects are prioritized,” said public finance specialist Zy-Za Nadine Suzara.

The Department of Budget and Management submitted the record spending plan to Congress on Aug. 11, a 6-percent or P407-billion increase from this year. The administration has described it as focused on education, health, food and social protection.

But a Congressional Policy and Budget Research Department document shows substantial cuts in several agencies under these sectors. Education faces a P39.2-billion reduction; health, P33.6 billion; social welfare, P28.7 billion; agriculture, P13.5 billion; and labor, P9 billion.

“It’s hard to characterize the 2027 proposed budget as a people-centered budget when funds for human capital development, livelihood support, agricultural productivity and commuter-centered transport programs suffered deep cuts,” Suzara said.
P107.4B for flood control

The Department of Public Works and Highways gets P113.1 billion more and the Department of Transportation P160.3 billion more. Debt interest payments rise by P164.3 billion and the National Tax Allotment by P129.3 billion.
The budget also sets aside P107.4 billion for flood control, a major corruption flashpoint.
Suzara said debt servicing, local government shares and government operating costs consume about 84 percent of the budget, leaving only P1.15 trillion in “real funding space.”
Blockchain budgeting

Amid the concerns, Sen. Bam Aquino renewed his call for passage of the Citizen Access and Disclosure of Expenditures for National Accountability (Cadena) Act, or Senate Bill No. 1506, the blockchain the budget bill.
The Senate approved the measure in December 2025, but it remains pending in the House.

The bill would require agencies to upload contracts, project costs, bills of materials and procurement records to a public Digital Budget Platform, making records accessible, tamper-resistant, traceable and verifiable. Officials who fail to disclose required documents or submit fraudulent information could face penalties.

Aquino said Cadena had fallen to 41st from third among the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council’s (Ledac) priorities. Socioeconomic Planning Secretary Arsenio Balisacan said he would raise the issue with Ledac leadership.
“The best way to address corruption is to have full transparency,” Aquino said, arguing that putting budget records on blockchain could help prevent misuse of public funds.
He said the measure was especially urgent amid renewed scrutiny of flood control spending and alleged misuse of public funds. /cb

articles.title: Flood control projects fail Central Luzon folk
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, ZAMBALES, Philippines — Flood control measures in Central Luzon region, including an ongoing river dredging program for the past seven years and the construction of flood control…

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, ZAMBALES, Philippines — Flood control measures in Central Luzon region, including an ongoing river dredging program for the past seven years and the construction of flood control structures along major waterways, have proved ineffective in the past days against flooding caused by the enhanced southwest monsoon or “habagat.”
Thousands of families were again forced to evacuate as the death toll in the region from the effects of the monsoon rose to 31 as of Monday, with most of the fatalities from Zambales and Bulacan.
In Zambales, the dredging of Bucao River in Botolan and Sto. Tomas River in the San Felipe-San Narciso area has been among the flood mitigation efforts being conducted by the provincial government.

Department of Environment and Natural Resources Administrative Order No. 13 also identifies dredging along the Bucao, Maloma and Sto. Tomas rivers as a measure to restore heavily silted channels and help prevent flooding.
All these dredging activities, however, proved to be ineffective as floodwaters submerged communities in Botolan and further wrecked flood control structures already damaged by previous floods.
Damage estimate
The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has so far reported P569.27 million in damage to flood control projects in Zambales, with P1.28 billion needed for recovery and reconstruction.

The DPWH 1st District in Zambales accounted for P472.42 million in damage, including sections of Bucao River Dike 7 in Barangay San Juan, Botolan, where more than 3 kilometers of slope protection were reportedly destroyed.
The DPWH 2nd District, on the other hand, recorded another P96.85 million in damage, including revetments along the Tamayok and Matain rivers in Subic and the Sto. Tomas River in San Marcelino.

blocks.caption: DESTROYED A section of Bucao River Dike at Barangay San Juan in Botolan, Zambales, is among the flood control structures reported destroyed in the latest assessment of the Department of Public Works and Highways. —Photo courtesy of Botolan LGU

blocks.text: The Zambales Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office reported that 710 families, or 14,052 people, had so far been evacuated. Of these, 552 families or 10,242 people were in evacuation centers as of Aug. 30.
Botolan recorded the highest number of evacuees in shelters with 3,491 people, followed by Cabangan with 1,938.

Agricultural damage and losses, on the other hand, reached P37.55 million, according to the Office of the Provincial Agriculturist. Rice accounted for P21.58 million, affecting 1,069.42 hectares and 1,267 farmers.
A state of calamity was earlier declared in Zambales following widespread flooding and damage from successive days of heavy rains.
‘Ground zero’
In Bulacan, the so-called “ground zero” of the flood control controversy, at least 15 people have died and three others injured since Aug. 10 amid heavy rains and widespread flooding.
The province also remains under a state of calamity with all 23 towns and cities affected by floods as high as 1.8 meters (6 feet) in some areas.

Fed up with the situation, at least 34 people’s organizations staged an anticorruption rally in Bulacan on Monday, demanding an end to reclamation projects and calling for accountability among officials linked to the flood control scandal.
The groups, under the banner of Kilos Bulacan, also called for comprehensive environmental and flood control measures, compensation for flood victims and stronger action on climate change.
The protesters first gathered at Malolos City Hall Amphitheater and near MacArthur Highway before proceeding to the provincial capitol to hold a short program.
Kilos Bulacan leader Obet Rodrigo said many of Bulacan’s rivers remain swollen, while Leonides Laderas of Hagonoy said the Aug. 31 rally was only the first in a series of planned street protests.
Heavy traffic on NLEx

In Pampanga, motorists traveling on the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) on Sunday were stuck in traffic for hours because of floodwaters ranging from knee to waist-deep in the San Simon and Tulaoc areas.
“Five hours hardly moving, with nowhere to go and no way to get off the expressway,” Kalookan Bishop Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David said of his “miserable” experience in a Facebook post on Monday.
Ironically, the Tulaoc overpass bridge had been raised by 0.7 meter three years ago to help prevent flooding in the area. It was also the first time the San Simon Interchange ended up under water.

The flooded portions along NLEx resulted in a long line of vehicles stretching about 8 km on the northbound side and roughly 6 km on the southbound side, NLEx Corp. assistant vice president for traffic operations Robin Ignacio said in a television interview.

For David, the ordeal was particularly “frustrating” because flooding in San Simon was hardly a surprise while NLEx Corp., which had access to real time traffic information, knew which sections were flood-prone.
“We pay substantial toll fees precisely because we expect a toll expressway to provide a reasonably safe, properly maintained and efficiently managed facility,” he said.
Monthlong death toll
Successive tropical cyclones, combined with the enhanced habagat, have caused widespread flooding in many parts of the country since Aug. 1, leaving 33 dead.
The Office of Civil Defense said on Monday that it is verifying reports about 14 additional fatalities.

Eleven of the fatalities are still under verification, supposedly drowned—nine in San Marcelino, Zambales; and one each in Olongapo City and Capas town in Tarlac. The remaining three were killed in landslides—two in Zambales and the third in Porac, Pampanga. OCD Assistant Secretary Raffy Alejandro IV said that four other individuals were missing after the collapse of the Agana Bridge in Tarlac City. This was on top of the three previously reported.

The death toll of 33 was reported earlier in the day by OCD Director Vicente Gregorio Tomas in a press briefing. He said that 19 others had suffered injuries, while the monsoon has so far affected a total of 8.8 million people nationwide.—WITH REPORTS FROM JOHN ERIC MENDOZA, AND JUN MALIG

articles.title: Built for floods: VinFast VF 6 has an IP67-rated powertrain
articles.summary: Techies might be familiar with the IP67-rating. It is typically a badge of honor for phones and action cameras, denoting their rugged and weather-proof design. Few cars can boast of a similar rating,…

blocks.text: Drive
The only car with an IP67 rating
Techies might be familiar with the IP67-rating. It is typically a badge of honor for phones and action cameras, denoting their rugged and weather-proof design.

Few cars can boast of a similar rating, save maybe for VinFast. The VinFast VF 6 is one of the few vehicles with an IP67-rated powertrain. This engineering design makes the VF 6 a weather-ready crossover, designed to withstand different roads and severe monsoon conditions in the country.

An IP67-rated powertrain can withstand dust exposure and water submersion for up to 30 minutes. Addressing one concern among prospective EV buyers in the country. The VF 6 features the said battery pack with a 59.6 kWh capacity, indicating protection against dust ingress and temporary water immersion. This ensures that no dust can enter the critical components of the VF 6, keeping its internal hardware safe from tiny debris and sudden floods. Likewise, the rating adds another layer of protection for the vehicle’s battery system, giving drivers peace of mind that their crossover remains safe in heavy rains, splashes, and spills during rainy season driving.

This weather-ready engineering answers the severe unpredictability of the Philippines’ rainy season. According to PAGASA, the enhanced Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) this August brought rainfall exceeding 200% of normal monthly averages. The MMDA also recorded 138 millimeters of rains in just two hours on August 17 – rates that mirrored 2009’s Tropical Storm Ondoy – triggering immediate flash floods across major thoroughfares. These downpours compound Metro Manila’s chronic gridlock, where the 2025 TomTom Traffic Index recorded a 57% congestion level and average speeds of just 18.9 km/h.

Rainy season gridlocks can turn a usual one-hour drive into a four-hour standstill – a scenario where traditional gas vehicles continue consuming fuel while idling. The VinFast VF 6, meanwhile, uses an electric powertrain that does not require the engine to idle while stationary. With over 450-km of NEDC-rated range and DC fast charging from 10% to 70% in 35 minutes, the VF 6 also offers the range and charging flexibility needed to fit into demanding daily routines.
Engineered for wet-weather conditions

Eager to address one of the major hesitations in EV adoption in the country, the VinFast VF 6 leverages its 170 mm ground clearance to navigate through urban flash floods. Its 1,650 kg curb weight provides the grounded physical footprint needed to maintain traction on pooled water. To keep the vehicle planted on slick surfaces, the Electronic Stability Program and Traction Control work alongside Electronic Brakeforce Distribution to help maintain stability and braking control when road conditions become unpredictable. Furthermore, Heated Side Mirrors and Defoggers help maintain clear sightlines when heavy rain and moisture compromise the driver’s view.

To reduce the mental strain of navigating busy, rain-soaked roads where torrential downpours blur lane markings and reduce visibility, the VinFast VF 6 is equipped with key Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) features. These include Adaptive Cruise Control, that maintains a safe distance from the vehicle ahead, helping reduce the need for constant speed adjustments in slower-moving traffic. Meanwhile, the 360-degree camera makes it easier to navigate tight streets and parking spaces by giving drivers a bird’s-eye view of their immediate surroundings. Blind Spot Detection and Rear Cross Traffic Alert add another layer of awareness. These features can be particularly useful in congested conditions, where reduced visibility and heavy traffic can make it more difficult to monitor vehicles approaching from different directions.
This is especially timely, given the MMDA recorded 23,260 road crashes in Metro Manila from January to May 2025 alone, underscoring the need for technology that supports driver awareness and safety.
For passive safety, the VF 6 Plus also comes equipped with eight airbags, while the Eco features four, providing additional protection for occupants in the event of a collision.
A mobility investment built for the rainy season

blocks.caption: Evoto

blocks.text: Evoto

The VF 6’s electric powertrain delivers 310-Nm of torque with responsive and controlled acceleration, helping drivers manage the frequent starts and stops of congested city traffic. When sudden rains conceal sharp potholes beneath standing floodwaters, the crossover’s rear multi-link suspension – a setup typical for higher-segment SUVs – helps provide a more composed ride over uneven roads.

Ownership is further protected by a seven-year or 160,000-km vehicle warranty and a 10-year or 200,000-km battery warranty, delivering vital long-term protection against the harsh wear-and-tear of the rainy season. VinFast also offers free unlimited charging at V-Green stations until March 31,2029, alongside complimentary accessories like a home wall charger with installation.

Priced at P1,699,000 (battery included) and P1,409,000 (battery subscription), the VinFast VF 6 fuses weather-ready engineering with intelligent driver assistance and comprehensive ownership support. Whether you are navigating rain-soaked city streets or braving the daily Metro traffic, the VinFast VF 6 is engineered to make the journey more confident, comfortable, and manageable.

articles.title: Lawmakers, lawbreakers
articles.summary: Congress’ power over the budget is supposed to discipline executive spending, not license legislative excess. Yet recent appropriations show how the constitutional ban on increasing the President’s…

blocks.text: Congress’ power over the budget is supposed to discipline executive spending, not license legislative excess. Yet recent appropriations show how the constitutional ban on increasing the President’s proposed budget has been repeatedly blurred, especially through unprogrammed funds and lawmakers’ own institutional budgets.

In a democracy, the power of the purse is meant to be a restraint, not a loophole. Congress authorizes spending so that presidents cannot build roads, erect monuments, or wage wars without public consent. But that power carries a matching duty: to protect taxpayers from waste and to ensure that public money is spent only as the Constitution allows.

The Philippine legislature has wide authority over the budget, taxes, and tariffs. It may decide how large government should be and how much citizens should pay for it, subject to constitutional limits. Its task is not merely to spend, but to make the state deliver value for money.

That discipline begins with the National Expenditure Program (NEP), prepared by the President. The General Appropriations Bill must be based on that proposal. This is not a ceremonial sequence. There can be no budget bill without the President’s submission, and Congress is not free to turn authorization into augmentation.
The rule Congress keeps testing

The constitutional rule is blunt. Article VI, Section 25(1) provides that Congress “may not increase the appropriations recommended by the President for the operation of the Government as specified in the budget.” Yet recent budgets suggest that this rule has been treated less as a command than as an inconvenience.

blocks.caption: Sources: Department of Budget and Management, various budget documents.

blocks.text: Sources: Department of Budget and Management, various budget documents.
A quiet expansion of the budget

In the programmed and automatic portions of the 2023, 2024, and 2025 budgets, Congress broadly kept to the President’s proposal. In 2025 it even approved slightly less than requested: ₱4.222 trillion against ₱4.247 trillion. On its face, that looked compliant.

The real expansion took place in unprogrammed appropriations. Congress added ₱219.0 billion in 2023 (or 37.2 percent), ₱449.5 billion in 2024 (or 159.5 percent), and ₱204.7 billion in 2025 (or 129.0 percent). Over three years, the additions reached ₱873.3 billion—close to ₱1 trillion. The form may have been legislative adjustment; the substance was budget enlargement.
When lawmakers budget for themselves

The Constitution is equally clear on another point: appropriations for Congress must follow the same procedure applied to other departments and agencies. Senators and representatives are not a budgetary class apart. The rules they impose on the Executive should apply, with equal force, to themselves.

Two principles therefore matter: Congress should not increase what the President proposes, and when it budgets for its own institutions, it should undergo the same pre-plenary scrutiny faced by executive departments. Fiscal restraint loses force when its authors exempt themselves from it.

blocks.caption: Legend: SET: Senate Electoral Tribunal; CA: Commission on Appointments; HOR: House of Representatives; HOR ET: House Electoral Tribunal; OP: Office of the President; OVP: Office of the Vice President.

blocks.text: Legend: SET: Senate Electoral Tribunal; CA: Commission on Appointments; HOR: House of Representatives; HOR ET: House Electoral Tribunal; OP: Office of the President; OVP: Office of the Vice President.

The pattern is clearest in the appropriations for the highest offices of government: the President, the Vice President, the Senate, the House, and their related bodies. These figures reveal not merely accounting choices, but the political economy of budgeting.

In the first four national budgets submitted by President Marcos Jr., lawmakers—particularly the Senate, the House, and the Commission on Appointments—approved appropriations above the President’s proposal. The constitutional ceiling became, in practice, a floor.

The fifth budget tells a different story. Lawmakers appear to have observed the “no increase” rule, perhaps chastened by public outrage over the misuse of public funds. That is progress, but not virtue. Obeying the Constitution is the minimum expected of those who write the laws.

The real test is still ahead. Will Congress now allow its own budget to be examined in public before plenary debate, as one legislator has proposed? The Senate and the House have long resisted such scrutiny. If lawmakers want the public to believe they have rediscovered fiscal discipline, they should begin by applying it to themselves.

articles.title: North Carolina teenager dies from rare infection caused by brain-eating amoeba
articles.summary:
Naegleria fowleri is commonly found in warm freshwater, and if it enters through the nose, can cause brain damage

A North…

blocks.text: A North Carolina teenager has died after contracting a rare and often fatal brain-eating amoeba.

The state’s health department (NCDHHS) confirmed the boy’s death on Monday, saying: “NCDHHS has been informed that the teen who developed a rare illness, caused by Naegleria fowleri died on Aug. 31, 2026. We extend our condolences to the family, friends and community impacted by this loss.”
Last Thursday, NCDHHS reported that the boy had contracted a rare illness caused by the single cell organism commonly found in warm freshwater.

The teenager – whose mother, Monica Mendoza, identified him as Moises Ponce Mendoza in an online fundraiser – was described earlier by the NCDHHS in its statement as “critically ill and receiving medical care”.
A Facebook post from a user who identified himself as a close relative of Ponce – also said that the teen had died by Monday.

In the online fundraiser, Mendoza described her son in Spanish as a “young man full of life currently fighting for his life in the hospital – in a coma”, adding that his illness started with severe headaches.
She said she initially took Moises to a Burlington hospital for severe symptoms on 21 August – but they were sent home after a doctor briefly examined him.

His condition quickly worsened and Mendoza said she rushed him to the University of North Carolina hospital’s emergency department at 7am the next day. Doctors there found he had an infection caused by Naegleria fowleri, which she described as “an extremely rare amoeba that can enter through the nose, reach the brain, and cause inflammation, infection, and brain damage”.
“From that moment on, our lives changed completely,” Mendoza added. “Moises is in a coma, and doctors are doing everything possible to fight this illness and give him a chance to pull through.”
Pictures posted online showed Moises intubated in a hospital bed and receiving intravenous fluids.
The Guardian has contacted Mendoza for additional comment.
Naegleria fowleri is often found in warm ponds, lakes and rivers. It is not found in saltwater or in properly maintained and chlorinated pools, the NCDHHS said.
The amoeba is harmless if swallowed – but is often deadly if contaminated water enters the nose and reaches the brain, such as while diving in water, water-skiing or engaging in similar activities.

Naegleria fowleri can cause an infection known as primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), according to the US Centers of Disease Control (CDC). Its symptoms can include severe headaches, fever, nausea and vomiting, followed by stiff neck, seizures and coma, with the illness often progressing rapidly and causing death within about five days.

Fewer than 10 cases are typically reported in the US each year, usually during prolonged periods of hot weather when freshwater temperatures rise, the NCDHHS warned. The CDC says more than 97% of people who contract PAM die from the infection.

Health officials advise swimmers to keep their heads above water in warm freshwater, use nose clips or hold their noses shut when entering the water, and avoid diving or jumping in. They also recommend avoiding submerging the head in hot springs or thermal waters and disturbing sediment in shallow, warm freshwater.

Ponce’s story gained attention after an eight-year-old Louisiana girl died after contracting a Naegleria fowleri infection. Lillian Smart may have been infected while she was swimming in Louisiana’s Lake Claiborne, the Louisiana health department said.
The girl died on 23 August, eight days after she was hospitalized.

As the climate crisis continues to alter environmental conditions, scientists warn that Naegleria fowleri is being detected in parts of the US where it has not traditionally been found, with the amoeba appearing to expand from southern states into the Midwest.
“It likes warm surface waters during the summer in the northern latitudes,” Charles Gerba, a University of Arizona microbiologist, told the Guardian in 2022.
