articles.title: Man who murdered Molly Ticehurst unlikely to face life in jail, court hears
articles.summary: Justice Natalie Adams says she is troubled by expert evidence about rape allegations in slain woman’s police statement

blocks.text: Molly Ticehurst’s ex-boyfriend is unlikely to face a life sentence for her domestic violence murder, a crime which galvanised a national movement against gendered abuse.
Ticehurst, a 28-year-old childcare educator, was found dead in her home at Forbes, in the New South Wales central-west, in the early hours of 22 April 2024.
Her former boyfriend Daniel Billings broke into her bedroom and stabbed her 15 times in a ferocious attack that lasted less than a minute.

Billings had been charged with several counts of raping Ticehurst and a string of domestic violence offences just over two weeks before the killing, but he was freed on bail by a local court registrar the next day.
Ticehurst’s death became a flashpoint in the nation’s fight against domestic violence and led to legal changes in NSW, including tighter bail laws.
Billings, 31, who has pleaded guilty to murder, is will face court in Orange for a two-day sentence hearing from Thursday.
During a mention in the NSW supreme court on Monday, Adams raised the issue of a life sentence, although she noted she did not expect it to be requested.
Crown submissions before the court do not seek a life term, but they argue Billings should not get any discount on his sentence because his level of culpability is “extreme”.
Adams said there would probably be mitigating factors to consider when sentencing Billings, as there were in almost all cases.
“It’s difficult to identify what’s [legally] unique about this case,” she said.
But the judge said she was troubled with how to deal with expert evidence about Ticehurst’s police statement that she was repeatedly raped by Billings.
The sexual assault charges were dropped when Billings pleaded guilty to murder in November 2025 after 18 months of legal negotiations.
Billings always denied raping Ticehurst and developed a dark obsession with clearing his name in the lead-up to the murder.
“If I’m going to do the time, I may as well do the crime,” he said in a conversation with a friend soon before the murder, according to a statement of agreed facts before the court.
Adams said she could not ignore the rape allegations, despite the charges being dropped, when it came to sentencing Billings for murder.
“It was him seeing the police facts that set him to spiral,” the judge said.
Acting out of spite over the allegations could push his crime into another serious category, she said.
after newsletter promotion
“The sense of grievance about a perceived false allegation, there’s no getting around that,” Adams said.
“Whether it’s almost a public-justice type murder or domestic-violence type murder.”
Adams said it was possible all the elements to satisfy the legal definition of sexual assault were in Ticehurst’s account to police.
Changes to consent laws in NSW, which included affirmative language in the legislation, meant it was a crime where both parties “feel they’re telling the truth”.
“The only witness who could have told us is dead,” the judge said.
Billings, who has been in custody in the supermax wing of Goulburn jail since he was charged, will face court in person.
He will hear victim impact statements from the Ticehurst family, along with expert evidence about his mental state at the time of the murder.
A series of videos he made before and after the murder are also expected to be played to court.
Adams has indicated she will sentence Billings later in September.

articles.title: Iran retaliates after first US strikes in a month
articles.summary: TEHRAN — Iran attacked US military targets in the Middle East on Monday in retaliation for the first American strikes on its territory in a month, in a fresh flare-up of the war that has…

blocks.text: TEHRAN — Iran attacked US military targets in the Middle East on Monday in retaliation for the first American strikes on its territory in a month, in a fresh flare-up of the war that has engulfed the region.

Tehran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said they had responded to Sunday’s American attack by striking two US air bases with ballistic missiles in Washington-allied Jordan, causing “heavy damage”.
Jordan’s army said it had intercepted eight missiles, without stating their origin.
Tehran also claimed it targeted US military personnel at an air base in the United Arab Emirates and shot down a US drone over the Strait of Hormuz.
The flurry of attacks came after the United States said Sunday it had attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the small island of Larak in the strategic shipping lane.
Washington said its attacks were aimed at preventing Iran from placing more sea mines in the strait, days after the US announced it had completed clearing explosives from the waterway.
“US forces took limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat in the Strait of Hormuz,” the US military’s Central Command wrote on X.
Iran’s Guards said the US strikes resulted in “casualties” and that their subsequent attack on Jordan was “in response to the US-Zionist aerial aggression”.
The Iranian foreign ministry condemned the US attacks on Larak and justified the Jordan strikes as “legitimate defence”.
“We are not seeking war, but we will deliver a decisive response to the aggressors,” added Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in a statement quoted by state TV.
Pezeshkian was speaking before traveling to Kyrgyzstan for a summit of a bloc that seeks to counter influence from the West, along with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping.
The exchange of fire between the United States and Iran came shortly after their war hit its six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.
In recent weeks, the administration of US President Donald Trump has prioritised “economic warfare” over military strikes.

Tehran has effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic sea lane through which one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the US and Israel triggered the war with strikes on Iran on February 28.
“Last week, CENTCOM completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes,” said Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for US Central Command.
“US forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” he said.
Unpopular war
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war.

While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming, and Washington has since declared “economic warfare” against Tehran.
A US naval counterblockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran during a shortfall in domestic production.
The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks — mainly around the Strait of Hormuz — have dimmed prospects for a final peace agreement.

The last US strike on Iran before Sunday came on July 29 in response to “an attempted surprise attack on US forces” in the region, the US military said. Earlier in July, CENTCOM attacked Iran for 13 consecutive nights.
Throughout the war, Iran has fought back by striking US facilities and allies in the Gulf region, hitting targets in Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, among others.
Its closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused pain around the world in the form of price hikes and shortages of fertiliser and energy.
Both main crude oil contracts rose at least two percent on Monday.
The war is also deeply unpopular with the US public, with midterm elections looming in November that could overturn Republican control of Congress.
In a statement on Friday, US Senator Jack Reed criticised Trump over the war.
“Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved,” said Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
“Indeed, he has weakened our position in the Middle East and the world significantly.” /dl

articles.title: South Korea’s medical tourism continues double-digit growth
articles.summary: SEOUL — Foreign card spending on medical services in South Korea jumped 66.5 percent in July from a year earlier, extending a rapid expansion in the country’s medical tourism industry. Foreign…

blocks.text: SEOUL — Foreign card spending on medical services in South Korea jumped 66.5 percent in July from a year earlier, extending a rapid expansion in the country’s medical tourism industry.
Foreign nationals spent 213 billion won ($145 million) on medical services and related products during the month, according to credit card-based data from the Korea Tourism Organization.
The increase follows annual growth of 65 percent in 2025 and 78.6 percent in 2024, suggesting the field is becoming a larger part of Korea’s inbound tourism economy.
Beyond beauty, beyond Asia

Korea has long been known for plastic surgery and dermatology, particularly among visitors from nearby countries such as China, Japan and Taiwan. In July, dermatology accounted for 54.9 percent of medical spending on foreign cards, while plastic surgery made up another 19.3 percent.
Ban Jun-seop, president of the Korean Association of Plastic Surgeons, said foreign patients accounted for as much as 70 percent of some plastic surgery clinics’ clientele.

But spending patterns show signs of diversification. The share of spending at pharmacies, for example, rose from 5 percent in March 2025 to 12.7 percent in July. Data from the Korea Health Industry Development Institute also shows demand spreading across a wider range of specialties and nationalities.
US nationals accounted for 24.1 percent of foreign patients who received health checkups in 2025, while patients from Mongolia and Kazakhstan featured prominently in other specialties.

“Patients from Japan, Taiwan, China, Singapore and Thailand tend to show a strong preference for dermatology and plastic surgery, while those from Kazakhstan, Canada and Mongolia often come to Korea for treatment of serious diseases such as cancer,” a Korea Health Industry Development Institute official said.
“Demand for treatment of serious diseases alone amounts to around 60,000 to 70,000 patients a year.”
Taking medical tourism beyond Seoul
The boom remains overwhelmingly concentrated in Seoul. In July, the capital accounted for 86.8 percent of total medical-related spending on foreign cards. Busan ranked second with just 6.4 percent.
That concentration has become a concern for local governments seeking to use medical tourism to encourage longer stays and generate additional spending at local businesses.
Experts say regions with fewer major medical institutions may be better off focusing on wellness and healthcare rather than trying to replicate Seoul’s medical tourism model.
Daegu, which ranked first outside the Seoul metropolitan area in the number of medical tourists in 2019, did not make the top five regions in terms of medical-related spending in July.

“It is practically impossible to distribute medical institutions across the country when they are already concentrated in Seoul,” Yoon Ji-hwan, a tourism professor at Kyung Hee University, told local media.
Yoon said Seoul could continue to focus on surgeries and procedures, while other regions develop healthcare tourism centered on wellness and traditional Korean medicine.
He said that would be a more realistic way to spread medical tourism beyond the capital. /dl

articles.title: 'Moonies' church leader jailed for two years over bribery offences
articles.summary: Han Hak-ja, 83, gave South Korea's former first lady two Chanel bags and a diamond necklace, a court found.

blocks.text: The leader of the controversial Unification Church has been sentenced to two years in prison for bribing South Korea's former first lady and other political funding offences.
A court found that Han Hak-ja's church gave Kim Keon Hee, the wife of ousted president Yoon Suk Yeol, two Chanel bags and a diamond necklace, together worth 80 million won ($57,900; £42,500).
Earlier this year, Kim was sentenced to 20 months in jail for accepting bribes from the church.
Han, the 83-year-old widow of the Unification Church's founder Sun Myung Moon, had repeatedly denied the allegations, calling them "false".
A special counsel team appointed to the case said Kim received the luxury products from the church between April and July 2022, in exchange for business and political favours.

The prosecutors said the probe was the first time the authorities have confirmed the church's attempt at buying influence in politics, and released photos of $19m (£14m) worth of cash found in Han's personal safe.
South Korea's former first lady admitted to receiving Chanel bags, but said she later returned them without using them.
Kim made a public apology when she appeared for questioning last August: "I am truly sorry that a nobody like me has caused concern to the people."
The Unification Church, known formally as The Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, was founded in South Korea in the 1950s by Sun Myung Moon, who proclaimed himself the messiah.
The church is probably best known for the mass weddings where thousands of couples were married by Han and her late husband and founder Sun Myung Moon in a stadium.

Critics have described the group as "cult-like". Lawyers have accused it of coercing devotees, known colloquially as "Moonies" after its founder, to donate large sums of money. "Moonies" is a term used by critics that many church members find offensive.

The Unification Church had come under the spotlight in Japan after the assassination of the country's former leader Shinzo Abe. The alleged assassin blamed the group for bankrupting his family and held a grievance against Abe for allegedly promoting it.
The church has boasted extensive links to politicians in Seoul, Tokyo, and even in Washington. Various politicians sent video message to its 2021 event congratulating the church's new think tank.
The list included US President Donald Trump, former US Vice-President Mike Pence, Shinzo Abe, as well as the mayors of Seoul and Busan.
The group is banned in parts of the world, including Singapore. In Japan, it has been ordered to dissolve.

articles.title: S. Korea considers in-flight meals for foreigners awaiting deportation
articles.summary: SEOUL — The South Korean government is reviewing a plan to provide regular in-flight meals to foreign nationals awaiting deportation, a move aimed at better protecting basic rights. The Korea…

blocks.text: SEOUL — The South Korean government is reviewing a plan to provide regular in-flight meals to foreign nationals awaiting deportation, a move aimed at better protecting basic rights.
The Korea Immigration Service said Saturday it was revising the meal policy for foreign nationals held at the detention facility in Incheon Airport before being sent back to their home countries.

The facility houses individuals ordered to leave the country for reasons such as illegal residency or unauthorized employment. Under the current system, they are given only bread and drinks upon arrival at the airport after deportation orders are processed.
Immigration officials say the change reflects deportees’ basic right to adequate meals.
“We are revising the plan to protect human rights and raise South Korea’s international standing,” an immigration official said. “This is an expansion of what we currently provide.”
Foreign nationals denied entry after failing to explain the purpose of their visit already receive in-flight meals while awaiting repatriation. The meals are valued at about 6,910 won ($5). /dl

blocks.text: New South Wales police have appealed for information to find the mother of a newborn baby boy, whose body was discovered in a rubbish bin in Auburn in Sydney’s south-west on Monday morning.

Police said emergency services responded to reports of the body of a baby located in a rubbish bin along Harrow Road in Auburn at 11.20am, with officers from the Auburn police area command finding the body of a newborn boy.
A crime scene has been established and detectives have commenced an investigation into the incident.
Police said they hold “serious concerns” for the welfare of the baby’s mother, and have urged the mother to attend the nearest hospital to receive urgent care.

Anyone with more information about the incident, or who was in the area at the time and may have dashcam or mobile footage relevant to the incident, are urged to contact Auburn police station or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

articles.title: Monday briefing: Nepal and Tibet’s floods are a warning for the future
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: As rescuers search for survivors after catastrophic floods, the disaster offers a stark warning about the climate risks facing the region, and the world

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. Over the weekend, rescue workers in Nepal and Tibet raced to find people who are still trapped in villages affected by catastrophic flash floods. As of this morning, the death toll stands at 903, and more than 4,000 people are missing.

For those of you reading this in a place where life continues as usual, the scale of devastation is hard to fathom. In a matter of minutes, a torrent of mud and debris engulfed entire villages, snapped bridges and swept away people’s homes and families. Some survivors are marooned on top of buildings that rescue workers can’t reach. Others are trapped in tunnels beneath the ground. Many have no idea if their loved ones are still alive.

The floods exemplify a wider threat. The delicate processes that have shaped our climate for centuries are unwinding at a terrifying pace. Scientists are still investigating the precise sequence of events that caused these floods, but as the planet heats up and glaciers melt, events like this will keep happening.

The Guardian has been covering the floods extensively – you can read our visual guide to the disaster, and our latest report on it here. For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen, who is on the ground in Kathmandu. She’s been speaking to survivors and reporting on the rescue operation since Thursday. That’s after the headlines.
Weekend roundup

items: UK politics | PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain in prison after Andy Burnham announced changes to the early release scheme that will see anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, excluded from the scheme.

Milo Yiannopoulos | Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US back to the UK by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in connection with what the agency said was expired authorisation to be in the country.

US-Iran | Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month.
Iceland | In a blow to Brussels, Iceland has held a referendum that has narrowly ⁠rejected ⁠the government’s proposal ​to hold ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU.

Nepal-Tibet disaster | A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.

blocks.text: In depth: An ‘absolute catastrophe’

blocks.caption: ‘Everything was either submerged in mud, or mangled’  Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters

blocks.text: At 8:37am on Wednesday morning, an enormous chunk of ice from a glacier in the Himalayas broke off and crashed on to a mountain near the border between Nepal and Tibet. It caused a fearsome avalanche of ice and rock, which surged downstream into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, submerging villages and sweeping roads away.

At first, the scale of damage was unclear. Nepal is prone to natural disasters, and many of the villages affected by these floods are extremely remote. Early satellite images of the region were obscured by thick clouds of dust, and scientists initially assumed that an earthquake must have caused the flood, rather than a glacier collapse. By Wednesday night, as more images and reports emerged, it became clear that the floods were an “absolute catastrophe,” Hannah says. On Thursday, she boarded a flight to Kathmandu, the capital city near the destruction.

When Hannah arrived in Bidur, a small city two hours from Kathmandu, on Friday morning, most of its buildings had been destroyed, their carcasses exposed like matchsticks. A team of rescue workers in yellow hard hats were working to clear the roads. “There was a bank, an ATM machine, and a truck that was lying on its side,” she says. “Everything else was either submerged in mud, or mangled.”
The race to save lives

The Nepali army has been organising the rescue operation from a military base in Bidur. Large sections of the road that links Bidur to villages higher in the valley have been washed away, so rescues are happening by air, and the sound of helicopters is nearly constant. Every two to three minutes, a chopper lands, deposits survivors, and sets off again. The mud is so thick in some places that helicopters have struggled to land. Rasuwa, an area where entire villages were destroyed, was still inaccessible when I spoke to Hannah on Sunday afternoon. “The ground zero of the floods has still not been reached by journalists, and is only just being reached by the army,” she says.

Hundreds, if not thousands, of people have been rescued, and hundreds of people are now waiting outside the army base in Bidur scanning lists of survivors posted on the walls. At hospitals in Kathmandu, health workers have put up photos of bodies that are so disfigured their families have struggled to identify them. Authorities have begun burying human remains because there isn’t enough mortuary space to prevent them from decomposing. “I’ve spoken to people who have up to 12 relatives who have gone missing,” says Hannah, who visited hospitals in Kathmandu on Saturday. “And there’s no phone signal in the more remote villages. So another big cause of suffering is this huge uncertainty.”
Thousands still missing

So far there are 4,247 people who are missing, according to Nepal’s disaster agency (592 of whom are foreigners, including 43 Australians, and 48 from the UK, including 15 reported missing in China). Among them are 933 workers from Nepal and neighbouring countries who were working on hydroelectric power projects along the river. These rely on vast tunnel systems that are built deep into the ground, and rescue teams have to dig through mud and bore through tunnel walls to extricate trapped workers. On Saturday, the Nepali army had a small breakthrough when it successfully inserted a pipe into a tunnel at a hydroelectric site in Trishuli, allowing air to be pumped into the tunnel. In the early hours this morning, rescue efforts were “intensified” at the site, with a team of 90 people deployed.

The army is racing against time to rescue the living. “People are stuck in areas that have no drinking water, or access to food. They’re completely cut off,” Hannah says. The picture of devastation has emerged more quickly in Nepal than in Tibet, where the Chinese government retains a tight grip on information. On Friday, as the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, China estimated that just five people had died in Tibet. The Chinese authorities have since revised their numbers, and estimate that at least 16 people are dead and 546 missing.
The long road to recovery

It will take months to clear away the mud, and some people will never find their relatives’ bodies. Some were pushed so far down the river that they have washed up in India. “People have lost everything,” says Hannah. “I saw one woman clutching a bottle of cooking oil, because it’s the only thing she had left.” Climate stories in the global south often struggle to break through, so it’s encouraging that these floods have been covered so widely. But when the news cycle has moved on, Nepal will be left with the enormous task of rebuilding. It estimates that cost could be between $4bn to $5bn, almost a tenth of its economy.

“It’s getting increasingly difficult for Nepal to pick itself up,” Hannah tells me. In Kathmandu, buildings destroyed by the 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people, are still in ruins. The EU has committed €2m to Nepal to help with the floods, and Britain has committed £5m. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for better early monitoring systems. All of this matters. But as Sunil Acharya, a climate policy specialist based in Kathmandu, wrote in this interesting Opinion column, it also obscures a more fundamental problem: systems to monitor these events were designed for yesterday’s risks, not today’s extremes. Nepal’s warning systems were destroyed before they could alert people near the source of the flood.

Looming over all this is the fact that nations like Nepal, which has contributed a minuscule amount to historic greenhouse gas emissions, will suffer the worst effects of the climate crisis. It needs far more assistance to cope with the consequences of richer nations’ actions. And it needs those nations to rapidly cut their emissions, before the crisis gets worse.
The week to come

Saturday | Officials from Jamaica will visit the UK to lodge a petition with King Charles to seek legal guidance from the privy council on the country’s request for reparations over Britain’s involvement in the slave trade, on the anniversary of the 1781 Zong slave ship departure from West Africa.

blocks.text: Results from a 15-year study suggest that statins, the cholesterol-busting drugs, can lower the risk of dementia by 15%. In the largest study of its kind, researchers tracked more than 132,000 people in Denmark between 2006 and 2021. Those who started on statins during the study period were 10% less likely to develop dementia. Those taking them early reduced their risk by 15%. The results were similar in women and men. The number of people living with dementia globally is forecast to nearly triple to 153 million by 2050. But, experts believe almost half of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed.

articles.title: Nepal flood death toll rises to 903, missing 4,247 – disaster authority
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Devastating floods near the border with China have killed at least 903 people in Nepal, while the number of missing in the country has soared to 4,247, its disaster authority said…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Devastating floods near the border with China have killed at least 903 people in Nepal, while the number of missing in the country has soared to 4,247, its disaster authority said Monday, as rescue efforts entered a sixth day.
Chinese state media earlier confirmed 16 dead and 546 people missing in Tibet following Wednesday’s disaster, taking the overall toll to 919 dead and 4,793 missing.
Nepal’s list of the missing includes 592 foreigners.
It also includes 933 workers on hydropower projects along the river which the torrent crashed through, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
Nepal’s disaster agency listed 3,655 missing citizens in its update on Monday morning.
That includes Nuwakot district, where the missing rose sharply to 1,158, up from 115 reported on Sunday, as well as a further 562 unaccounted for in Rasuwa district.
The missing includes 45 Nepali army soldiers, 38 police and armed police officers, and 19 customs and immigration officers.
In India, authorities in Uttar Pradesh state said they had recovered 17 bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.
Indian authorities are seeking to identify the bodies, and they are not included in the toll. /dl

articles.title: Annual Pacific Islands summit: At least 5 leaders won’t attend
articles.summary: KOROR, Palau — At least five leaders will skip the Pacific Island region’s annual summit, officials said Monday, hours before the opening of talks overshadowed by Taiwan-China tensions.…

blocks.text: KOROR, Palau — At least five leaders will skip the Pacific Island region’s annual summit, officials said Monday, hours before the opening of talks overshadowed by Taiwan-China tensions.
The gathering aims to grapple with thorny regional issues including climate change, drug crime, and the Chinese test-firing of a ballistic missile that landed in the Pacific Ocean in July.
China’s security and economic influence has added resonance this year, because the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum is being hosted by Palau, a diplomatic ally of Taiwan.
Beijing has protested against Taiwan’s inclusion among aid partners invited to attend, along with China, Singapore, Japan, Britain and the United States.
China, which claims self-ruled Taiwan as part of its territory, also declared Palau an “unsafe” place for tourists.
The Pacific forum has been touted for decades as a symbol of regional unity.
“The Pacific is our home, not a theatre for geopolitical competition,” Palau President Surangel Whipps said in an interview on Sunday.
Tensions between the Pacific’s partners should not detract from island priorities on renewable energy, drug crime, food security and climate change, he urged.
But a growing number of leaders are skipping this year’s forum and sending lower-ranked ministers in their place.
Samoa’s government said in a statement its delegation would be led by the deputy prime minister.
The prime minister of Vanuatu and the head of government of the French territory of New Caledonia will also skip the summit, a forum official told journalists.
No confidence motion
Kiribati’s president has already said he will not be attending the talks.
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale unexpectedly flew out of Palau on Sunday to deal with a political crisis at home after a no-confidence motion was lodged against his leadership.
Solomon Islands had been China’s closest partner in the Pacific until Wale was recently elected, vowing to review a secret security pact and repairing ties with the United States and Australia.
Fiji, a founding member of the forum, said its delegation to Palau would be led by the foreign minister but it was not known whether the prime minister might join at a later stage.
The leaders’ absence may weaken any joint Pacific statement on the Chinese missile test, said Oliver Nobetau, Pacific analyst at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney-based think tank.
“Not having these leaders there really lowers the expectation of whether or not we will see a strong statement come out of the Pacific Islands Forum,” he told AFP.
Some Pacific leaders were staying at home to tackle domestic political priorities, said Nobetau, director of the institute’s Pacific Islands programme.
But the leaders may also have decided that one-on-one discussions with external powers are more useful than forum negotiations in some areas.
“Some matters may be better dealt with in the realm of individual sovereignties, like when it comes to security, economic support, development support,” Nobetau said.
Around 110 police drawn from various Pacific islands will provide security at the forum, the first large-scale demonstration of Pacific-wide cooperation on policing.
Australia, the biggest forum member and aid donor, has led efforts for the Pacific to provide its own security, arguing there is no need for China to have police in Kiribati and the Solomons. /dl

articles.title: American wanted in US nabbed in Dumaguete City
articles.summary: BACOLOD CITY, Philippines — A 45-year-old American wanted by United States authorities for a parole violation involving an underlying dangerous drugs charge has been arrested by the Bureau of…

blocks.text: BACOLOD CITY, Philippines — A 45-year-old American wanted by United States authorities for a parole violation involving an underlying dangerous drugs charge has been arrested by the Bureau of Immigration (BI) in Dumaguete City, Negros Oriental.

The BI said on Saturday, Aug. 29, that its Fugitive Search Unit (FSU), working with US law enforcement agents, the Philippine National Police and local police and maritime authorities, apprehended Jason Michael Hill at Purok St. John in Barangay Calindagan on Aug. 11.

Hill was reportedly wanted in the United States for violating his parole, with an underlying dangerous drugs charge, based on an outstanding warrant issued by the Sacramento County Superior Court in California.
BI records showed that Hill entered the Philippines in March 2023 as a temporary visitor but had overstayed his authorized period of stay.
He was also the subject of existing BI derogatory records for being an undesirable alien and a fugitive from justice, the bureau said.
BI Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado said the arrest should serve as a warning to fugitives seeking refuge in the Philippines.
“Let this be a clear message to fugitives: The Philippines is not a safe haven for those escaping justice,” Viado said.

“If you come here to hide from the law, the BI will find you. We will work with our foreign law enforcement partners to locate you, arrest you, and ensure that you face the appropriate legal and immigration consequences,” he added.
Hill will remain in BI custody while undergoing immigration proceedings. /dl

articles.title: Iceland votes ‘No’ to resuming EU talks
articles.summary: REYKJAVIK, Iceland — Iceland voted ‘No’ to resuming membership negotiations with the European Union, referendum results showed Sunday, dealing a blow to Brussels which had been keen…

blocks.text: REYKJAVIK, Iceland — Iceland voted ‘No’ to resuming membership negotiations with the European Union, referendum results showed Sunday, dealing a blow to Brussels which had been keen to welcome a new wealthy member.
Almost 53 percent of Icelanders rejected the resumption of EU entry talks suspended 13 years ago, while some 47 percent voted in favour in Saturday’s referendum.
Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, who favoured a ‘Yes,’ stressed she didn’t “see this as a setback”.
“I see this as a victory for democracy,” she told reporters, pointing to voter turnout of over 80 percent.
“I want to make it absolutely clear, this government is not going forward with the accession talks this term.”

This means any discussions of Icelandic accession are frozen at least until 2028 — an apparent disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues to facilitate Iceland’s accession.
EU chief Antonio Costa nonetheless told Frostadottir the bloc “fully respects the democratic choice” made by voters, a spokesperson said.
“Iceland remains one of the EU’s closest and most trusted partners,” said the spokesperson.
Far-right, eurosceptic leaders in Britain and France hailed the result.

“At a time when some are pushing for greater federalism and the transfer of sovereignty to the European Commission, this vote reminds us that another Europe is possible, a Europe of free, sovereign nations cooperating voluntarily on matters of common interest,” France’s Marine Le Pen wrote on X.
“Congratulations to Iceland on voting to keep their independence,” Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who was one of the faces of Britain’s Brexit, wrote on the same platform.
Iceland, a country of just under 400,000 people applied to join the EU in the wake of the 2009 financial crisis that devastated its economy.
Membership talks were then suspended in 2013 when a eurosceptic government came to power.
The island is, however, already closely linked to the EU as a member of the European Economic Area and the free-movement Schengen zone, ties which will remain unchanged.
The referendum result was non-binding but the government had vowed to respect it.
High turnout

Debates ahead of the vote had mainly revolved around domestic and economic issues, though the war in Ukraine and US President Donald Trump’s ambitions for neighbouring Greenland — which he has mixed up with Iceland on several occasions — also featured.

The campaign had “lifted discussions about the EU, about Iceland’s place in the world, about our general geopolitical situation and status, to a higher level”, Frostadottir said after casting her ballot Saturday.
Political analysts had said it was unlikely the government would resign in the event of a ‘No’ victory, though it could emerge weakened by the rejection.
According to RUV, voter turnout was 82.5 percent, the highest participation in any Icelandic vote since April 2009 parliamentary elections during its crippling financial crisis.
The campaign divided Icelanders.
“It’s hard to grasp that it’s a ‘No’,” 37-year-old artist Elisabet Anna Kristjansdottir told AFP.
“It’s quite sad that the Icelandic people don’t even want to see the possibilities of joining the EU.”
Anna Maria Bogadottir said meanwhile she was “really happy”, but acknowledged it would now “be a challenge to unite 50 percent on each side.”
Wooing from Brussels

A ‘Yes’ vote would have given the government a mandate to resume negotiations with Brussels, including on the hotly contested issue of fishing — a pillar of Iceland’s economy and part of its national identity, and over which Reykjavik wants to retain exclusive control.
Any accession agreement would then have then been put to another referendum in Iceland.

The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc — 90 percent of companies in the industry are against the idea — and the EU had tried to woo it with a conciliatory approach ahead of the vote.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos had said Brussels and EU member states would be willing to “find creative solutions” to Iceland’s “unique specificities on fisheries and agriculture”.
An EU source in Brussels told AFP: “I don’t think anyone (in the EU) wants to block an accession over a question of fish.”

Brussels had hoped to be able to present wealthy Iceland as an example of positive enlargement that could also make it more palatable for member states to agree to take in poorer countries like Montenegro.
It would also have enabled it to enlarge its presence in the strategic Arctic region, and perhaps helped change some minds in ultra-wealthy non-EU member Norway. /dl

articles.title: Countries gear up to create lunar standard time amid global race on Moon
articles.summary: Countries are gearing up to establish a unified lunar time standard, with a key international conference in Paris set to take up the issue amid a global race to establish a presence on the Moon.…

blocks.text: Countries are gearing up to establish a unified lunar time standard, with a key international conference in Paris set to take up the issue amid a global race to establish a presence on the Moon.

Member states will try to work it out at the plenary meeting of the General Conference on Weights and Measures, which decides global measurement standards, as operations including the construction of a permanent base and lunar navigation are expected to be in full swing from around 2030.
China and the United States are among the countries pursuing plans to land astronauts on the lunar surface and secure lunar resources.

Under the theory of general relativity, time on the Moon passes slightly faster than on Earth because lunar gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth’s, meaning lunar time runs ahead of time on Earth by around 56 microseconds per day.
The difference between time on the Moon and on Earth is believed to pose problems for future lunar missions.

In building a lunar base, for example, operators must know the exact location where work is being done. Signals from satellites orbiting the Moon are expected to be used to calculate positions, similar to Earth’s Global Positioning System.
Lunar time needs to be accurate, because a timing error of just 1 microsecond can change a calculated position by about 300 meters, potentially affecting robots working at a lunar base.

Mamoru Sekido, a research manager at Japan’s National Institute of Information and Communications Technology, said international cooperation to coordinate and unify time standards for satellites operated by different countries is vital for lunar development.

There are two proposals for setting lunar time. One assumes a hypothetical clock at the Moon’s center of mass and calculates lunar time from it, while the other uses a real clock placed at the Moon’s average surface height as the reference, an approach that would be closer to how time is defined on Earth. /dl

articles.title: Barrier lake near Nepal-China border fully drains, China says
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — A barrier lake formed near the Nepal-China border after last week’s massive ice-rock avalanche has fully drained through natural outflow, China’s Ministry of Water Resources said on…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — A barrier lake formed near the Nepal-China border after last week’s massive ice-rock avalanche has fully drained through natural outflow, China’s Ministry of Water Resources said on Sunday, easing fears of another sudden flood downstream.

The lake had formed near the confluence of Nepal’s Chhochen Khola and China’s Purepu Tsangpo following Wednesday’s glacier collapse on the northern face of Langtang Ri, which triggered a devastating flood in the Bhotekoshi river system.

Citing the ministry, China Daily reported that around 2 million cubic metres of water had accumulated behind the blockage. The ministry’s hydrological emergency monitoring team said water was now flowing normally through natural channels and the impounded water had been almost completely discharged.

Nepali scientist Nitesh Khadka, who works at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Chengdu, also shared photographs sent by colleagues showing that the lower barrier lake had drained. He said more than half the water in an upper lake had also flowed out.
The development comes as river levels rose again in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems on Sunday, raising fresh concerns in areas already devastated by Wednesday’s disaster.

The swollen Trishuli river has eroded riverbanks in Nuwakot and Dhading districts. Flood-induced erosion and a subsequent landslide at Krishnabhir in Dhading have completely blocked the Muglin-Kathmandu section of the Prithvi Highway.
Floodwaters also swept away a suspension bridge over the Trishuli river linking Ghyachok in Gorkha with Charaudi in Dhading on Sunday.

Chinese authorities had earlier warned that the barrier lake posed a high risk of breaching, with continued rainfall expected to increase the volume of water behind the natural dam. Satellite monitoring later showed that the lake had begun draining gradually, reducing the immediate threat. /dl

articles.title: Nepal buries dead as rescuers seek thousands missing after floods
articles.summary: BIDUR, Nepal — Nepal was burying on Monday some of the hundreds of bodies retrieved after a deadly, tsunami-like flood crashed through the Himalayan region, sweeping away villages and leaving…

blocks.text: BIDUR, Nepal — Nepal was burying on Monday some of the hundreds of bodies retrieved after a deadly, tsunami-like flood crashed through the Himalayan region, sweeping away villages and leaving thousands still missing.
Distraught families have packed rescue stations and hospitals in search of their missing relatives, while others have faced the grim task of identifying bodies at overflowing morgues.

The huge wave of ice, rocks and debris that smashed into villages and towns on Wednesday claimed at least 797 lives in both Nepal and Tibet — across the border in China — with reports of some bodies possibly swept downstream as far as India.
At least 3,048 people remain missing, including many tourists and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash. There are also 933 workers at hydropower plants among those unaccounted for in Nepal.

Nepali army troops and engineers drilled through debris on Sunday towards workers believed trapped in a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site in the Himalayan river valley after they successfully inserted a pipe into the passage.
Workers who managed to get out described horrifying scenes when the disaster struck.
Surendra Dowluri, 33, from India’s Andhra Pradesh state, said raging water swamped the Upper Trishuli-1 site, where he was working.

“We heard a very loud sound… and saw that the turbine floor was submerged with slush, and six workers were stuck in that,” Dowluri told AFP in the Nepali capital Kathmandu after his rescue four days into the disaster.
“We managed to rescue five of them, but one person lost his life,” he said, describing how some workers reached higher ground or construction areas out of reach of the torrent.
Overnight rain and rising river waters also hampered rescue operations on Sunday, filling the excavation area with water before conditions eased, the Nepali army said.
DNA samples
The disaster was caused by a glacial collapse, sending a wall of water and debris downstream, the US Geological Survey said.
The torrent caused the formation of huge lakes, closely watched by emergency workers for risks to their operations.
Chinese rescuers near the Tibet border port that was hit by a deadly mudslide were “moved to a safe location” on Sunday after a new lake was formed by a landslide, state media reported.
China has so far put the death toll in Tibet at 16, with the number of missing at 546.
In Nepal, the disaster agency raised the total number of people missing on its side of the border to 2,502 on Sunday, saying there were also 781 confirmed deaths.
Overwhelmed by the number of bodies and without proper freezing facilities, Nepali authorities have had to begin burials before completing the identification process.
Officials said DNA samples were taken from the bodies so that families could later claim them and perform traditional funeral rites.
Grieving relatives gathered at identification centres to watch LED screens showing pictures of retrieved bodies, occasionally closing their eyes when the grim exercise overwhelmed them.
Walking out from one such building next to a makeshift morgue, Shobha Adhikary told a local coordinator she believed one image showed her childhood best friend.
“It looks like him, for sure,” she said, showing coordinators a photograph of a smiling, middle-aged man.
“My husband and I are best friends with Rajkumar and his wife Geeta,” she said. Geeta has also been missing since Wednesday.
‘Swept away’
Survivors were also faced with the daunting prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away,” resident Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.
“There is nothing left.”
The United States and Canada said they would provide $3.6 million each in humanitarian aid to Nepal.

The UK has offered $6.8 million, while the UN released $2.5 million in emergency funding, and aid pledges were made by the European Union, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, and others.

Nepal’s economy is already under pressure, with limited resources to respond to a disaster of this scale. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the reconstruction bill could run into “billions of dollars”.
He appealed for specialised assistance, including heavy-lift drones and technology to help locate people who are trapped.
Khanal also called for forensic testing kits to identify corpses and freezer units to store them, saying bodies that have been in water could decompose at a faster rate.
The minister has highlighted the inequity that Nepal should suffer the extreme impacts of climate change when it has one of the world’s lowest per-capita carbon emissions.
That is due to its location in the Himalayas, the world’s highest mountain range, where glaciers are melting at rapid speed as the planet heats.
In Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists and where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, a total of 2,141 personnel have joined search and rescue operations.
In an illustration of the difficulties of access, Chinese rescuers seeking to establish a route to the Tibet epicenter of the disaster, Gyirong Port, only advanced 285 meters (935 feet) on Sunday.
They have another 1.25 kilometers to go before reaching the site, the state-run Xinhua news agency reported. /dl

articles.title: Families scour Nepal morgue for loved ones swept away by flood
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Raj Kumar Tamang of Bidur, Nuwakot, had fed his five-year-old son Prince and sent him to school in his uniform when he learned that the Trishuli river had flooded. Raj Kumar was…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Raj Kumar Tamang of Bidur, Nuwakot, had fed his five-year-old son Prince and sent him to school in his uniform when he learned that the Trishuli river had flooded.
Raj Kumar was safe, but Prince never returned home.
He searched desperately for his son. Then, while scrolling through photographs of recovered bodies published on the Nepal Police website, he spotted a child wearing a school tie.

The body had been taken to Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences. Raj Kumar travelled to Pokhara on Saturday and identified his son by his school tie, a necklace and an earring. The tie bore the name of Uttargaya Secondary School in Bidur, where Prince was an LKG student.

His body had been recovered on the banks of the Narayani river in Nawalparasi on Thursday, far downstream from the flood zone. Rajkumar collected his son’s body and returned to Bidur later on Saturday.

For Satya Krishna Prajapati of Bhaktapur, it was a tattoo that helped identify his elder brother, Satya Sundar Prajapati. He recognised the body from a tattoo on his brother’s shoulder and took the remains back to Kathmandu on Friday.
Satya Sundar had been working as a site engineer at the under-construction Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project in Rasuwa for the past year and a half.

Relatives of 45-year-old Narayan Thapa, a schoolteacher from Arghakhanchi who had been teaching at a community school in Betrawati, arrived in Pokhara on Friday after suspecting that a body recovered in Nawalparasi East was his.

A photograph released by Devchuli Police and a silver pendant worn around the man’s neck helped relatives identify the body. Thapa’s wife and other family members formally identified the body on Saturday and took it away.
Following the Bhotekoshi flood, 102 bodies recovered from Gorkha, Tanahun, Dhading and Nawalparasi East were brought to Pokhara. By Saturday, relatives had identified and claimed 10 of them.

More than 1,000 relatives of people missing in the Rasuwa flood arrived at Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences on Saturday alone to search for their loved ones, according to Deepak Rijal, acting spokesperson for Kaski Police.
Police have set up a help desk at the hospital.
Photographs and identifying details of the bodies are displayed in a hall at the academy, allowing relatives to search for missing family members.

“Where faces are no longer recognisable, relatives are identifying bodies through school ties, tattoos, necklaces and earrings,” Police Inspector Rijal said. “More relatives are continuing to arrive.”
The help desk provides assistance including free help with filing reports, free ambulances for transporting bodies and free food and accommodation for relatives searching for missing family members.
With support from the Hotel Association, police accommodated 47 people in Lakeside hotels on Friday and another 19 on Saturday, Rijal said.
Of the 102 bodies brought to Pokhara, 46 had undergone post-mortem examinations by Saturday.

Five forensic specialists, including three from Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences and one each from Manipal College of Medical Sciences and Gandaki Medical College, have been deployed for the examinations. They have been working from 9am to 6pm.
Two specialists from Nepal Police’s Central Forensic Science Laboratory arrived in Pokhara on Friday to collect DNA samples and analyse fingerprints.
Bodies to remain in Pokhara for several more days
The mortuary at Pokhara Academy of Health Sciences has 72 refrigerated compartments, but it is currently holding more bodies than its official capacity.
Authorities have managed the shortage by arranging the bodies carefully, including smaller bodies and dismembered remains.
A container was placed inside a cold room at the academy on Saturday, and authorities are preparing to transfer up to 25 bodies into it under controlled temperatures.

According to the academy’s information officer Sushil Aryal, the facility has one of Nepal’s largest and most modern mortuaries outside Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj. Bodies can be preserved at temperatures between 2 and 6 degrees Celsius for around 10 days to two weeks.
The process of handing over identified bodies to relatives is continuing.

For bodies that remain unidentified, authorities must follow the government’s 2021 directive on the management of unidentified and unclaimed bodies. Under the rules, a body management committee led by the district police chief is responsible for the process.
Photographs, fingerprints and DNA samples are collected and preserved before burial.

If a body remains unidentified for a prolonged period, it must be buried at a site designated by the local government. The burial site must be chosen so that no structure is built there for at least 12 years.
“We bury the bodies with tag numbers and geo-location records,” Rijal said. “If relatives come forward within 12 years, the remains can be exhumed and identified through DNA analysis.”
Kaski Chief District Officer Kuman Singh Gurung said Pokhara could continue storing the bodies for several more days.

“Relatives are arriving in Pokhara after checking bodies recovered in Chitwan and Nawalparasi,” he said. “The situation here is not like Chitwan, where an improvised mortuary led to a foul smell. We have refrigerated facilities here, so there will be no immediate problem.”

Authorities will wait for several more days before deciding whether to bury unidentified bodies, he said. The decision will be taken jointly by the District Security Committee and the body management committee. /dl

articles.title: Trump calls for ‘punishment’ of NBC reporter Kristen Welker
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Sunday threatened a prominent NBC broadcast journalist with possible punishment by US media regulators as the Republican expressed disappointment with…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Sunday threatened a prominent NBC broadcast journalist with possible punishment by US media regulators as the Republican expressed disappointment with coverage of his candidate endorsements ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Trump took to his Truth Social platform to attack Kristen Welker as the “unpopular ‘hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press” talk show.

He objected to her having said the president had had “mixed results” on his endorsement of political candidates in party primaries, insisting the races had gone his way 98 percent to 100 percent of the time.
Welker, speaking early Sunday to a local NBC affiliate, said Trump would “loom large over these midterms.”
When it came to endorsements, she added, he “had some mixed results, but most recently, his pick of Senator Darline Graham… was successful in her primary battle.”

Trump, in his comments, said “because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment”. The Federal Communications Commission assigns and oversees licenses for radio and television broadcast frequencies.
“Unfortunately, she is not the only one,” he added. “The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP.'”
Welker is an award-winning journalist who earned bipartisan praise after moderating a 2020 presidential debate featuring Trump and Joe Biden, the Democrat who won that year’s election.
An NBC News spokesperson, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, defended Welker on Sunday, telling AFP that “Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her.”
Lawsuits and restrictions
Trump’s endorsements overall have proved helpful for Republican candidates running for statewide office.

But his approval ratings have slid, and at least 10 of Trump’s picks have been defeated this cycle, according to a tally compiled by Ballotpedia. They include four US House hopefuls and six candidates for governor, among them conspiracy theorist Mike Lindell in Minnesota.

Billionaire Trump has used American media to his advantage over the years as a provocative real estate developer in New York. But as president he dramatically turned against the press and what he called “fake news.”
He has sued several newspapers including the Wall Street Journal and New York Times, and ordered federal funding slashed for public media.
His administration has ramped up restrictions and attempts to intimidate journalists, and the FCC — headed by a close Trump associate — has pressured broadcasters to toe the line.
“I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” Trump said.
The latest attack is part of the Trump administration’s months-long offensive against media outlets it deems overly critical.

Such efforts are facing growing resistance from news organizations and major broadcast networks. Several of them have filed lawsuits against the FCC, arguing such pressure constitutes political retaliation that violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which protects freedom of speech.

Relations between Trump and Welker have been under pressure for months. In June the president abruptly cut short an interview with her following a tense exchange, during which he grew irritated by Welker’s questioning, particularly on the war against Iran.
Experts argue the FCC lacks the legal authority to punish broadcasters or reporters for their viewpoints.
According to a 2025 paper by the Yale Journal on Regulation, the US Supreme Court has confirmed that US law “does not grant the FCC the power to ban controversial speech.” /dl

articles.title: Nepal floods: Brother searches tunnel for fifth day for missing sibling
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Ram Budha traveled once again on Sunday morning to the mouth of a tunnel in Rasuwa where he believes his younger brother has been trapped for five days. Standing a short distance…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Ram Budha traveled once again on Sunday morning to the mouth of a tunnel in Rasuwa where he believes his younger brother has been trapped for five days.

Standing a short distance inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project at Hakubesi, Ram shouted repeatedly, hoping to hear the voice of his 20-year-old brother Prabin Budha from somewhere in the darkness.
There was no response.
Ram waited for a while before walking back out, disappointed but still unwilling to abandon hope.

A resident of Patarasi Rural Municipality-5 in Jumla, Ram has been returning to the tunnel every day since floods swept through the area, cutting off contact with his brother and other workers inside.

“I went to the mouth of the tunnel again this morning and called out to my brother. There was no response,” Ram told the Post on Sunday morning. “My hope is fading. We know nothing about the conditions inside the tunnel.”
Ram and relatives of other missing workers arrived in the Trishuli area on Sunday morning. On Saturday, he entered the tunnel himself in search of his brother and the others.
He managed to go around 100 metres inside, despite thick mud deposited by the floodwaters.
“The mud came up to my chest. I went about 100 meters inside and shouted as loudly as I could, but there was no response,” he said. “Then I had to come back out.”
Since the first day of the disaster, Ram has repeatedly appealed to the Nepali Army to rescue his brother and other workers trapped inside. The army has told him that rescue efforts are underway.
“The rescue could not happen quickly,” he said. “I have now heard that a Chinese team has also arrived. I just hope we can soon find out what the situation is inside the tunnel.”
Ram and Prabin had both been working at the Upper Trishuli-1 project in Hakubesi, Rasuwa. Ram had been employed there for about a year.

Prabin, who had recently completed Grade 12, had been preparing to go abroad for work. His paperwork was being processed in Kathmandu, and he had joined his elder brother at the hydropower project to earn money for his planned journey overseas.
“Rather than sitting idle while his documents were being processed, I brought him to work with me so he could earn some money,” Ram said.
Back home in Jumla, their parents have been anxiously waiting for news. Ram said he has been trying to reassure them that search efforts are continuing.

He said he had received information that around 25 people from Patarasi, including his brother, were trapped inside the tunnel. Relatives of the missing workers have been calling him constantly, asking for updates.
The day before the flood hit the Bhotekoshi river system, Ram had left Hakubesi for Kathmandu, leaving his younger brother at the project site.
On the day of the disaster, Prabin and around 25 other workers from Jumla were working inside Tunnel No 216 of the Upper Trishuli-1 project.

The project is being built by Sinohydro Corporation. Ram had joined the project about a year ago and brought his younger brother to Rasuwa around a month ago because the work offered relatively good earnings. /dl

articles.title: Torrential rain to lash South Korea on Monday
articles.summary: SEOUL — Heavy rain accompanied by gusty winds, thunder and lightning is forecast across most of South Korea through Monday. The central west coast is expected to bear the brunt of the…

blocks.text: SEOUL — Heavy rain accompanied by gusty winds, thunder and lightning is forecast across most of South Korea through Monday. The central west coast is expected to bear the brunt of the downpours.

Rain was already falling in southern parts of the country Sunday, where heavy rain warnings were in effect as of 5 p.m., according to the Korea Meteorological Administration. The rain will spread across most of the country by Monday, hitting hardest in southern Gyeonggi Province, southwestern Gangwon Province, the central Chungcheong region and North Jeolla Province.

South Chungcheong Province and the cities of Daejeon and Sejong are expected to receive 80-150 millimeters of rain through Tuesday — totals could climb past 250 millimeters along the coast and 200 millimeters inland. North Chungcheong Province could also see up to 200 millimeters.

Southern Gyeonggi is expected to get 50-100 millimeters, with certain areas topping 150. Seoul, Incheon, northern Gyeonggi and Gangwon Province are in line for 30-80 millimeters, though mountainous parts of southern Gangwon could get more than 120.
In the greater Seoul area, the heaviest rain is expected between the predawn hours and Monday morning.
The rain should end in southern regions and on Jeju Island by Monday night but will linger over central parts of the country into Tuesday morning.
The weather agency warned of possible damage from the downpours, saying rainfall will vary sharply from one area to the next with strong bursts alternating with lulls.

The rain will do little to cool the southern half of the country, where heat advisories remain in place. The heat index there and on Jeju is expected to reach around 33 degrees Celsius in the coming days. /dl

articles.title: Grand Canyon flash flood: About 15 people missing
articles.summary: LOS ANGELES — About 15 people may be missing after a flash flood in Grand Canyon National Park, the National Park Service said in a statement Sunday. The floods hit the Bright Angel Canyon and…

blocks.text: LOS ANGELES — About 15 people may be missing after a flash flood in Grand Canyon National Park, the National Park Service said in a statement Sunday.

The floods hit the Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area on Saturday, the service said, adding that it was working with Arizona authorities to evacuate people and account for missing individuals.
Earlier, the park service said that more than 20 people were believed missing.
There were no confirmed deaths or injuries, the park service said in an email.
The flash flood, which began about 2:30 pm on Saturday, was caused by rainfall on the Kaibab Plateau, it said.
As of Sunday morning, 62 people have been evacuated, and others were scheduled to be evacuated, it said.

More thunderstorms and heavy rainfall were possible through Monday, possibly leading to “additional flash flooding, debris flows, rockfall and changing trail and river conditions,” the park service warned. /dl

articles.title: Google Maps renames Lake Ontario ‘Lake America’ in US — but not Canada
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — Google redesignated Lake Ontario as “Lake America” on maps seen by US users Sunday after President Donald Trump announced he was renaming the body of water, with a…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON — Google redesignated Lake Ontario as “Lake America” on maps seen by US users Sunday after President Donald Trump announced he was renaming the body of water, with a Canadian official slamming the cross-border tensions as “absolutely backwards.”
People in Canada will still see the body of water labeled Lake Ontario, the Indigenous-rooted name used since the 17th century, on their devices and computers, the US-based tech giant said.

The nomenclatural spat erupted as the latest element of Trump’s “America First” narrative, with the longtime allies ramping up a trade war that has seen Washington and Ottawa slap tit-for-tat tariffs on each other.

Trump launched a new salvo of criticism Sunday, taking aim at the auto industry — even as the United States and Canada have deeply interconnected auto manufacturing sectors, with a hefty amount of Canadian parts used in US-made vehicles.
“I don’t want Canadian cars, I don’t want Canadian parts, I don’t want Canadian anything,” Trump seethed in a post on his Truth Social platform.
Apple as of Sunday has maintained the name Lake Ontario on its Maps app, which comes installed on iPhones in the United States.
Google said it made its change in line with the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the official federal database for geographic names.

“Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using Maps in the US will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said on its blog.
The change mirrors Trump’s unilateral altering of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in January 2025 — a move Mexico has also rejected.
Ontario is the smallest by surface area of the five Great Lakes, which straddle the Canada-US border between Ontario province and the US state of New York.
The province’s premier, Doug Ford, offered fresh criticism Sunday of the trade dispute and Trump’s lake name change.

“It’s absolutely backwards. It was like something out of (US comedy TV show) ‘Saturday Night Live’ when he signed a document saying — changed to ‘Lake America.’ No one’s going to call it Lake of America,” Ford told ABC talk show “This Week.”
“It’s just so disappointing,” he said.

Ford also warned that while a trade war would harm both countries, “it’d be definitely devastating on the US” given that Canada has been by far the largest purchaser of US vehicles. Should those buys dry up, US auto factories would be hit hard.
“A tariff on Canada is nothing more than a tax on American people,” he said. “It’s probably the worst move you could ever do.”
In his comments, Trump highlighted the success of Ford Motor Company’s plant in the Detroit area that is working overtime to assemble F-150 pickup trucks.
“They’ve been ripping us off for decades, and it’s going to stop,” he said of Canada.
Many F-150 engines are built just across the border in Windsor, Ontario. But Trump has threatened to double tariffs on such auto parts to 50 percent, along with other Canadian products.
Canada has slapped its own counter-tariffs on US goods ranging between 15 and 50 percent, intensifying the trade war between the historically close allies. /dl
