articles.title: How the US-Canada trade war is being felt on both sides of the border
articles.summary: The US-Canada trade war is being felt on both sides of the border.

blocks.text: The US and Canada appear no closer to resolving their ongoing trade dispute.
Tensions have been simmering between the two neighbours since President Donald Trump returned to the White House just over 18 months ago, and unleashed a wide-ranging global programme of tariffs.
Canada was one of the first countries the Trump administration hit with levies, and is one of two countries to respond with its own reciprocal measures.
Currently, the US has hit Canada's key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles with tariffs, and last week imposed an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods.
Canada has hit back with its own counter-tariffs on American goods, announcing on Tuesday what it calls a "dollar-for-dollar" and "strategic" retaliation designed to match the US tariffs.
With no resolution in sight, how has this enduring trade war affected Canada and the US, and what could come next?
Here are five charts to help break it all down.
The US economy is much larger and the impact of Canada's counter-tariffs won't be as stark.
But some states will feel the pain of Canada's retaliation more than others, with tariffs levied on C$28bn worth of US goods from steel to furniture, cosmetics and toilet paper, as of 8 September.
According to data by Statistics Canada, the swing state of Ohio will be hardest hit, with C$3.2bn - or 12% - of its exports soon to be tariffed by Canada, followed by Illinois and Pennsylvania.

For Ohio, it's the tax on steel that will particularly hurt, as well as the tax on laundry machines. In Illinois, where farm equipment giant John Deere is based, it will be the new tariffs on farm and construction equipment.

Derek Holt, an economist with Scotiabank, noted that Canada's counter-tariffs appear to be "very deliberately oriented" towards some swing states that could decide the US balance of power in the upcoming midterm elections.
Some businesses are adapting to find customers elsewhere.

Matteo Sgaramella, who owns Toronto-based menswear clothing company Outclass, told the BBC he has started attending trunk shows in Paris instead of New York, helping him reach more customers in Europe.
"The reception has been amazing," he said, adding that some European stores are particularly enthused about supporting Canadian products due to the ongoing trade war with the US.
"We're kind of seen as the one country that's kind of standing up to the Americans right now," Sgaramella said.
Other businesses, however, are struggling to diversify their trade, particularly in Ontario manufacturing sectors that are deeply integrated with the US.
A recent report by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce pointed out three such regions in Ontario - Oshawa, London and Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo - as being particularly vulnerable.

"These cities remain heavily tied to the US market, while growth in exports outside the US has been limited or insufficient to offset broader weakness in trade activity and local economic conditions," the report said.
While some businesses are lagging, foreign direct investment into Canada hit C$96.8 billion in 2025, the highest inflow of capital to the Canadian economy since 2007.
Canada's economy also strongly rebounded in the second quarter of 2026 to 3.3% growth in the country's GDP, thanks to a jump in exports and domestic investment.
These latest figures have warded off recession concerns, at least for now.

Carney is hoping to attract even more investment. In September, his government will host the first-ever Canada Investment Summit, bringing major investors, CEOs and business leaders to Toronto for two days.

articles.title: US strikes Iran for first time in a month
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — The United States said Sunday it had carried out strikes on Iranian rocket launchers on a small island in the Strait of Hormuz, its first attacks on Iran since late July.…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — The United States said Sunday it had carried out strikes on Iranian rocket launchers on a small island in the Strait of Hormuz, its first attacks on Iran since late July.

“Earlier today, US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island,” a US Central Command spokesman said, adding that Iran’s Revolutionary Guards “were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz.”
The strikes came shortly after the US-Iran war hit the six-month mark, and at a time when hostilities had been subsiding.
In recent weeks, the Trump administration has prioritized “economic warfare” over military strikes against Iran.

Iran has effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic sea lane through which one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the United States and Israel started hostilities with airstrikes on Iran on February 28.
“Last week, CENTCOM completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes,” said Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for US Central Command.
“US forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” he said.
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war to no avail.

While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming and Washington has since declared “economic warfare” against Tehran.
A US naval counterblockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran amid a shortfall of domestic production, as the US ramps up pressure on its foe.
The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks, mainly around the Strait of Hormuz, have dimmed the prospects of a final peace agreement.
In a statement on Friday, US Senator Jack Reed criticized President Donald Trump over the war.
“Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved,” said Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
“Indeed, he has weakened our position in the Middle East and the world significantly.” /apl

articles.title: At least 2 dead and several missing or unaccounted for after Grand Canyon flash flood, park service says
articles.summary: At least two bodies have been recovered since a major flash flood swept through the Grand Canyon, park officials said Monday, as search and recovery efforts continued for about 15 people still…

image.caption: This U.S. National Park Service photo shows remnants of a destroyed footbridge along Bright Angel Creek in the Grand Canyon following a flash flood Saturday. (James Thompson/National Park Service/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

At least two bodies have been recovered since a major flash flood swept through the Grand Canyon, park officials said Monday, as search and recovery efforts continued for about 15 people still missing.
Flooding knocks out water pipeline serving tourists and residents at national park, officials say

Weather forecasters warned rain and thunderstorms could bring more flooding to the popular tourist attraction from where scores of visitors were evacuated following the storm-fuelled flood Saturday in Bright Angel Creek.

The deluge also seriously damaged the only water pipeline in the canyon, leading to emergency water restrictions for year-round residents, and tourists have been barred from staying at lodges and hotels inside the park.

Video from the area showed a force of muddy, debris-filled floodwaters carrying what appeared to be remnants of a bunkhouse and rocks through the canyon. Four "waves of rainfall" over two creek drainages during the weekend resulted in rapid onset flash flooding, the National Weather Service said.
The National Park Service says the area gets less than 25 centimetres of rain per year on average.
Bodies recovered

The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the park service said without providing additional details. At least one other body has been recovered, according to a statement posted on Facebook by the Grand Canyon National Park. It provided no other details
Torrents of water wiped out footbridges over the creek and significantly altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and creating what appeared to be a new river rapid.
"This is a reminder of what a dynamic and active landscape Grand Canyon is," said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University.

Popular tourist spots including the Bright Angel Campground, Phantom Ranch and parts of the North Kaibab trail remained closed on Sunday while park officials surveyed the damage, the park said. Rafting trips on the Colorado River have also been halted for now.
'Up, up, up, up!'
Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with a group of fellow physicians and a park ranger when the downpour started.
"We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere," he said.

Later, as they made their way toward Phantom Ranch, a colleague shouted "Up, up, up, up!" as a one-metre debris wall headed toward them and they ran up into a patch of cacti, he said. They were finally rescued by helicopter that evening after making it to the Phantom Ranch area, he said.

Erica Viola said she was at Bright Angel campground when the rain started Saturday afternoon, and she and about 50 other hikers watched the creek rise and then debris start to flow by, including what looked like a bunkhouse.
The group was taken by helicopter to safety, ending her adventure two days early, Viola said.
About 1.2 to 2.5 centimetres of rain fell within about 30 minutes in the rocky area where there's a steep drop in elevation, said National Weather Service meteorologist Justin Johndrow in Flagstaff.
"Most of it ran off instantly," Johndrow said.
He said the flooding happened on the north side of the Grand Canyon, where Bright Angel Creek comes from the North Rim down to the Colorado River, dropping about 1,830 metres.
More rain and thunderstorms were possible for the area into Monday.

articles.title: Hikers feared missing after flash flooding hits Grand Canyon
articles.summary: More than 20 people are thought to be unaccounted for after flash flooding on Saturday.

blocks.text: More than 20 people are thought to be missing or unaccounted for after flash flooding swept through parts of the Grand Canyon.
It hit at around 14:30 local time (22:30 BST) on Saturday in Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area, according to the National Park Service (NPS).
Sixty-two people have so far been airlifted out of the area, with more expected to follow. No injuries have been reported.
The NPS said flooding had caused significant damage in some areas and that trails in the area have been closed.

It warned that more thunderstorms and heavy rainfall were forecast for Sunday and Monday, which could lead to "additional flash flooding, debris flows, rockfall and changing trail and river conditions".
The NPS asked anyone who knew of hikers or backpackers who were in the inner canyon along the Bright Angel Creek corridor on Saturday to get in touch.
The Grand Canyon is one of the most popular national parks in the US, with about five million people visiting each year. The Bright Angel trail is its most popular hike.
The Phantom Ranch area can only be reached by foot, mule or by rafting the Colorado River, according to Grand Canyon National Park Lodges.

articles.title: US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak Island in first known attack in weeks
articles.summary: Iran says the attack killed some civilians and is the first known US strike on Iran since late July.

blocks.text: Larak Island is just offshore from the key port of Bandar Abbas and sits right on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global shipping.
Iran is currently making tanker traffic pass by this island for checking and reportedly forcing vessels to pay $2m (£1.5m) to cross.

Hossein Mohebbi, the IRGC's spokesman called the attack a "strategic and fatal mistake by the Trump regime" and said that the "enemy will pay the consequences of this miscalculation in both the economic and military fields".
Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, said earlier that the attack was carried out by drones. Reports indicate that two people were killed and two others injured, it said.

Trump ​said last week that all mines‌ placed in the Strait of Hormuz by Iran as part of its efforts to blockade the route had been detonated or removed. He said Iran had been warned that any ship ​or boat deploying new mines would be ​destroyed.
Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi described Trump's claim as a "propaganda" deception.
Iran is facing renewed economic pressure after Washington announced a fresh sanctions campaign on 24 August aimed at further isolating Tehran and expanding secondary sanctions against its allies.

Iranian officials and state media have largely dismissed the campaign as a continuation of previous US economic measures, which they argue followed Washington's military failure in the recent conflict.

The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic. The Iran war has now crossed its six-month mark.
Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel through before the war began.

blocks.text: Number of Australians missing in Nepal rises to 43
The total number of Australians missing in the deadly Nepal floods is now 43.
The department of foreign affairs has received more than 650 calls in relation to the disaster.
Nepali and Chinese authorities confirmed an updated death toll of at least 810 on Sunday.
More than 3,000 people are believed missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas on Wednesday engulfed Gyirong port on the Nepal-China border.

blocks.text: Australian personnel still unable to access Nepal flood zone
Australian personnel has not been able to get access to the Nepal flood zone yet, the assistant minister for immigration, Matt Thistlethwaite, confirmed.
Speaking on ABC’s Radio National, Thistlethwaite said roads remained cut off in the disaster and most of the telecommunication infrastructure was down.
double quotation markThere has been about eight power stations that have been affected as well, so it’s very difficult to get into the area.
He said the Australian government had “offered support” to the Chinese government, with six Australians missing on the Chinese side of the border.
double quotation markThey’ve said at this stage they don’t require that support.

blocks.caption: A man walks through the sludge in the aftermath of flash floods at Trishuli in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on 30 August. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Australia to send $3m in additional aid to Nepal
The government will send $3m in additional aid to Nepal, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, has announced, bringing the total package to $8m.
Of this additional aid, the Australian defence force will coordinate $2m worth of hygiene kits, solar lighting and other emergency supplies following a request from Nepal’s government.
double quotation markThe Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) will transport the first of these supplies from Queensland in the coming days.
In addition, the government will donate $1m to the Emergency Action Alliance appeal, which has reached $1.4m in donations from the public.

There is now 14 Australian personnel on the ground in Kathmandu – including crisis response, consular officers and Australian federal police – to assist staff in the humanitarian disaster. Two more will be deployed this week.

“I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak island. Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guards Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz,” the official said.

Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported the US had carried out ‌a drone strike on the island.

US president Donald Trump said last week that all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait of Hormuz and Iran had been told that any ship or boat placing new mines will be destroyed.
The last known ‌US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks, with Washington threatening ​to impose costly sanctions on countries that support Iran.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. The Iran war has now ⁠crossed its six-month mark.
US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on ​Lebanon have killed thousands ​and displaced millions. Eighteen US service ​members have been killed in the conflict.

articles.title: 39 kg of bread dumped in park roadside in Japan
articles.summary: JAPAN — A total of 39 kilograms of bread was recently dumped along a roadside in a national park in western Japan, prompting police to investigate who discarded it and why. The loaves were left near…

blocks.text: JAPAN — A total of 39 kilograms of bread was recently dumped along a roadside in a national park in western Japan, prompting police to investigate who discarded it and why.

The loaves were left near guardrails in Daisen-Oki National Park in Tottori Prefecture between Aug. 14 and 20. The incident has prompted the spread of fake images and videos attempting to link the dumping to a sharp increase in bear encounters in Japan over the past year.
“When I first heard of the reports, my head was full of question marks,” said Koji Iwaihara, director of the Natural Parks Foundation’s Tottori branch.
The bread was initially believed to have been used as bait for cameras livestreaming images of animals, but no such equipment was found.
The foundation later came to believe the bread had been left to feed animals after 1.3 kilograms of chicken was found in the same area.
Bear bait?
Bread was also found scattered around the prefecture’s Hakuto coast, but the brand appears to be different from that found in the national park.
Neither the bread nor the chicken was poisoned.
The prefecture has since installed security cameras in Daisen-Oki National Park, but no further dumping has been reported.

“I don’t understand why it was left on the side of the road” as opposed to inside the mountain, said Tottori Gov. Shinji Hirai, questioning the theory that the food may have been placed there as bear bait.
If that really is the aim, “it may become a dangerous precedent as bears become accustomed to the taste of bread,” he added.
Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated videos and images showing a bear looking at or eating the bread have spread on social media.
The prefectural government plans to ask social media platforms to remove them over concerns the false content could cause reputational damage.
Prefectural police said the perpetrator may have violated a law against illegal dumping or regulations governing national parks. /cb

articles.title: Fact check: Germany's Merz misstates record in ARD interview
articles.summary: Migration, debt and electric vehicles: Chancellor Friedrich Merz made several misleading claims in his ARD summer interview. DW Fact check reviewed them live.

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke with ARD's Markus Preiss in this year's summer interviewImage: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

blocks.text: As part of an annual tradition, Chancellor Friedrich Merz sat down with public broadcaster ARD on Sunday evening for a wide-ranging summer interview. Amid drooping poll numbers, Merz tried to use the interview to tout his government's work on economic, migration and energy policy.
At the same time, Merz made a number of misleading claims, often overstating his administration's work and misrepresenting climate science.
DW Fact check, in collaboration with colleagues across the ARD fact-checking network, reviewed Merz's interview live.

blocks.caption: Asylum applications have dropped sharply, but not by 60% as Merz claimedImage: Joko/IMAGO

blocks.text: Did Merz cut asylum numbers by 60%?

Claim: "One of the main issues in the last federal election campaign was the migration crisis, and together with the federal government, we've been able to reduce the numbers by over 60% in just over a year."
Verdict: Misleading
This is misleading for several reasons — it is both questionable what exactly Merz meant by migration, and also not clear to which period he is referring.

The number of asylum-seekers in Germany has fallen significantly, but not to the extent Merz said. According to the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF), a total of 56,547 asylum applications were filed in the first half of 2026, including 39,646 first-time applications. Compared with the same period last year, the number of first-time applications fell by 35.4%.
In July 2026, the number of first-time asylum applications was 4,311, around 48% below the figure for the same month last year.

To reach 60%, Merz was likely referencing a figure that compares initial applications from August 2025 to the same month a year prior. That decline, is indeed, 58%, close to what Merz stated. But a more complete comparison of January through August 2025 to the prior year shows just a 51% decline.

In addition, the downward trend began even before the Merz government took office in May 2025. After the fall of Syrian ruler Bashar Assad in December 2024, the number of asylum-seekers in Germany declined. At the European level, the number of asylum applications also fell in the first half of 2025.

Official statistics also show a decline in general migration. According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 235,000 more people immigrated to Germany in 2025 than emigrated. This means that net immigration was 45% below the previous year's figure of 430,000 people. But that's mostly due to the number of arrivals falling, while the number of departures remained almost stable.

blocks.caption: Merz cast his vote for a historic amendment to Germany's debt brake in March 2025, ahead of taking officeImage: MICHAEL KAPPELER/AFP

blocks.text: Germany's debt, in context

Claim: "We are still one of the least indebted countries in Europe. We are still a country that has by far the best credit rating of any European nation. No one doubts the debt sustainability of our country or our economy; we are operating within reasonable limits here."
There are three important ways to measure how much debt EU countries hold: debt-to-GDP ratio, deficit spending and credit rating.

On the first — debt-to-GDP ratio, or how a country's total debt compares to its annual economic output — Germany receives a failing grade. The eurozone requires countries to keep this ratio below 60%. Germany and 11 other countries are above that limit, versus 15 countries which are in compliance, putting Germany smack in the middle of the eurozone.

On the second — government deficits, or a country's net borrowing — Germany is just scraping by. The eurozone asks its members to keep this figure below 3%. Germany's net borrowing is at 2.7%, joining 16 other countries that are also below the limit. Of the 17 countries that meet that requirement, Germany comes the second closest to hitting the 3% limit.

As for credit rating — a grade from investors on how likely a country is to repay its debts — Germany does indeed earn the highest marks possible. But it shares that grade with several other countries. There are only 11 countries in the world with an AAA rating from S&P: Germany joins Denmark, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and Switzerland in earning the grade.

In 2009, Germany amended its constitution by adding a so-called "debt brake," mandating the government to keep deficits to 0.35% of GDP. In 2020, that restriction was suspended to deal with the COVID pandemic and then again in 2022 and 2025 to allow for an increase in defense spending.

blocks.caption: Merz claimed the CO2 balance of electric vehicles is often overstated — but the data tells a different storyImage: MiS/IMAGO

blocks.text: Real CO2 balance of electric cars

Claim: "At the European level, the issue with internal combustion engines has nothing to do with CO2 emissions. We want climate-friendly and climate-neutral cars, but we don't want to dictate the technology — it's not up to politicians to decide that. What matters is how much CO2 such a car emits, and the CO2 balance of electric mobility isn't as rosy as it's often portrayed."

Battery electric vehicles produce, on average, 73% less CO2 emissions than internal combustion engine vehicles, according to the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), a US-based nonprofit think tank.

Battery electric vehicles do generate about 40% higher production emissions, mostly because of the processes involved in manufacturing the battery, though these are usually offset after about one or two years of driving.

Merz was likely referring to a new paper from researchers at the Technical University of Munich, which right-wing media seized on this week. The paper, which took an average of 19 studies, claimed that battery electric vehicles only reduce CO2 emissions by 41%, compared to traditional cars.

But there's a key issue with the TUM paper: including all those studies means older analyses with outdated electricity mixes are given equal weight. The ICCT analysis, on the other hand, uses a more current estimate.
Either way, there's an overwhelming scientific consensus that electric vehicles are better for the environment than traditional cars.
Is Germany's weak economy boosting the right-wing AfD?

articles.title: Headteacher saves 900 children from deadly flash flood in Nepal
articles.summary:
Rajendra Dawadi ordered students to higher ground with moments to spare after receiving warnings from upstream

A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a…

blocks.text: A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.
Rajendra Dawadi decided to halt classes and order children to higher ground after receiving warnings about the scale of the flooding heading their way.

Dawadi, the headteacher at Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot, which has 1,600 pupils, said he had received four warnings from different people within minutes, including one from Betrawati, a town directly upstream.

blocks.caption: Rajendra Dawadi, the headteacher of Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school in Nuwakot

blocks.text: This prompted him to take immediate action. “I decided I shouldn’t delay any more,” he told the BBC. “Even if the flood was not coming, it was just a matter of a single day’s classes.”
Dawadi said during the evacuation of the school he saw a hostel building about 100 metres from the river being engulfed by the torrent of flood water.
“If we had made the decision 10 minutes later, all of us, including the students and me, would not be able to speak to you today,” he said.
One student said Dawadi’s decision had saved their lives with moments to spare. Yunisha, 16, told reporters: “I, along with my friends, survived by just 10 seconds.”

She described the children running up a muddy path to escape as water and debris inundated the town. “Within no time, the bazaar was swept away in front of my eyes,” she said. She was reunited with her family three days later.
At least 69 schools have been destroyed or damaged by the floods, affecting nearly 19,000 children, according to the charity Save the Children.
In Dhading, one of the areas worst hit by the floods, a group of schoolchildren survived the disaster when they left their classroom for their lunch break.
Others in the area escaped when teachers told them to quickly evacuate classrooms just before the waters came crashing in.
The mother of one child told the Associated Press that teachers had warned students: “There is a flood and you should leave bags and tiffins. That’s how they managed to survive.”
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. The country said on Sunday 2,502 people, including 592 foreigners, were out of contact. It reported an updated death toll of 781 people.

The disaster, which struck the Nepal-Tibet border region of the Himalayas on Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a wall of water and debris cascading downstream, the US Geological Survey said.

Nepal’s foreign minister has called for a global response to the climate crisis, saying the Nepali people had disproportionately become “major victims of climate change” despite having contributed a fraction of the planet’s fossil fuel emissions.

articles.title: Fifteen Britons among 261 foreigners missing in China after floods
articles.summary: Total number of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal at 48 as Beijing mobilises more than 2,100 rescue workers

blocks.text: Fifteen British nationals are reported to be missing in China as the search continues for survivors of the devastating flooding in Nepal and Tibet.

Nepali and Chinese authorities confirmed an updated death toll of at least 810 on Sunday. More than 3,000 people are believed missing after flash floods brought upon by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas on Wednesday engulfed Gyirong port on the Nepal-China border.

The 15 missing British people are among 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries missing in China, according to figures released by Chinese authorities, bringing the total of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal to 48. The Tibet autonomous region’s government said the total missing there also included 104 Nepalis, 49 people from India, 33 from Latvia and 18 from the US.

Thirty-three British people had already been declared missing on the Nepal side of the border. Some were on a pilgrimage at the time of the flood, including Hemangini Jitendra Patel and Hema Sunil Amin, two sisters who were last seen on the Friendship Bridge on the border.

The figure for missing Americans has been disputed by the US state department, which declared on Sunday that at least 85 US citizens were missing. The department’s spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said getting accurate information from the region had been difficult, “made even more so by the devastation and the remoteness that we see”.

Chinese authorities have said at least 16 people have died on their side of the border. But there are concerns over a possible lack of transparency from the Chinese government, which has prevented footage of the floods from being shared in the countryand may have downplayed the casualties.

Police in Nepal said 794 people had been confirmed to have died there and at least 2,742 injured. Numerous areas remain at risk of fresh flooding and people who have returned to their homes have been told to remain alert and be prepared to evacuate again at short notice.
Rescue efforts have been affected by the threat of landslides and dangerous weather as well as confusion over which side of the border victims had been on when the waters struck.

Chinese state television reported that officials in Beijing, far better resourced than their Nepalese counterparts, had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated more than 220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts.

Equipment and supplies have been airdropped to frontline workers, while Chinese soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing, CCTV said. The Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had already travelled to the region.

Numerous countries have pledged to help Nepal, including the US which has offered $3.6m in humanitarian aid, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households”, on top of $500,000 previously pledged, and Australia, which will donate more than $3m in assistance.
Britain has committed £5m to Nepal and sent a rapid deployment team, which arrived in Kathmandu on Saturday.

A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: “We are working around the clock to support British nationals and their families affected by the devastating floods on the Nepal-China border. We are coordinating closely with the Nepali and Chinese authorities and have deployed consular support staff to the region to ensure British nationals can access support.”

articles.title: German churches speak out against AfD ahead of state election
articles.summary: As the far-right AfD party leads the polls ahead of Sunday’s election in Saxony-Anhalt, Church leaders warn against downplaying its 'ethnonationalist' agenda.

image.caption: Saxony-Anhalt's churches have been reminding voters of their Christian values ahead of the state election on September 6Image: Christoph Strack/DW

blocks.text: Flags flutter in the wind outside Magdeburg's Catholic cathedral. "Love thy neighbor, dialogue, human dignity, solidarity. VOTE CONSCIOUSLY!", they proclaim. Just a few minutes' walk away, a sign on the building of the Protestant Cathedral Congregation reads: "DIVERSITY IS DIVINE." Other Protestant churches across the region display banners reading "Heart Instead of Hate."

For many months now, warnings about the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is particularly strong in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, have been part of everyday church life. During a sermon at a pilgrimage event in September 2025, Magdeburg Bishop Gerhard Feige remarked almost in passing that pilgrims of hope do not cast their votes on a whim, "into the blue." He was interrupted by prolonged applause — blue is the AfD's party color.

The AfD holds a commanding lead in the polls ahead of the state election on September 6. The prospect of a government led by the party alone appears increasingly plausible. At the same time, Germany's domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
Churches speak out against AfD
In Saxony-Anhalt, 10% of the population is Protestant and 3% is Catholic; only a few thousand people belong to the Muslim or Jewish faiths.

More than 85% of the state's 2.1 million residents have no religious affiliation, compared with a national average of 47%. Nevertheless, the churches play an important role as defenders of democracy — and that, apparently, is precisely what troubles the AfD.

With its so-called government program, adopted at a state party conference in April, the party launched a broadside against both the Protestant and Catholic churches. The program calls for an end to all state payments to the two churches and for the abolition of church tax collection by public authorities, a service for which the churches themselves pay.

blocks.caption: Bishop Gerhard Feige has said he could never have imagined that so many people could once again be so easily led astray by the far rightImage: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In cases of so-called church asylum, where refugees seek shelter on church premises for fear of renewed persecution in their countries of origin, the AfD is calling for churches to be held financially accountable on a "permanent" basis.

The Protestant Academy of Saxony-Anhalt should also no longer receive any state funding whatsoever. The reason, according to the AfD, is its "political agitation in line with the established parties: climate dogma, gender ideology, and the rainbow cult." The academy is said to advocate "unchecked mass immigration." Yet in scarcely any German federal state is the proportion of foreign nationals as low as it is in Saxony-Anhalt.
From estrangement to open confrontation

The sharpness of the criticism goes far beyond anything typically heard from other regional branches of the Alternative for Germany or from the party's national leadership. Long gone are the days when representatives of the then-emerging party complained about not being invited to church congresses or Catholic conventions.

In February 2024, the plenary assembly of the German Catholic Bishops' Conference unanimously adopted a declaration entitled "Ethnic Nationalism and Christianity are Incompatible." In it, the bishops identified an ethnonationalist mindset within the AfD and spoke of a "genuine right-wing extremism." The document was prompted by the state elections scheduled to take place later that year in the eastern German states of Thuringia, Saxony, and Brandenburg. Now, in September 2026, elections are due to follow in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
At present, the confrontation between the AfD and the churches is nowhere more intense than in Saxony-Anhalt.
Germany's churches get creative about new ways to worship

For Bishop Feige, the AfD's current direction is "without question" an expression of ethnonationalism. "Until now, Saxony-Anhalt's motto has been 'Thinking Modern'. The AfD wants to replace it with 'Thinking German'," he told DW. "The AfD's election posters speak a very clear language: 'Save your country', 'Take your country back', 'Deport from day one!' What else could that be but ethnonationalism?"

The 74-year-old said he "could never have imagined that so many people today could once again be so easily led astray, or that arsonists, pied pipers and respectable-looking agitators could emerge, and that so many would fall for them."

As an example, Feige cited the so-called flag assembly that the AfD wants to reintroduce in the state's schools: the raising of the flag and the singing of the national anthem. "This existed during the Nazi era and was later adopted by the GDR," he said, referring to the former East Germany. "And now it is supposed to return? I find that inconceivable."

blocks.caption: Bishop Friedrich Kramer said Christian messages should not be interpreted as an endorsement of any particular political partyImage: Martin Schutt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Both major Christian churches emphasize they are speaking out not against a particular party, but in defense of a Christian view of humanity. Whether the issue is climate protection and the safeguarding of creation or the treatment of strangers, the churches' interventions are "primarily not political messages, but Christian ones, and should not be interpreted as an endorsement of any particular political party," Friedrich Kramer, bishop of the Protestant Church in central Germany, recently told the online magazine Die Eule.
Religious freedom, according to the AfD

Jews and Jewish life, incidentally, are never mentioned in the government program. By contrast, Islam appears repeatedly. According to the AfD, it will "restore religious freedom to appropriate limits." Islam is described as a "religion alien to our culture." Freedom of religion, the party argues, does not oblige Germans to "fulfill every demand of the Islamic lobby."

Representatives of the state's Jewish association, which includes the synagogue of the Jewish community of Halle targeted in a 2019 right-wing extremist attack, as well as representatives of the largest mosque congregation in the state, declined to comment when asked.

Notably, the AfD's platform speaks of a "Christian mission" that, in its view, the churches supported by church tax, which it labels the "church-tax churches," no longer fulfill. This evokes the support that US President Donald Trump receives from influential evangelical and conservative Christian groups in the United States. In Saxony-Anhalt, however, there is only a limited presence of comparable religious milieus.
Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough?
Why bishops are sounding the alarm

"A government involving the AfD would have devastating consequences," Kramer said. That is why, he added, cultural institutions and civil society organizations are joining forces to warn against the AfD.

His Catholic counterpart, Feige, likewise cautioned against "downplaying" the prospect of an AfD-led government. During the election campaign, he said, the party is presenting itself "with messianic ideas" and promoting slogans such as "Everything will be fine" or "Anything is possible."

Because the AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, "comes across as highly polished and enthusiastic," some people ask what could possibly be "right-wing extremist or dangerous" about him. "But behind him stand forces that give cause for concern," said Feige. "If an AfD single-party government comes to power here, it will be a pilot project. Then Saxony-Anhalt will become a gateway to national politics."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: EU wants drones to spray pesticides — but it could backfire
articles.summary: The EU wants to lift a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air, allowing drones to be used for greater precision. But experts warn the plan could lead to even more pesticides being used…

image.caption: Using drones to spray pesticides is common in other parts of the world — for example on this rice field in ChinaImage: CFOTO/IMAGO

blocks.text: In theory, the idea doesn't sound bad: Instead of using tractors to spray large quantities of pesticides over fields, drones could precisely spray herbicides, fungicides and insecticides only where they are actually needed.

The plan would be to scan a field, identify affected areas and treat them selectively — significantly reducing pesticide use, according to the European Union's Omnibus X legislative package, which aims to simplify EU food and feed safety rules. After all, the bloc aims to halve the use of chemicals for plant protection by 2030.

Until now, however, the EU had a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air over agricultural land. Exceptions applied only to difficult-to-work terrain, such as steep vineyard slopes. Omnibus X is now set to change that. In May, the European Council gave the legislative package the green light.
Drone use doesn't automatically mean less pesticides

"I think it makes sense in principle to distinguish spray drones from conventional aerial application from a regulatory perspective," said Thomas Daum, an agricultural economist and human ecologist at the School of Global Studies at the University of Gothenburg. Daum studies new technologies and their impact on agriculture. Compared with an airplane or helicopter, he said drones can generally spray more precisely.
How toxic is the industry behind pesticides?

However, Daum also cautioned that "the drone itself does not save any pesticide." He sees potential for using drones to respond more selectively to pest infestations — and thus reduce overall pesticide use. Another advantage for farmers could be the ability to respond quickly to an infestation "even when soils are wet or in difficult-to-access terrain."

"At the same time, this flexibility lowers the barriers to treatment and could therefore also lead to spraying being carried out more frequently overall," Daum said. This could result in a technological lock-in — meaning that more efficient application could reinforce dependence on chemical crop protection.
Omnibus X aims to save administrative costs, cash
Chemical pesticides have been cause for concern for many researchers. Omnibus X is intended not only to make it easier to use spray drones, but also to change the way pesticides are approved.

When the European Council approved Omnibus X in May, a group of researchers from 27 European research institutions voiced strong criticism. Among them was Carsten Brühl, a biologist at the Institute for Environmental Sciences at the Rheinland-Pfalz Technical University of Kaiserslautern-Landau. Brühl, who studies the effects of pesticides on the environment, called Omnibus X a "deregulation package" and is deeply alarmed by it.

To date, pesticide active substances have generally been approved at the EU level for a period of 10 years. Once that period expires, manufacturers can apply for renewed approval and must once again submit data on the safety of the active substance. Since this review process was introduced in 2011, it has resulted in 59 active substances not being reapproved, as they were deemed harmful to human health and the environment.

The main aim of the Omnibus X package is to cut administrative costs, reduce bureaucracy and "ensure fair treatment for companies while safeguarding fair competition within the internal market [...]," according to an EU press release.
Researchers warn Omnibus X could harm people, environment

European scientists have been critical of the EU proposal to cut red tape and deregulate the industry, because it could lead to many active substances being approved indefinitely, eliminating regular reassessments. They also say the transition periods after an approval expires would be extended from 18 months to three years.

Brühl called the idea "reckless." It would mean that even active substances suspected of being harmful to human health could remain on the market — like weedkiller glyphosate, for example, which has been linked to cancer in humans.
Bayer wins in US court, but at what cost to public health?

But the precautionary principle should apply, Brühl argued. This political principle holds that potential harm to people and nature should be prevented proactively, even when there is not yet conclusive scientific evidence.

The scientific evidence on pesticides is already incomplete. The risks posed by an active substance are inferred from the results of laboratory studies, Brühl said. But how that substance actually behaves over the long term under different environmental conditions and in combination with other pesticides is unclear at the time of approval. That is why regular reassessments are so important.

Brühl now fears Omnibus X could undermine scientific interest in studying these active substances. It would be unappealing for researchers "to engage with a system that can no longer be influenced anyway," he said.
Agriculture can work without pesticides

Brühl is certain the new EU legislation will not lead to lower pesticide use — not even with the help of drones and more targeted spraying. This approach, for example, does not work at all with fungicides, he pointed out. Fungicides combat fungal infections and have to be applied preventively because once a plant has become infected, it can no longer be saved.

But Brühl stressed there is another way: doing without pesticides entirely, through what is known as "integrated pest management." And this isn't some hippie eco-fantasy, but rather a concept for the sustainable management of harmful organisms enshrined in German law in 2012.
Pesticides banned in Europe linked to bees deaths in Kenya

Shortly after the European Council gave the green light to Omnibus X and its new rules on drones and pesticides in May, the Scientific Advisory Board of Germany's National Action Plan for the Sustainable Use of Plant Protection Products reminded the German government of its own law in a statement. Brühl was the lead author.

Researchers wrote that integrated pest management calls for the use of synthetic chemical pesticides only as a last resort. The goal is to secure yields and quality while also minimizing negative consequences for people and nature and preventing resistance to plant protection products. This can work if certain crop rotations are taken into account and mixed cropping is favored. Pests can be controlled by attracting natural predators through flower strips or hedges, while weeds can be removed mechanically.
The problem: Spraying pesticides is often the less time-consuming and therefore cheaper option. There is also a persistent narrative that pesticides are necessary to ensure food security.

What this narrative leaves out is that monocultures and ecosystems disrupted by pesticides make agriculture more vulnerable to changing environmental conditions. That threatens food security, said Brühl, "because you have a system in place that can't cope with climate change."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez says oil deal with Trump has ‘endless’ benefits
articles.summary:
Deal that will reportedly see US take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil has provoked outrage in her country

Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has defended her…

blocks.text: Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has defended her government’s highly controversial energy deal with Donald Trump, insisting the South American country will maintain ownership and sovereignty over its massive oil reserves.

Rodríguez, who assumed power in January after Trump ordered the abduction of the president, Nicolás Maduro, took to the airwaves on Saturday to push back against criticism of what the US president has called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
“The benefits are endless,” claimed Rodríguez, a former vice-president who Trump backed after ordering Maduro’s capture during a special forces raid on the capital, Caracas.

During a six-minute television broadcast, Venezuela’s acting leader claimed the deal would help her resource-rich country develop its economy, earn revenues of more than $209bn (£154bn), and become “an energy powerhouse”.

Rodríguez said: “As everyone knows, our country has the biggest oil reserves in the world. But having resources underground isn’t enough. We need investment, technology, infrastructure [and] production capacity to convert this wealth into wellbeing for our people.”
She added: “It’s no use having our oil reserves underground, only to appear in statistics or bookkeeping … and for us not to be able to convert and translate them into development for Venezuela.”

Trump announced the “groundbreaking” deal on Friday, calling it a “historic transaction [that] more than doubles American oil reserves … while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity”.

On Sunday, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan Oil is fill up the Strategic National Reserves which, because of Sleepy Joe Biden, has been virtually emptied.”
Trump added: “The ‘topping out’ process will begin very shortly, and is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.”

Hours after seizing Maduro on 3 January, Trump warned Rodríguez she would face an even worse fate if she failed to toe the US line. “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” Trump said.
Details of the agreement – struck during months of secret talks – remain sparse but it will reportedly see Washington take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.

The South American country has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn. Rodríguez said the deal involved 17 “strategic oilfields” where it was hoped more than 1.5m barrels could be produced each day.
But the deal has provoked outrage, both among members of Venezuela’s opposition and within the Chavismo political movement of which Rodríguez is part.
Speaking on Friday, one prominent opposition figure, who asked not to be named, called the agreement “a massive land grab” by a “a rapacious, mafioso United States”.

Writing on X, Rafael Ramírez, the former head of Venezuela’s state-owned oil company PDVSA, accused Rodríguez’s administration of “driving a dagger straight into the heart of the homeland” with the “neo-colonial” transaction. “They are handing over 65bn barrels of our reserves to the United States. That has never happened in Venezuela, and I think nowhere else in the world,” Ramírez added in an interview with the newspaper El Nacional.
On Saturday, dozens of leftwing protesters marched through Caracas with banners reading: “We are neither a colony, nor a backyard” and “Yankees go home!”
Critics of the agreement shared an ironic meme on social media suggesting the state oil company’s name should be changed from PDVSA to “PDUSA”.

In her broadcast, Rodríguez, the daughter of a Marxist guerrilla who spent years denouncing “imperialist” attempts to snatch her country’s oil reserves, countered claims she was surrendering Venezuela’s natural resources to a foreign power. She thanked Trump and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, for striking the deal but added: “There is something that must be made absolutely clear: Venezuela retains the ownership and sovereignty over its resources.”
“We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” claimed the politician, whose country was plunged into authoritarian rule and one of the world’s worst peacetime economic crises during Maduro’s 13-year rule.
The deal represents an astonishing U-turn from Rodríguez and the socialist, anti-imperialist political movement she and Maduro inherited from Hugo Chávez after his 2013 death.

In one 2024 speech, footage of which circulated on social media after Friday’s announcement, Rodríguez lambasted the Venezuelan opposition, accusing it of seeking to surrender the country’s oil, natural gas and gold reserves to their “masters” in Washington.
Last September, as the US tightened the screws on Maduro, Rodríguez told the New York Times: “The Pentagon always had a strategic objective of obtaining Venezuelan reserves.”

The deal will reportedly involve the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, which channels funds into projects seen as important for national security. It will also involve a private company owned by Alejandro Betancourt, a controversial UK-based tycoon who has emerged as a key intermediary between the Trump administration and Rodríguez and owns mansions in Oxfordshire and London.

Opposition politicians fear the deal will scupper attempts to recover Venezuela’s democracy and hold fresh presidential elections. Maduro is widely believed to have stolen the last vote, in 2024, and Rodríguez has deflected questions about a future election, saying vaguely that it will happen “some day”. Trump has also said Venezuela is “not really ready” for elections.

Writing on X, the opposition leader Juan Pablo Guanipa, said: “The only way to truly reactivate the Venezuelan economy in the long term and make this agreement benefit both parties is through a free election that leads to a representative government, clear rules of the game, rule of law, and institutions that allow our resources to be managed transparently and for the benefit of the nation.”
Without that, the energy deal was like “a skyscraper [built] on pillars of clay”, Guanipa added.

articles.title: Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates
articles.summary:
Meanwhile, Trump posts video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America sign

Donald Trump…

blocks.text: Donald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel on Saturday over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the country erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting a video of him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA.

Rhetoric over the naming of Lake Ontario is the public face of an escalating trade dispute between the US and its northern neighbor involving a 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.

Trump’s order for the US government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America by Sunday had at least one prominent impact. Google Maps had changed Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America for US users to reflect the president’s executive renaming order.

Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney has flat-out rejected the renaming, explaining that Lake Ontario derives from an Indigenous Wendat word meaning “the lake is beautiful, the lake is great” that dates back more than 400 years.
With talks to resolve the trade dispute stalled, Trump issued an executive order on Thursday directing US agencies that the lake was now Lake America.
It revived memories of a dispute earlier in his second presidency with Mexico, which saw Trump direct US agencies to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters before he signed an executive order renaming the body of water among US federal agencies.

In a statement explaining why it was acquiescing to Trump’s desired name for Lake Ontario, Google said its practice is to “reflect name changes in official government sources”. Trump’s order affects the US’s federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), “which sets the standard for official US maps”, the tech company said.

blocks.caption: Lake Ontario renamed as Lake America on US-facing Google Maps. Photograph: Google Maps

blocks.text: The Lake of Ontario’s name change “does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or ​how the rest of the ‌world refers to the ‌lake,” Google said in a statement. And it said “those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’” on Google Maps, “and those outside … the US and Canada will see both names.”

Google had done similarly in Trump’s executive order for the US government to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. US Google Map users for now see that body of water named as the “Gulf of America”.
Meanwhile, on Saturday, the US president raised the volume again by resorting to the kind of AI-generated imagery for which he has shown a penchant.

He posted one such video of an army of Canada geese with Trump-like blond hair firing rifles in protection of Lake America. He published another of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America while he danced in his distinctive to a soundtrack of the Village People hit YMCA, which he has implemented into his public appearances for years.

Across the US’s northern border, Ontario premier Doug Ford replied with a two-stories high billboard declaring “Lake Ontario. Now and Always,” near Grimsby, Ontario. Ford said Trump was trying to rename the lake because Ontario and Canada were “standing up for ourselves”, and he argued the name would outlast the president.
“Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said in a video posted on social media.
In an interview with the Associated Press earlier, Ford said the late Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over Trump’s tariff policies.
Meanwhile, Manitoba’s premier, Wab Kinew, said Trump’s Lake America provocation was akin to an aging rock band trying to revive an old hit.

“You know when, like, a rock band is really over the hill and you see them like in a casino playing some song from like 50 years ago, I think that’s the part of Donald Trump’s presidency we’re at now,” Kinew said. “Like he thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie, with the Gulf of Mexico.
“He’s trying to bring back that, and he’s trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it’s a little sad, and it’s not his best work.”

Wendat Nation grand chief Pierre Picard called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said.
Lake Ontario is one of North America’s five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie. At 7,340 sq miles, Lake Ontario is the smallest of those in terms of surface area.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet death toll rises amid new flood fears and race to free group trapped in tunnel
articles.summary: Combined toll of more than 750 dead and 3,000 people missing in Nepal and Tibet after devastating flood

blocks.text: Rescuers in Nepal and Tibet have battled through leg-sucking mud amid the threat of fresh flooding to search for thousands of people still missing after a deadly wall of water swept through the Himalayan border zone, engulfing entire villages.

The latest updates on Sunday put the number of missing at 3,048, including hundreds of foreigners. There were 768 confirmed deaths, and reports of some bodies swept downstream possibly as far as India.

Nepal said it had begun the grim task of burying some of the hundreds of bodies after first taking DNA samples so that families could later reclaim them and perform traditional funeral rites after identification.
The disaster, which struck the border on Wednesday morning, was caused by a glacial collapse, sending a wall of water and debris downstream, the US Geological Survey said.
Nepal’s foreign minister called for a global response to the climate crisis, saying the small, poor Himalayan nation was bearing a disproportionate share of its impact.
“Despite having only 0.1% contribution to the global emissions, people of Nepal have become major victims of climate change,” Shisir Khanal said on Saturday.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. Chinese authorities on Sunday reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, of whom 261 were foreign nationals, including 104 from Nepal, 49 from India, 33 from Latvia, 18 from the US and 15 British citizens.
In a breakthrough at the weekend, Nepal’s army was able to insert a pipe into a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydroelectric site where more than 100 workers are believed to be trapped.
The home minister, Sudan Gurung, said: “We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside.”

It is a race against time to reach the workers, who may still be alive inside the tunnels, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites. They are among 933 hydropower workers who are among the missing, according to Nepal’s disaster authority.

blocks.caption: Soldiers search for bodies as rescue operations shift into search and retrieval in Nepal.  Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

blocks.text: Nepal warned on Sunday of rising flood waters and urged rescue teams to exercise caution. “We have received information that the flood flow in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa has increased further,” the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.
Flood warnings were sent to people’s phones early on Sunday as rescue crews worked to clear a highway connecting Kathmandu to one of the areas hit by the devastating floods.

In Dhading, one of the worst-hit regions in Nepal, some people began returning to ruined homes to see what could be salvaged. Residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they had received since the initial floods.

One resident, Govind Shreshta, told the Associated Press: “Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain. It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and 70-year-old mum. I must carry them and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”
The government estimated Nepal’s reconstruction bill could run into the billions of dollars.
Officials in Nepal called for forensic testing kits to identify bodies and freezer units to store them in, saying bodies that had been in water could decompose at a faster rate.
Survivors face an agonising wait to learn the fate of missing relatives and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away,” Buddhi Ram Dangol told Agence France-Presse in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. “There is nothing left.”

blocks.caption: Firefighters conduct search and rescue operations along a river in Gyirong county in Tibet. Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters

blocks.text: In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, rescue operations were temporarily paused at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of more flooding from a newly formed lake.
A total of 2,141 rescuers were near the Gyirong site, the Xinhua state news agency reported, including more than 500 in the worst-hit area.
In Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, relatives and friends gathered outside the main government hospital from early morning desperately searching for news of missing loved ones.
Many shuffled between the help desk and the hospital noticeboard, clutching photographs and scanning injured patients’ lists in the hope of finding them.

Dil Maya Lama stood weeping outside the help desk at the hospital, searching for information about her missing 26-year-old brother, a driver for a hydropower company in Rasuwa. She had travelled from Ramechhap, about 80 miles (130km) away.
“I came here with the hope that I might find him,” she told the Associated Press. “There is no information about him.”
Nelza Moktan anxiously sought information about her missing cousin, who also worked as a driver in Rasuwa. “I feel hopeless. It has already been four days,” she said.
With Associated Press, Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas
articles.summary: Turkey has announced the creation of two protected zones in a disputed area of the Aegean Sea, sparking an angry reaction from Greece. Does this mark a new chapter in a long-running dispute between…

image.caption: Turkey recently designated two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean, one off the Greek island of Lemnos (seen here in May 2025)Image: Diogenis Dimitrakopoulos/DW

blocks.text: A stint of unfamiliar calm between Greece and Turkey lasted less than three years.

After a devastating earthquake struck Turkey in February 2023 and Greece provided substantial aid, the two countries came closer together. They then signed the Athens Declaration on Friendly Relations and Good-Neighbourliness in December 2023, a further step to improved relations.

During this unusual time of calm, neither government moved to resolve long-lasting Greek-Turkish disputes, which mostly involve marking maritime boundaries. As a result, even a measure ostensibly aimed at protecting the environment has reignited regional tensions.

The latest dispute was triggered by Turkey's designation of two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean earlier this month. The park in the northeastern Aegean includes a protected area in the waters between the Greek islands of Lemnos and Samothrace. The southern park lies east of Rhodes and surrounds the Greek island of Kastellorizo.
For decades, Greece and Turkey have been at odds over the delineation of their maritime borders in the Aegean and the related economic rights, such as claims to natural resources like oil.

Greece's Foreign Ministry was quick to react to the announcement, calling the establishment of the parks "illegal." In a statement, it said the designation of Turkish marine parks in areas outside Turkey's territorial waters has no legal validity.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said at a Cabinet meeting earlier this week that he wanted to maintain good relations with neighboring countries. However, he stressed that "areas under Greek sovereignty are determined by international law" and that Greece is "always ready to defend them."
Competing to protect the Mediterranean?

For its part, Greece also announced two marine parks in 2025 — in the Ionian Islands and the southern Cyclades, both within Greek territorial waters. At the time, Turkey reacted in a clearly worded statement: "Unilateral actions should be avoided in closed or semi-closed seas such as the Aegean and the Mediterranean."

But Turkey has now declared its own marine parks — and without consulting Greece. Environmental protection appears to have been, at most, a secondary concern for the two countries in announcing their respective conservation parks. Instead, the move appears to be a new tactic for asserting dominance in the disputed maritime area — the latest chapter in a decades-long regional spat.
Kastellorizo caught up in Greece-Turkey dispute (09.2020)

Greece believes Turkey sees the marine parks as a way to challenge the sovereignty of Greek islands. It fears the designation of the two parks is part of Turkey's revisionist "Mavi Vatan" doctrine, Turkish for "Blue Homeland."

Under the doctrine, Turkey lays claim to the exclusive economic zones of Greece and Cyprus — maritime areas in which a coastal state has special rights, including over fishing and the exploitation of natural resources. It also challenges the sovereignty of numerous Greek islands and islets.

Until now, the doctrine has largely remained theoretical and strategic in nature. It is now being advanced through legislative initiatives in Turkey's parliament, and Turkey intends to use the parks to formalize its claims to greater control over parts of the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.
Greece invests in defense

Greece itself is content with the status quo in the Aegean but feels threatened by Turkey, which is significantly better armed. As a result, Greece has invested heavily in fighter jets, frigates, submarines and air defense systems.

After spending significantly less on arms imports for several years, Greece ranked 19th worldwide among the largest importers of major arms from 2021 to 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Even as Athens builds new or closer alliances, Turkey is factored into decisions. In 2021, for example, the Greek government sent Patriot air defense missiles to Saudi Arabia, despite objections from the Greek opposition, to protect Saudi oil refineries from Houthi attacks — at a time when Riyadh and Ankara were at odds politically.
During a state visit with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Prime Minister Mitsotakis explicitly referred to Turkey's "destabilizing and counterproductive" role.

blocks.caption: Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis (right, seen here with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Athens in July 2022), has worked to build closer ties with Saudi ArabiaImage: dDimtiris Papamitsos/Greek Prime Minister's Office/AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Relations between Ankara and Riyadh have since improved. In early August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Defense Pact, a major joint defense agreement.
An 'Iron Dome' for Greece

With Turkey in mind, Greece has also pursued strategic cooperation with Israel. Despite heavy criticism in Greece over the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza, Mitsotakis continues to maintain close ties with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The Greek Defense Ministry is planning an air defense shield over the Aegean modeled on Israel's Iron Dome. The project, dubbed the "Achilles Shield," is designed to protect against all conceivable threats — including those from neighboring countries — and is expected to be fully operational by 2029.

For now, Mitsotakis continues to strike a conciliatory tone toward Turkey. But Greece is due to elect a new parliament by spring 2027 at the latest, and Mitsotakis may face growing pressure to take a tougher nationalist stance As the election approaches.
Greece's Santorini: Balancing tourism and the environment
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: S. Korea: COVID-19 surges; masks, test kits return to shopping lists
articles.summary: SEOUL — As COVID-19 infections begin to climb in South Korea, pandemic-era shopping habits are making a comeback, with people once again reaching for masks and self-test kits. All three major…

blocks.text: SEOUL — As COVID-19 infections begin to climb in South Korea, pandemic-era shopping habits are making a comeback, with people once again reaching for masks and self-test kits.
All three major convenience store chains — 7-Eleven, GS25 and CU — have seen a sharp rise in sales of related products over the past month, according to news reports Friday.

Sales of COVID-19 self-test kits at 7-Eleven, for example, recorded a 62 percent on-month rise from Aug. 1-26, while those of masks, cold medicine and fever and pain relievers rose 17 percent, 15 percent and 14 percent, respectively, data showed.

blocks.caption: Masks sit on sale at a GS25 convenience store in Seoul. (Yonhap)

blocks.text: GS25 also reported a 30.3 percent increase in test kits and a 10.3 percent gain in cold medicine over the same period. Demand was particularly strong for masks for children and infants, with sales more than quadrupling from the previous month, up 341 percent, officials said.
CU saw a similar trend from Aug. 1-23, with sales of test kits and cold medicine up 45.7 percent and 12.2 percent, respectively, from the same period a month earlier.

“Since mid-August, we’ve been asking parents to send their children to day care with masks after a series of cold-like illnesses accompanied by high fevers among 1- and 2-year-olds,” Hwang Ji-mi, a teacher at a day care center in Dongjak-gu, Seoul, told The Korea Herald.
Industry sources say the recent uptick in COVID-19 infections is bringing back the shopping habits that became commonplace during the pandemic.
The country’s COVID-19 detection rate reached 9.1 percent for Aug. 9-15, roughly 2.8 times the 3.2 percent recorded three weeks earlier, according to the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.
The number of patients hospitalized with COVID-19 at general hospitals also rose 2.4-fold over the same period.
Cases are also on the rise in China, with about 522,000 new COVID-19 cases reported in July, including 487 severe cases and one death, according to local media reports.

“With schools back in session, we expect demand for test kits, masks and cold medicine to remain strong for a while. The change of seasons is also likely to give sales a further boost,” a GS25 official said. /dl
