blocks.text: Closing summary
We’re wrapping up the Nepal-Tibet flash flood for the time being. Here are the latest developments:

items: Reuters reports the death toll from the catastrophic flash flood that hit the China-Nepal border on Wednesday has today risen to 626, according to Nepal police, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.

At least 2,478 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday said 1,924 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.

At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.

A Chinese rescue team reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time yesterday, finding “nothing but ruins.” More than 550 ‌remain unaccounted for in Tibet’s Gyirong County after the massive flash flood.

Reversing an earlier decision, Nepal’s foreign minister has said the country needs specialised and technical help from other countries for a tunnel rescue and for identifying and storing bodies. It has also asked China and India for bailey bridges that can quickly be erected.

The number of Australians who were reported missing in the catastrophic Nepal flooding disaster has risen to 41, with one family celebrating after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.

blocks.text: A Chinese rescue team reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time yesterday, finding “nothing but ruins.”
More than 550 ‌remain unaccounted for in Tibet’s Gyirong County after Wednesday’s massive flash flood, including 260 foreigners, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
A rappelling rescue team descended into the once-bustling border-crossing area from wooded mountain slopes, the state broadcaster China Central Television said.

“As far as I can see, it’s nothing but debris,” rescue official Zou Mingqi told state media. The area where travellers went through border control to enter or leave China has been flattened to a muddy area, according to satellite images.
You can read more on that story here.

blocks.caption: In this photo released by Xinhua news agency, rescuers from the People’s Armed Police Force search for victims at the mudslide-hit area near Gyirong Port in China’s Tibet autonomous region on Friday. Photograph: Liu Shuang/Xinhua/AP

blocks.text: Nepal asks for foreign help with tunnel rescue, identifying and storing bodies
We’re just learning that Nepal’s foreign minister has said the country needs foreign help for a tunnel rescue and for identifying and storing bodies.

The country needs foreign ⁠help ⁠in specialised and ​technical areas in ⁠which it does ⁠not ​have expertise but not in ⁠search and rescue, ​foreign minister ​Shisir Khanal told ​Reuters late on Friday.
“We have already made requests for such specialised services and technical assistance in areas ‌where we don’t have enough expertise and technical knowhow,” Khanal said.

The Nepalese army has undertaken a dangerous and difficult rescue operation of people trapped in a tunnel of a hydropower project in the flood-hit district of Rasuwa. Rescuers are seen crawling on thick mud towards the trapped people and carrying them out to safety.

Khanal said Nepal has also asked India and China for bailey bridges – portable, prefabricated truss bridges made of standardised panels that can be assembled quickly – to reopen early transport and communication in the disaster-hit area where about two dozen bridges have been destroyed.

blocks.caption: One of the many bridges swept away by the flash floods, this one in DeviGhat village, Nepal.  Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images

blocks.text: The number of Australians who were reported missing in the catastrophic Nepal flooding disaster has risen to 41, with one family celebrating after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.
It means three additional Australians were confirmed missing overnight – up from 38 who remained unaccounted for on Friday evening.

Other countries are regularly updating tallies for citizens missing or accounted for. Ninety US citizens are missing, according to the state department while three have been rescued. Tourism board figures released by Nepal on Friday showed 98 people from India were missing, but 85 others were rescued.

The Australian government’s Department of Foreign Affairs has been urgently working with local authorities to contact Cara Severino, 25, who became the first Australian reported missing who has been confirmed safe.
Interim summary
If you are just joining us, here’s the latest information coming out Nepal and elsewhere about the Nepal-Tibet calamity. It is 6.18am in Nepal on Saturday.

items: At least 2,478 people are missing after the catastrophic flash flood hit the China-Nepal border on Wednesday. Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday said 1,924 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency early today reported the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554, with seven people confirmed dead.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.

At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.

Nepal on Friday reversed an earlier decision and said it would allow foreign teams and experts to help with rescue efforts, apparently under pressure from other countries, especially those whose citizens are unaccounted for, a leading English-language newspaper, the Kathmandu Post, reported.

The number of Australians who were reported missing has risen to 41, according to the Australian government, while one family celebrated after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.
Three American citizens have been rescued but at least 90 Americans are unaccounted for, the US state department told USA Today. It said it was not aware of any US citizen deaths so far.

Nepal is continuing to monitor two lakes upstream of the flood zone where hundreds died ⁠on Wednesday, an official with Nepal’s disaster management authority said. Flood risks will remain until the two lakes have ⁠fully drained, the official added, as one of the two lakes began overflowing on Friday.

blocks.caption: A flash flood survivor is taken to a medical camp in the Nuwakot district of Nepal on Friday. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP

blocks.text: The day so far

items: Nepal’s disaster authority raised sharply the number of missing to 1,924 on Friday, two days after devastating floods that killed at least 579 in the country. The number of missing includes 517 foreigners, as well as 933 workers on hydropower projects on the rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The AP is reporting a higher figure, with almost 2,500 are missing and nearly 600 people killed.

Authorities in Nepal and China issued warnings about the risk of a second wave of flooding. Chinese authorities said an artificial lake had formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border, which risked “sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media. Nepal’s disaster authority said a lake that had formed by debris blocking a river at the site was also rising and ‌at risk of bursting. Amid the mounting fears over a second wave of flooding, families are rushing to Nepal to search for the 33 British nationals who are still missing.

Rescuers were forced to suspend their search for survivors, while residents who had returned to Rasuwa were told to evacuate their homes, with many seen fleeing up the hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river.

The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by the disaster, triggering a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.

The European Union has promised €2m ($2.3m) in aid for Nepal. European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X that the “immediate humanitarian aid” would help “deliver life-saving assistance to families and communities hit hardest.”

Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search and rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of bridges and roads across the mountainous region – continues. “The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

Rescue teams have reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

blocks.text: The number of missing individuals in the deadly flash flood has risen past 2,400, according to a count by AFP.
Nepal’s disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list already including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, AFP reported.
The news agency also reported that emergency teams have recovered 586 bodies so far – with some of the dead swept downstream as far away as India.
Our most recent reporting indicates that 1,924 individuals are missing and at least 579 were killed, as of Friday, two days after the devastating floods.
Chinese control of information hampers assessment of Tibet flood damage

blocks.caption: Amy Hawkins

blocks.text: Amy Hawkins

As the scale of the devastation caused by the flash floods in Nepal and Tibet unfolds, the picture is emerging far more quickly in Nepal than in China, where strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.

The floods devastated villages along the Himalayan border region that straddles Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet. On Friday, the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, while in China it was just five, despite the fact that the villages around the Gyirong border crossing are home to several thousand people.

“Everything about Tibet is seen through the national security prism. And therefore nobody is going to say anything or report anything that has not been cleared from the very top,” said Steve Tsang, the director of the China Institute at Soas University of London.
For anyone on the ground, “you can’t report a higher figure of deaths, even if you have seen more bodies yourself, until the official statement says that the figure has gone up”.

Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country. Sporadic protests, including self-immolations, by Tibetans calling for more autonomy and religious freedom have been cracked down on by the authorities.

International journalists cannot visit Tibet apart from on tightly choreographed government tours. Many Tibetans are not allowed passports and have very limited contact with the outside world. Tibetans can be punished for speaking to journalists. Human rights groups have for years criticised Beijing’s policies on Tibetan language and culture, which activists say are under attack.
As the Chinese government’s tight controls on information limit international coverage of its relief efforts, it continues to stress that the disaster is a national priority.

China’s leader, Xi Jinping, chaired a meeting on Friday to direct rescue work, according to state media, in which he called on the authorities to “make every effort to search for missing people from China and abroad”.

He also dispatched his number two, premier Li Qiang, to visit the affected area. According to the state-run Xinhua news agency, Li “emphasised that General Secretary Xi Jinping is deeply concerned about the people in the disaster-stricken areas”.
'Now I have nothing left to live for,' survivors grieve relatives and homes swept away in Nepal flooding
Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Bidur, Nepal.

Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.

“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”

blocks.caption: Sangke Dolma Tamang (in red), 61, grieves her family and home in the aftermath of the deadly flooding in Nepal. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: As a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas between Tibet and Nepal splintered and crashed into the valley below, it set off a deadly cascade of water, mud and debris down the Bhote Koshi River. The Nepali village homes that lined the riverbank and clung to the mountainside stood little chance.

Two days after the disaster, at least 579 people have been confirmed dead and more than 1,900 are still missing, the numbers rising by the day. Many in Nepal fear that the true scale of the disaster has yet to emerge, as the worst-hit areas in districts such as Rusawa are only accessible by helicopter. The situation remains even more opaque in Tibet, which is under tight Chinese media control. Though it was at the centre of the disaster, Chinese authorities insist only five people there have died.

In the army barracks in the town of Bidur, where Nepal’s rescue efforts were being coordinated, helicopters carrying those rescued from flooded areas continued to arrive every few minutes, while others carrying vital supplies of food and clean water flew out and high up into the mountains.

blocks.caption: Flood victims evacuate to Nepal army camp - loop

blocks.text: On Friday morning, ground rescue efforts were halted over fears that the river levels were rising once again. But the Nepali army spokesperson, Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet, said the helicopter rescues would continue for as long as people were missing. He accepted that the death toll was hard to calculate. “Right now, our focus is mostly on finding the living,” he said.

Among those recently brought to safety was 60-year-old Murali Maiya Tamang, who had been in Rusawa and was found hanging in a tree. As the flash floods came down the valley, she had watched as her house was washed clean away. She convulsed with tears as she waited desperately for news of her son, who was in their village when the floods struck and has been missing since.
“My husband had already died in Nepal’s 2015 earthquake,” she said. “Now this flood has taken away the only son I had left. I am all alone now. What is the point of living now?”
You can read the full piece, with photographs and video by Ahmer Khan, here:
Here are some images coming through on the news wires of residents salvaging their belongings after the deadly flash flooding in Nepal.

blocks.caption: Residents salvage their belongings from damaged houses after flash flooding in the Devighat area of Nuwakot district in Nepal today.  Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP
A woman carries a bag and suitcase of her belongings after her house was heavily covered in mud.  Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/Getty Images
Residents salvage belongings from their destroyed home.  Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

blocks.text: Footage shows glacier collapse that led to deadly flooding in Nepal – video

This drone video shared with the Guardian shows the moment of glacier collapse that led to the devastating flash flooding in Nepal. The numbers of people missing, killed or injured are feared to continue to rise as rescue efforts are under way.
The UK has deployed a rapid response team of specially trained volunteers to Nepal to help with the disaster there.
The foreign secretary Ed Miliband said: “The scenes from Nepal are devastating, and our thoughts remain with everyone affected.

“The safety and welfare of British nationals is our top priority. That is why we are deploying a Rapid Deployment Team to Nepal to provide additional support on the ground for British nationals and their families at what is an incredibly difficult time.
“Our staff are working closely with the Nepali authorities, emergency responders and our embassy in Kathmandu to ensure those affected can access the assistance and information they need.
“We will continue to do everything we can to support British nationals impacted by this tragedy.”
British nationals in Nepal who require consular assistance should contact the British Embassy in Kathmandu or call the FCDO on +44 (0)20 7008 5000.
Death toll in China rises to seven
The death toll has risen to seven and 554 remain missing after the mudslide at a border port in China’s Xizang region, according to local reports.

articles.title: Dolly Parton's dad couldn't read - it inspired her to send books to millions of children
articles.summary: Families across the globe share how free books from Parton's Imagination Library helped their children.
articles.byline: Sheila Flynn, Claire Keenan and Emily Holt

blocks.text: Dolly Parton's dad couldn't read - it inspired her to send books to millions of children
Dolly Parton first launched Imagination Library in her home county in Tennessee
BySheila FlynnReporting fromColorado, US and Claire Keenan and Emily HoltReporting fromAustralia and UK
One child in Denver called her "The Book Queen".
Another in Alabama calls her "Ms Dolly".

Across the globe in Australia, a toddler with speech delays delighted her family with her first word - "orange" - after she and her twin sister received a free book in the post about colours. It came from Imagination Library, the literacy programme begun by late global superstar Dolly Parton.

Parton, who died this week aged 80, launched the philanthropic effort in 1995 to honour her father - whose difficult Appalachian upbringing never allowed him to finish school or learn to read and write.

"He was the smartest man I have ever known, but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," wrote Parton in an open letter on Imagination Library's website.
"Inspiring kids to love to read became my mission."

blocks.caption: Image caption, London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe signed her daughter up for the scheme when she was three months old

blocks.text: Image source, Harriet Anscombe
London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe signed her daughter up for the scheme when she was three months old

Imagination Library sends one free book a month to children from birth to age five. It first launched in Tennessee's Sevier County, where Parton grew up, before expanding across the US in 2000. The programme, which partners with local organisations, launched in Canada in 2006, the UK the following year, then Australia in 2013 and Ireland in 2019.
By 2025, as Imagination Library celebrated its 30th anniversary, it had distributed more than 300m books - equating to one book mailed every 78 seconds, according to the organisation.
And for the families in receipt of the storybooks, the impact has been invaluable.

"It just blows my mind that it's readily available for every family that lives in my borough," said London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe, whose four-year-old daughter has been receiving Imagination Library books since she was three months old.
The free books helped Anscombe establish a reading-focused nighttime routine.

"I think that, if I didn't get those books, maybe I wouldn't have started doing bedtime stories till she was two - but because we were getting them so early, it embedded story time into our routine from when she was just a couple of months old," Anscombe said. "She probably doesn't remember a time when we weren't reading stories."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Colorado mother Ciara Fernandez Faber's son called Parton 'the Book Queen'

blocks.text: Image source, Ciara Fernandez Faber
Colorado mother Ciara Fernandez Faber's son called Parton 'the Book Queen'

Imagination Library became part of the family routine for Ciara Fernandez Faber, too, after she signed up her son about eight years ago in Colorado. His favourite book for years was one written by Parton herself: I Am A Rainbow.
"We read it almost every night, and I never got tired of reading it to him," said Faber, 42.

"It's a book about different emotions, and so we would act out the different emotions, the different faces," she said. "At the back of the book, there's a little excerpt by Dolly talking about how everybody has a rainbow of feelings, and we would read that - and he would always point to her picture and say, 'There's the Book Queen.'"
Families like Faber's repeatedly remarked on how well curated the books were - detailing how topics helped their children not just with reading, but also with social and emotional development.
"There were themes that were addressed in a lot of the books that would have really helped us navigate issues," said Helen Cashell, of Dublin, Ireland.

She signed up both of her children, now aged seven and five, for the scheme. "Whether it was same-sex families or just different types of families, things about bravery, courage, bullying, things about different identities."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fernandez Faber's son, Aster, reads a book to his younger sister, Maya, in Colorado

blocks.text: Fernandez Faber's son, Aster, reads a book to his younger sister, Maya, in Colorado
Author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice Is Best was selected for distribution through Imagination Library, noted how the plotline features a black protagonist.
The programme also helps promote authors like herself; because of the selection, it "means 14,000 copies of my book have been sent to children in the UK".
"To choose between gas, electric, food or a book, you're going to choose a core need - but with the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, you don't have to do that," she said.
In inner-city Sydney, Australia, first-time mum Paige Stewart was astounded as she watched her children's progress with the programme.
Her twin girls, now four, "had a speech delay and some learning difficulties" - but Stewart noticed a change after just the second book.
"Not only did they learn their colours from that book… it kind of set the tone for them speaking and their joy for books."
She's become a vocal advocate for the programme, telling others: "It's so helpful, honestly."

blocks.caption: Image caption, In Dublin, Ireland, Helen Cashell's two children read books atop a pile of other titles they received in the post through Parton's Imagination Library

blocks.text: Image source, Helen Cashell
In Dublin, Ireland, Helen Cashell's two children read books atop a pile of other titles they received in the post through Parton's Imagination Library
Alabama grandmother Kristina Hadley also promotes the programme to friends and family - even incorporating Imagination Library into baby gifts.

"I'll pull up the Imagination books website, and I'll print that, and I'll put it in a picture frame, and I'll get little newborn books and stuff like that, and I'll put it with that for like a suggestion for new mothers," said Hadley, 53.

She signed up her nearly three-year-old granddaughter, Eillie Elaine, "before she was actually born". Now the child has her own bookshelf in their shared household - "and one whole shelf is for her Dolly books".
"She likes to go to go to the mailbox, and she's like, 'Ms Dolly! Ms Dolly!' and I'm like, 'Well, let's go see if Ms Dolly sent you a book!'"
A lifelong Parton fan, Hadley chokes up while detailing how she was at work when a friend texted to say the singer had died.
Imagination Library, she says, "is going to keep her memory going with the younger generation, and I hope and I pray that this is something that goes on for years and years and years."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Children's author Selina Brown saw 14,000 copies of her book sent to kids in the UK

blocks.text: Image source, Selina Brown
Children's author Selina Brown saw 14,000 copies of her book sent to kids in the UK
It's a legacy that Parton built quietly in the background as she presided over pop culture for more than six decades.
"The biggest thing that I like is the fact that she didn't do anything for recognition," said Geoff Blacklin, 67, of Manitoba, Canada.
He and his wife signed up their grandchildren for Imagination Library after a local doctor brought the programme to their region.
"She gave families more than books," Blacklin said. "She gave children a love of reading, precious moments with loved ones, and opportunities to learn and dream."
Such family stories and gratitude would undoubtedly have been music to Parton's ears; the expansion of the programme was truly a realisation of her own dream.

"In the beginning, my hope was simply to inspire the children in my home county, but here we are today with a worldwide programme that gives a book a month to well over 3 million children," she wrote on the Imagination Library site - also taking care to thank the partners "who have embraced my dream and made it their own".
At the centre of it, always, was her love for children - and her love for her father.
"Before he passed away, my Daddy told me the Imagination Library was probably the most important thing I had ever done," Parton wrote.
"I can't tell you how much that meant to me, because I created the Imagination Library as a tribute to my Daddy."

articles.title: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela
articles.summary:
US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves

Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy…

blocks.text: Donald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves.

The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.
The administration, Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more ​than 65 BILLION ‌BARRELS of proven Oil ‌Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the ‌American Taxpayer”.
Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves.
“This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubio wrote on social media.
Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the ⁠reserves.
Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest.

Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying ‌to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment ​into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude.
Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, ​which could ​be eased through ​cheaper oil supplies and expanded output.
The US ​also has ‌been looking ​for solutions ​to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers.

Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was “in advanced talks with Venezuela for the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”. Axios also reported on the negotiations, quoting a US official who claimed the deal would be “massive”.
The discussion was reportedly over a US stake in Venezuela’s most promising oil-and-gasfields, with some 90bn barrels of proven reserves.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.

“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticizing the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States.”
The announcement comes as Chevron and other US energy companies are expected to sign a deal next week investing billions in Venezuela’s oil fields, according to the Journal.
Tom Phillips and Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Venezuelan opposition up in arms over reports US wants big stake in oil and gas
articles.summary:
Critics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’

Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s…

blocks.text: Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.

Several media outlets this week reported that the Trump administration – which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn.

On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal said Trump officials were in “advanced talks” with Venezuelan officials to take “a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields” containing 90bn barrels, nearly a third of Venezuela’s energy reserves.

“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” a source told Reuters, which said the fields being negotiated were in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.
Axios claimed the deal would be “a legacy-defining moment for President Trump”, with one unnamed official telling the US outlet: “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement … It is massive.”
Bloomberg, citing sources familiar with the negotiations, said one deal under discussion was a 100-year lease on several oilfields.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.

“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticising the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States,” they added.

Since January’s special forces raid on Caracas, Venezuela has been led by an interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president and minister of petroleum. Other key members of Maduro’s regime have also retained positions of power, including the interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, who has been collaborating with Trump officials – despite having a $25m (£18m) US bounty on his head for alleged drug trafficking. Meanwhile, the exiled opposition leader, María Corina Machado, whose movement is believed to have won the 2024 presidential elections, has been sidelined.

Ricardo Hausmann, an exiled former minister and opposition supporter, wrote on X: “An illegitimate interim government with an illegitimate hydrocarbons law has no legitimacy to strike this unconstitutional deal. It will be a fiasco for all involved.”

The economist Francisco Rodríguez urged Venezuela’s national assembly to reject what he called a “predatory deal”. “Handing over Venezuela’s oil wealth to the US contravenes the constitution and is not in the interest of the Venezuelan people – much more when it is done at gunpoint,” Rodríguez said.
Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent journalist and government critic, sarcastically called the “surrender” of Venezuela’s natural riches “the deal of the century”.

Gregory Brew, an energy historian and Eurasia Group analyst, anticipated “quite a lot of suspicion and rejection of any deal that would hand the United States government effective control over Venezuelan resources”.
after newsletter promotion
Brew said the reported deal reminded him of how BP, then the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, controlled the oil resources of Iraq and Iran at the start of the last century.

“Anglo-Persian was given a concession by the shah of Iran in 1901 … in exchange for what was essentially a bribe to the Persian government, and it gave the company sweeping rights. The company was essentially in total control of any oil it found and would be able to retain virtually all the profits of any other oil it found and exploited and exported,” Brew said.

“From Trump’s point of view, the control over oil is something of an end in and of itself. But if you do try to rationalise it, I think US dominance over Venezuelan oil reserves allows the US to regard Venezuelan reserves as its own reserves: a source of oil from which the United States can draw and that nobody else has access to. I think that’s how the administration is conceiving of this – excluding China, excluding Russia, but I think also excluding other potential customers for Venezuelan oil,” he said. “It sounds colonial, because it is.”

Venezuela’s post-Maduro conversion into what many call a US protectorate is the most dramatic play in Trump’s push to reassert Washington’s influence over Latin America as part of the so-called “Donroe Doctrine”.

That policy is a 21st-century adaptation of the 19th-century Monroe doctrine by which President James Monroe sought to keep European powers out of the Americas. Trump’s version is about countering China’s growing footprint in the region and imposing US will through economic and military pressure.
Maduro’s downfall has brought some change to Venezuela, with hundreds of political prisoners freed under Rodríguez and talks about reforming the regime-controlled supreme court taking place.

But no date has been set for a fresh presidential election and Machado has been unable to return from exile. “Delcy’s been doing a fantastic job,” Trump told reporters last month, claiming Venezuela was “not really ready” for a vote.

articles.title: At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross
articles.summary: Federation says it fears death toll of nearly 600 will continue to rise as rescuers reach cut-off areas
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Bidur, Sam Jones and agencies

blocks.text: The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, which have killed nearly 600 people, left another 1,900 missing, and triggered a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.
“The trauma of this event is enormous,” David Fisher, the IFRC head of delegation for Nepal, said on Friday.

“Thousands of homes have been destroyed or suffered significant damage. We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in great need. The death toll is very high and unfortunately likely to continue to rise.”

The deadly floods occurred on Wednesday morning after an enormous section ⁠of a glacier in the Himalayas broke loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive surge of water, mud, rock and ice that thundered down rivers and valleys. The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed power stations, roads and bridges.

Nepal’s steep slopes and the lush valleys below are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events, such as intense monsoons, and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.

“The damage is just incredible,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN resident coordinator for Nepal, said on Friday, adding that more than 40 bridges had been destroyed or badly damaged and “over 40km of road completely destroyed”.

By Friday afternoon, the death toll stood at 584 people: 579 in Nepal and five across the border in Tibet, China. Authorities in Nepal said 1,942 people were still missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals who were in the area to work, trek with guides or make a pilgrimage.

blocks.caption: On the ground in Nepal after deadly flash floods - video

blocks.text: Rescue teams have reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Indian border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

Rescuers were forced to suspend operations on Friday morning after a dam of debris overflowed on Friday, increasing the risk of further flooding. Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses.

blocks.caption: Relatives display photos of missing people outside a hospital in Kathmandu, where they have travelled from Rasuwa to seek information about family members. Photograph: Subaas Shrestha/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.

Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the border overflowed.
Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

blocks.caption: People surveying the aftermath of the flooding in Bidur. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.
Nearby, people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.

blocks.caption: A woman among the ruins of Bidur. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: Most areas battered by the flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, from where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned in a matter of minutes.
The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.
Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search and rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of bridges and roads across the mountainous region – continues.

“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search and rescue teams to assist in the operation.

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with Tibet.
“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.
But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities.

Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only five deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.

blocks.caption: Excavators clear debris to restore a road damaged by the flash floods on the Tibet side of the border. Photograph: China News Service/Getty

blocks.text: With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
articles.summary:
Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours

Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum…

blocks.text: Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.

Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.
The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

blocks.caption: A visitor takes a picture of the platinum and diamond necklace, which dates from 1939 and belonged to Queen Nazli of Egypt, at the Pierres Précieuses exhibition in Paris. Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”

Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.

MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.

Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.

blocks.caption: Queen Nazli of Egypt, right, wearing the necklace at Princess Fawzia’s wedding in Cairo, 1939. Also pictured, from left, are: Queen Farida, King Farouk, Fawzia and Crown Prince Mohammad. Photograph: Bettmann Archive

blocks.text: The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.
A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.

European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.
after newsletter promotion
In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.
This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.

Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.

A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.

articles.title: BBC tracks one week of Israeli settler violence in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: The BBC's Lucy Williamson reports on settler attacks on Palestinians, which have been observed over the last week alone.

articles.title: Midnight blaze hits Mabolo warehouse; damage reaches P1.4M
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — A fire broke out shortly after midnight on Wednesday, gutting a hardware warehouse along St. Jude Street in Barangay Mabolo, Cebu City. Fire authorities estimated the damage…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — A fire broke out shortly after midnight on Wednesday, gutting a hardware warehouse along St. Jude Street in Barangay Mabolo, Cebu City.
Fire authorities estimated the damage caused by the fire at P1.4 million.
Ronieglen Lopez, a 20-year-old mechanic at the warehouse, said he noticed smoke coming from inside the building at around 11 p.m. on Tuesday, August 25.
Lopez lives in a company-provided workers’ housing facility adjacent to the warehouse.

“Pag-abli nako sa bintana, didto nako nakita nga nagbaga na. Mao to nibaba ko kay nagkuha og tubig kay abi namo nga matabang ra namo pero wala na jud. Mao to namukaw nalang ko sa akong mga kauban,” he said.

(When I opened the window, I saw that the fire was already blazing. So I went downstairs to get some water because we thought we could still put it out, but we really couldn’t anymore. So I just woke up my companions.)
The fire was reported to authorities shortly after midnight.
The first alarm was raised at 1:06 a.m. as flames rapidly spread through materials stored inside the facility. The fire was placed under control at 1:14 a.m. and declared out at 1:24 a.m.
As of this posting, fire investigators are continuing to determine the cause of the fire.
The 13 warehouse employees displaced by the fire were also transferred to another area, where they will stay temporarily.

articles.title: Ligutan tells defense: Post not for you, but for law students, public
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Counsel for the prosecution Amando Virgil Ligutan has countered the defense panel’s criticism of his Facebook post about misleading questions not being allowed even during…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Counsel for the prosecution Amando Virgil Ligutan has countered the defense panel’s criticism of his Facebook post about misleading questions not being allowed even during cross-examination, noting that the statement was not issued for them, but for law students and the general public.

In his counter-manifestation on Wednesday, at the start of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, Ligutan said nothing in his post was personal, noting that he intended to clarify to the public that misleading questions are not allowed.

Last August 12, Ligutan made a post stating that a “principle all lawyers and law students know by heart” is that “misleading questions are not allowed even on cross-examination” — which led counsel for the defense Sheila Sison to claim was an attack on counsel for respondent Kristine Ferrer — particularly the exchange between Ferrer and private prosecutor Atty. Lorna Kapunan.

“To the defense, the post is not about you. It is not personal. It is about the law that we all adhere to. It is about what we teach the public who are watching our trial. Correcting a mistake is never wrong. Doing it while a hearing is ongoing, online, does not make it wrong,” Ligutan said.
“Ang pagtatama ng mali ay hindi kailanman ipinagbabawal. Kahit sa loob ng impeachment court na ito (Correcting any mistake is never prohibited. Even inside of this impeachment court),” he added.
LINK TO POST: https://www.facebook.com/share/p/19JKzuzt2a/

Ligutan also reminded the defense and the Senate Impeachment Court that, beyond being a lawyer, he is a teacher—a law professor—and he cannot help but correct wrong perceptions being floated on social media.
According to the lawyer, his instincts as a teacher kicked in amid questions on whether misleading questions were really applied.

“But more than just a lawyer, first and foremost I am a teacher. Isa po akong guro and I am proud to be one […] At alam ng ating mga magigiting na guro sa buong kapuluan na ang pagtuturo ay likas sa atin. Ang pagtuturo, ang pagtatama ng mali, ay walang pinipiling lugar, at walang pinipiling panahon. That’s why I made that post,” Ligutan said.

(But more than just a lawyer, first and foremost I am a teacher. I am a teacher, and I am proud to be one […] And our honorable teachers across the archipelago know that teaching is second nature to us. Teaching and correcting mistakes don’t pick an area or a time. That’s why I made that post.)

“I was concerned that the statement made in open court — that misleading questions are allowed — will go unchecked. My teacher’s instinct kicked in. I wanted the students I left in Cebu and in Diliman, and all law students out there, to know that a teacher had heard that wrong statement in open court, and he is correcting that mistake on Facebook, as I have been doing the past years,” he added.

In a tense moment during the cross-examination of state auditor Xylene Mae del Campo, Kapunan strongly objected to Ferrer’s habit of cutting the witness off before she is even able to provide an answer to the questions, and insisting that questions be answered by yes or no only.
Ferrer asked that she be allowed to conduct the cross-examination in her own manner, but Kapunan noted that some questions are not simply answerable by yes or no.
Later, Kapunan said that “misleading questions are not allowed,” to which Ferrer responded by saying that “it is allowed.”

But Sison said that Ferrer’s “it is allowed” quip was not a reply to Kapunan’s “misleading questions are not allowed” even on cross-examination statement — making Ligutan’s social media post as something done in “bad faith.”

But several members of the prosecution team stood by Ligutan, like Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon, who told Sison not to gaslight the country, as the transcripts would show that Ferrer really was responding to Kapunan and to her insistence that misleading questions are not allowed.

After Sison’s manifestation, Presiding Officer and Senator-judge Francis Escudero warned both the defense and the prosecution after both were observed making social media posts in relation to the proceedings.

“The presiding officer is already in the process of drafting a ruling and a warning and an order pertaining to this. Because clearly, I can even name all of you who’ve been commenting on social media in violation of Rule 18 of the impeachment rules,” he announced.

In response, lead public prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said in an interview with INQUIRER that the prosecution has been following the rules — that they have been very mindful not to go over the prohibition, and that their interpretation is that as long as they do not touch on the merits of the case, they can speak about these matters.
Luistro also stressed that Rule 18 of the Senate’s Rules of Impeachment applies not only to the prosecution and the defense lawyers, but also to Duterte and even senator-judges. /mr

articles.title: Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?
articles.summary: Lawmakers in Iran have once again raised the possibility of leaving the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as tensions over Tehran’s nuclear program and its standoff with the United States…

blocks.text: Lawmakers in Iran have once again raised the possibility of leaving the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as tensions over Tehran’s nuclear program and its standoff with the United States continue.
Iranian MP Ghasem Ravanbakhsh said a proposal to withdraw from the landmark treaty had been submitted and was being considered.
Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, said a withdrawal would be the “best response” to increased US economic pressure.

The idea is not new. Iranian officials and lawmakers have repeatedly raised it during periods of tension with Western governments. However, it remains unclear whether Tehran is actually preparing to leave the treaty or whether the threat itself is the objective.
What would leaving the nuclear treaty mean?
In 1970, Iran ratified the agreement, which is the main international treaty on nuclear non-proliferation.

blocks.caption: Iran has been repeatedly accused of having hidden its nuclear programImage: Planet Labs PBC/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: The NPT has 191 member states and is based on preventing the spread of nuclear weapons, promoting peaceful nuclear cooperation and pursuing nuclear disarmament.
Any member can withdraw if it believes that extraordinary events related to the treaty have put its supreme national interests at risk.
It must give three months’ notice to the other members and the UN Security Council and explain its reasons. Leaving the treaty is therefore legally possible.
Behrooz Bayat, a nuclear expert and former consultant to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), told DW that the process would take time.
“A withdrawal would almost certainly be seen internationally as a signal that Iran intends either to keep open the option of developing nuclear weapons or to move toward doing so,” Bayat said.
He said such a perception could sharply increase political and economic pressure and potentially raise the risk of further military action.
For that reason, Bayat believes Tehran’s repeated threats are more useful as diplomatic leverage than as a policy it actually intends to pursue.
Why withdrawal may not benefit Tehran

Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst and researcher at LUISS University in Rome, told DW that the renewed debate should be seen in the context of stalled negotiations over uranium enrichment and Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
Iran has about 440 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%, according to the IAEA.
Inspectors from the UN’s nuclear watchdog were unable to verify the location of much of the material after the June 2025 US and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities.

blocks.caption: Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?

blocks.text: Iran has already sharply reduced international oversight. In July 2025, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian signed legislation to suspend access for IAEA inspectors into the country until the “security” of its nuclear facilities is guaranteed.
That created what Modarres describes as a potentially more useful position for Tehran than formally withdrawing from the treaty.
“Withdrawal would remove that ambiguity without offering any clear advantage, turning a dispute over compliance into an explicit declaration of intent,” the analyst said.

“By remaining formally within the NPT while limiting inspections, Iran can maintain uncertainty about its capabilities and intentions without openly leaving the global non-proliferation system,” he added. “Withdrawing would remove much of that uncertainty.”
A countdown could increase military risk

Withdrawal could also have security implications for Tehran. Under Article X of the treaty, states must give three months’ notice before withdrawing. That period would give Israel, the United States and other governments time to reassess Iran’s intentions.

Some analysts argue that governments already concerned about Iran’s stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium could interpret a withdrawal as a sign that Tehran was moving closer to a nuclear weapons capability.
Bayat said that makes actual withdrawal considerably less attractive than threatening to do so. He added that leaving the treaty could also “complicate Iran’s civilian nuclear cooperation.”

Membership in the treaty “provides the broader legal and political framework through which non-nuclear states gain access to peaceful nuclear technology,” he said. “Russia remains involved in Iran’s civilian nuclear sector, particularly at the Bushehr nuclear power plant.”
“Formally withdrawing from the treaty could make future cooperation much more difficult politically and legally, even though existing agreements would need to be assessed separately,” added Bayat.
Opposition inside Iran

There is no clear consensus in Iran. Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based analyst who has written extensively about Iran’s nuclear program, told DW that withdrawing from the treaty has been discussed repeatedly but has never become government policy.

“The issue of leaving the NPT is not new and has been raised many times before,” he said. “But right now, there are significant legal and political obstacles, and there is still no full consensus within Iran.”
Ghahremanpour said the international community would closely examine any attempt to invoke Article X. He points to the ongoing legal debate over North Korea’s withdrawal as an example.

North Korea announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003. Although Pyongyang is generally treated internationally as no longer being a party to the treaty, some UN documents note that its formal status remains uncertain.
The treaty itself, however, does not require UN Security Council approval for withdrawal. It requires only that states notify the council.
For Ghahremanpour, the political message is more important than the legal process.
He believes talk of leaving the NPT is mainly aimed at pressuring Washington, and particularly European governments, to make concessions. /dl

articles.title: Dolly Parton’s greatest songs, philanthropic works
articles.summary: Dolly Parton was more than a musician, actor, author, philanthropist, or theme-park entrepreneur. Parton, who died Tuesday at age 80, occupied a space in our global cultural imagination — a figure of…

blocks.text: Dolly Parton was more than a musician, actor, author, philanthropist, or theme-park entrepreneur. Parton, who died Tuesday at age 80, occupied a space in our global cultural imagination — a figure of American mythology, someone best described as larger-than-life and then a little bit more. But from the very beginning, at the heart of everything she accomplished, she was a songwriter.

Selecting 11 songs across her many decades of recorded music is a fool’s errand, but there are some classics that stand above others. Here are a few across her discography — from country songs that challenge traditional gender dynamics to the greatest ballad ever committed to record.
1968: “Just Because I’m a Woman”

Parton was long celebrated for the feminist themes throughout her music. That progressive sociopolitical stance is evident from the beginning of her career, which overlapped with the emergence of the women’s liberation movement. On the country classic “Just Because I’m a Woman,” Parton’s protagonist reminds her partner he need not judge her for having previous sexual partners — after all, he’s had some, too. “My mistakes are no worse than yours,” she sings, “Just because I’m a woman.” She said the song was inspired by a conversation with her late husband, Carl Dean, who asked her if she’d been with any men before they met.
1971: “Coat of Many Colors”

The quintessential example of Parton the raconteur is “Coat of Many Colors.” It’s an autobiographical tale about her mother, who made a coat for Parton out of rags. She was mocked by other kids but understood its value. “Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be,” she sings, “In my coat of many colors my momma made for me.”
1973: “Jolene”

It is not only one of Parton’s best-known hits, but also one of the best-known country music songs of all time. “Jolene” was inspired by Dean; Parton told NPR in 2008 that she wrote the song about a flirty bank teller who seemed to take an interest in him.

“She got this terrible crush on my husband,” she said. “And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention. It was kinda like a running joke between us — when I was saying, ‘Hell, you’re spending a lot of time at the bank. I don’t believe we’ve got that kind of money.’ So, it’s really an innocent song all around, but sounds like a dreadful one.”
1974: “I Will Always Love You”

The second single from Parton’s 13th studio album, “I Will Always Love You” is most known for its rendition by Whitney Houston. But the Parton original was written for Porter Wagoner ahead of her departure from “The Porter Wagoner Show.” (She left in 1974, having collaborated with him since 1967.) There have been several versions, but none as resonant as Houston’s, recorded in 1992 for the soundtrack to “The Bodyguard.” The song topped the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, where it stayed for a then-record-breaking 14 weeks.
1977: “Here You Come Again”

Parton wrote an overwhelming number of her hits, which makes “Here You Come Again” an interesting outlier. It was penned by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, first recorded by B.J. Thomas and originally conceived with the idea that Brenda Lee would record it. The song made its way to Parton and became a tentpole pop crossover hit for the country artist. But make no mistake — Parton made sure the steel guitar was heard loud and proud.

Enter Parton, the Hollywood star. It begins with the sound of a typewriter. (That clacking sound? Parton originally conceived of it by striking her long acrylic nails together.) The ebullient “9 to 5” was written for the 1980 film of the same name, which starred Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Parton in her acting debut. The song also appears on her album “9 to 5 and Odd Jobs.” Lyrically, it celebrates women in the workplace and serves as a battle cry for pay equity; it earned Parton her first Oscar nomination.
1983: “Islands in the Stream,” with Kenny Rogers

By the 1980s, Parton had fashioned herself as a mainstream celebrity. On “Islands in the Stream” with Kenny Rogers, her clarion soprano makes for perfect harmonies. That shouldn’t come as any surprise, but perhaps this will: The song was written by the Bee Gees. Barry Gibb maintained it was meant for Diana Ross, while Robin Gibb said it was meant for Marvin Gaye. Whatever the case, it got to Parton and Rogers, and the rest is history. It’s also a reminder of how R&B and country music are inextricably linked.

blocks.caption: Dolly Parton, left, and Kenny Rogers rehearse a song for their appearance on the TV show “Live… And in Person” in Los Angeles on Sept. 27, 1983. (AP Photo/Doug Pizac, File)

blocks.text: 1989: “Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That”

Before this triumphant return to capital-C country music, there was a deeper detour into ’80s drum machine-heavy pop. (If there’s a single Parton album to consider skipping, it is 1987’s “Rainbow.”) But what came after, 1989’s “White Limozeen,” should be celebrated for “Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That,” with its steel guitar, banjo, mandolins, Pedabro and a fierce fiddle courtesy of Ricky Skaggs — all while Parton playfully objectifies a man with a cheeky wink.
1999: “The Grass Is Blue”

“I’ve had to think up a way to survive,” Parton opens the title track to her 1999 album “The Grass Is Blue.” She said she wrote the bluegrass ballad in 30 minutes, during a lunch break while filming “Blue Valley Songbird,” a made-for-television musical drama about a woman who tries to leave an abusive partner. It features her scratch vocals — a demo meant to serve as a blueprint for the final recording — providing an additional rawness to a song of impossible pain. “And the sky is green / and the grass is blue,” she sings. “And I don’t love you.”
2001: “Little Sparrow”

If there is anything resembling a dip in Parton’s overwhelming popularity, it arrived in the ’90s, when country listeners instead embraced the glossy pop-country of Shania Twain and LeAnn Rimes. A pivot arrived at the end of that decade and into the one that followed, when Parton endeavored to make roots albums — pulling from bluegrass, country, gospel and Appalachian folk — that reinvigorated her music career. The heartbreaking a cappella harmonies of the title track on her 2001 album “Little Sparrow,” released one year after the death of her father and dedicated to him, are further evidence of her greatness. Parton’s is a voice that knows no bounds. But to remind people of that fact? Sometimes it takes going back home.
2014: “Blue Smoke”

No one writes place like Parton. On “Blue Smoke,” with its youthful choo-choo spirit, Parton brings the listener into her childhood home in the Blue Ridge Mountains, gorgeous, desolate and nostalgic. “Blue Smoke climbin’ up the mountain, Blue Smoke windin’ ’round the bend / Blue Smoke is the name of the heartbreak train that I am ridin’ in,” she sings. “I left a note, I wrote, ‘I’m leaving and I won’t be coming back’ / Blue Smoke rolling, rolling, rolling, rolling, rolling down the track.”
Philanthropic works

Beyond her music and entertainment career, Parton has built a lasting philanthropic legacy, particularly in education and literacy. In 1988, she established the Dollywood Foundation, initially focusing on scholarships for students in her hometown of Sevier County, Tennessee.

Her best-known initiative, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, was launched in 1995 as a way to encourage children to develop a love for reading. Inspired in part by her father, who could not read or write, the program began by sending free, age-appropriate books to young children in her hometown before expanding across the United States and other countries.

The program has since grown into a global literacy effort, with more than 270 million books mailed to children as of 2026. Its reach has made Parton synonymous with childhood literacy, earning her the affectionate nickname “The Book Lady.”

Parton’s charitable work has also extended to communities affected by disasters. Following the 2016 wildfires in Sevier County, Tennessee, which destroyed thousands of structures and killed 14 people, Parton and the Dollywood Foundation established the My People Fund. The initiative provided $1,000 a month for six months to families whose homes were damaged or rendered uninhabitable. It ultimately raised more than $9 million for wildfire survivors, while a subsequent partnership with the Mountain Tough Recovery Team provided an additional $3 million for longer-term recovery.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center for research into the coronavirus. Her contribution supported research that became part of the work that led to Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccine, making her one of the notable entertainment figures whose philanthropy helped advance vaccine research.

She also made major donations to pediatric infectious disease research. In early 2026, the East Tennessee Children’s Hospital announced it was naming its campus the Dolly Parton Children’s Hospital in honor of her ongoing support.

Her commitment to disaster relief continued in 2024 after Hurricane Helene devastated parts of the southeastern United States, including East Tennessee and western North Carolina. Parton pledged $1 million of her own money to the Mountain Ways Foundation, with her East Tennessee businesses, including Dollywood, matching the contribution and bringing the total from her side to $2 million.

Her philanthropy has earned major recognition, including the Library of Congress’ David M. Rubenstein Prize for her work through the Imagination Library. In 2022, she also received the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy, which recognized her contributions to education, poverty alleviation and medical research, among other causes.
Following her passing, her family requested that in lieu of flowers, fans send donations to continue supporting Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library./ra

articles.title: Sara Duterte: Prosecution is resorting to 'theatrics, insults'
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday blasted the prosecution in her impeachment trial for allegedly using “theatrics” and “insults.” She said that doing these…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday blasted the prosecution in her impeachment trial for allegedly using “theatrics” and “insults.”
She said that doing these actions is a sign of “feigning confidence” in presenting what she says is a weak case.
Duterte made the pronouncement as her trial before the Senate impeachment court entered its 19th day.
“They should not be fishing for evidence during the trial or desperately try to turn something they wish to be true into a wild story of alleged wrongdoing,” said Duterte in a statement.
“A strong case does not need the adornment of theatrics,” she noted.
“A Senator calling a witness ‘stupid,’ a lawyer calling me the ‘mastermind of a scam’ or another witness referring to me as a ‘brat,’ does not prove a case, nor does it produce evidence,” she added.
According to Duterte, resorting to such insults does nothing but reveal the need to “feign confidence in the face of a weak presentation.”
Meanwhile, the vice president then alluded to the flood problem in the country, including the flood control scandal—accusing the administration of preparing to divide the 2027 budget.
“Lubog na ang bansa sa baha at kahirapan, pero tila walang mananagot, dahil ang impeachment, ang paghati-hatian ang 2027 budget,” Duterte said.
(The country is already inundated with floods and poverty, but it seems no one is taking responsibility, because the impeachment, will divide the 2027 budget.)
“At ang paghahanda kung papaano baliin ang Constitution para manatili sa puwesto ang prayoridad ng administrasyon at lahat ng kaalyado nito,” she added.
(And preparing how to break the Constitution to stay in office is the priority of the administration and all its allies.)
Duterte is currently facing the Senate impeachment court through her lawyers on allegations of misusing confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery and grave threats. /apl

articles.title: Keeping flu protection within reach: Watsons makes vaccination more accessible to Filipinos
articles.summary: With frequent rain and the rainy season, many Filipinos are finding themselves moving between rainy streets, air-conditioned spaces, and crowded areas as they go about their daily routines. While flu…

blocks.text: With frequent rain and the rainy season, many Filipinos are finding themselves moving between rainy streets, air-conditioned spaces, and crowded areas as they go about their daily routines. While flu remains a year-round health concern, the rainy season serves as a timely reminder to pay closer attention to respiratory health and the preventive steps that can help protect ourselves and our loved ones.

Flu can begin with symptoms that may seem simple or familiar, such as fever, cough, colds, sore throat, headache, or body aches. Most people recover without serious complications, but some may be more vulnerable to severe illness, including older adults, young children, pregnant women, and people with certain underlying health conditions. Staying informed and taking preventive measures, including flu vaccination, can therefore be an important part of maintaining good health.

For many Filipinos, however, knowing what to do is only part of the challenge. Busy work schedules, school activities, family responsibilities, and everyday errands can make it easy to put preventive healthcare on hold, especially when getting vaccinated means making a separate trip to a healthcare facility.

Watsons is helping make vaccination more accessible by bringing these services closer to where Filipinos already live, work, and shop. Vaccination services are available at more than 300 Watsons stores nationwide, many of which are located in SM Malls. Of these, 22 vaccination hubs offer daily services, giving individuals and families greater flexibility and more opportunities to make preventive care part of their regular routines, at a time that works for them.

More than 85,000 patients have already received vaccinations through Watsons, reflecting the growing demand for accessible preventive healthcare. Among the vaccines offered, flu vaccines remain the most in demand, followed by HPV, pneumonia, shingles, and pertussis vaccines.

“We understand that with busy schedules, preventive care can sometimes be put off, so we continue to make vaccination services more accessible through our stores. With flu vaccines among the most in-demand vaccines, and as the rainy season continues, we hope to give more Filipinos the flexibility to get vaccinated as part of their everyday routines and take an important step toward protecting themselves and their loved ones,” said Danilo S. Chiong, Managing Director of Watsons.

Beyond vaccination, simple everyday practices such as washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes, and staying home when feeling unwell can also help reduce the spread of respiratory illnesses. Those experiencing severe, persistent, or worsening symptoms should seek appropriate medical advice.

Whether you’re heading to work, bringing the kids to school, or simply doing your weekly errands, staying protected against the flu can be one simple step toward keeping yourself and your loved ones healthy.
For the latest updates on vaccination schedules and participating stores, customers can also follow Watsons Philippines on social media or visit the Watsons website.
